div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS,
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS,

NOBODY has been able to convince the coal-deale, of the error of his weighs. EVERY bride is beautiful, and it is a mystery where all the plain married women come from. A CLERGYMAN who married a couple of deal mutes the other day wished them "unspeakable
bliss!" A MAN was recently arrested in Maine who had wives in half a dozen States, including a state of

indignation. Mn. COBB has married Miss Webb. He knew that they were intended for each other as soon as he spider. IT is said that there are more lies told in the sentence, "I am glad to see you," than in any other six words in the English language. A SI7BURBANEB was recently asked how his house had fared during the snowstorm. "Oh, badly," was the reply; "my cistern is the only dry place

in it." - A WELL-KNOWN playwright and wit, having taken a new house, said to a friend, "Well, all will go on now like clockwork." "Aye," said the friend, "tick, tick 1" ONE lady said to another—" Have you been to church to-day IWe had a most beautiful sermon on training children." "No ; I was at home doing it,"
was the reply. OLD lady (to grocer's boy)—" What makes the price on them potatoes so stiff, my boy ?" Grocer's boy—" It's because there's so much starch in 'em,
111171 m." MAMIE—" What are you writing, Minnie—your will I" Minnie—" No; I'm writing my won't. George proposed last night, and I told him I'd
answer to-day." "SHOULD a man shave up or down?" asked a youthful city clerk. "That depends. When I "shave you, for instance, I always shave down," _ .
-- • replied the barber. A JAPANESE story-writer has just finished a novel In 90 volumes. If a Japanese messenger-boy gets hold of that story, the company might as well get a

new boy. "WHAT is that dear, delightful, old-fashioned chair worth?" she inquired. "It is worth, madam," said the honest dealer, "just about 115 dols. ; the price of it, however, is nine dols." FIRST SYRACUSE CITIZEN—" Ever seen Buffalo Bill, Jim ?" Second Syracuse Citizen—" Ever seen a Buffalo bill? I should say I had. I stayed a week at a hotel once, and the bill nearly piaralysed me." PATERFAMILIAS "Why, Ethel 1 You don't mean to tell me you want to marry that bald- headed Professor Wiseman I" Ethel—" It is true he is bald, but think how many young men of to- day are bald on the inside of their heads." MISS SHAWSGARDEN (of St. Louis)—" Oh, yes,

SM proud of our city. We have changed the saying about Naples to See St. Louis and die.' " Miss Dearborn (of Chicago)—"lndeedl Is it so sudden?" THE rumour that a Kentucky father has disin- herited his son because the young man signed the temperance pledge and introduced water into the house lacks confirmation, but it sounds plausible enough. "I TELL you, Candidus," said Scribbler, "the public its fairly going wild rivet my poems." " Indeed, ' replied Candidus ; "I'm sorry to hear that. If you wish to conceal yourself until it calms down, why, my house is at your service." "JIM," said an honest coal dealer to one of his men—" Jim, make that ton of coals two hundred pounds short. It is for a poor, delicate widow, and she will have to carry all of it up two fights of stairs. I don't want to overtax her strength." "GUARD (to country-looking party)—" Do • you know you've been riding second-class with a third- class ticket? You'll have to pay excess." Country L. P.—" Oi'll be biled if I do. I paid tuppence for my ticket, and I got in a carriage wi' a 2 on it." He was let off. PARSON—" I am astonished to hear a man with three married daughters say marriage is a failure.'" Chicago citizen—" Well, sir, when you have three families besides your own to support you will learn that marriage is a positive bankruptcy." JOHNNY'S mother, who has been reading to him about Africa—" It is dreadful to think that there are benighted tribes who do not know what soap is, and who do not wash from one year's end to another." Johnny—" I wish I was a 'flighted tribe." BUTCHER—" What can I sell you to-day, my dear 2 " Servant Girl—" I've come to order some roast beef for to-morrow, but let there be plenty of bones." Butcher—" Plenty of bones? How's that ? " Servant—" Ye see the money as I gets for the bones is my parkist." LITTLE JOHNNY (to Merrit)—" Won't you take me fishing with you some day ? " Merrit (surprised) —"Why, I never go fishing." Little Johnny (as though he has got him cold)—" Oh, yes, you do. Corn told ma the other day that you were always fishing for compliments." IV CERTAIN judge having been called on at a public meeting for a song, replied that it was not in his power to gratify the company. A wag, who was present, observed he was much surprised at the re- fusal, as it was notorious that numbers had been transported by his voice. HE—" At last, Clara, I find you alone and now solemnly put the question to you—Are you willing to unite your lot with mine? May I ask your papa to bestow your hand upon me 7 " She—" Ah 1 lam really sorrow that you have come so late. Only half an hour ago I was betrothed to another." A WISE boy, like a wise lawyer, considers how he will answer possible objections before he puts in his plea. "Papa," said Charlie, "will you buy me a drum?" " Ah, but, my boy, you will annoy me very much if Ido !" "Oh, no, papa I won't drum only when you are asleep." "YOU women don't know when you are well off," sneered old Brown. "Here you are complaining just because you have to do the housework. Why, in ancient times wives used to be slaves." "Yes, my dear," returned his better half, "but that was before the invention of brooms." IT was in a railway carriage, and a young lady got out whose face was much disfigured by small- pox and pimples. "Oh, dear me," exclaimed a pretty girl to her male companion; "if my face was like that poor girl's I do believe I should die." "Oh, no, you wouldn't dye," replied the gentleman, "you'd paint." "KNOW JIGBEE ? Of course I do, and what's more, I know him to be a man of nerve." "Non- sense I He's as timicl as a mouse. A man of nerve Ha, ha 1 What in the world put such a notion in your head ?" "Well, sir, I heard him contradict his own wife the other day, and in public, too, at that." A COUNTRY schoolmistress gives the following sentences from the pen of her youngest and brightest scholar, given in answer to the request —"Write in 20 words a definition of ' Man.' " It read thus—" Man is an animal that stands up ; he is not very big, and he has to work for a living." " GRANDMAMMA," said a West-end young lady Indignantly, "Clara Guggins says that you and grandpapa kept a corner grocery shop when you were young." "She is mistaken," said grand- mamma. "I knew she was, the mean, spiteful thing! The idea I" "Yes, she is mistaken, went on the old lady retrospectively; ft wasn't on a

corner." A PORTLY lady, endeavouring to skate on the ice at a loch in the neighbourhood the other week, suddenly fell with a thud. A gentleman ran to her assistance; and, as he helped her to her feet, he remarked, "I presume you are skating for the first time." "No ; for the last time," she replied, with disgust. PRIM SPINSTER—" Well, if you say, Mr. Feather- wing, that the parrot has been well brought up and IS perfectly strong, I think I may as well take him." Parrot (who knows life and is somewhat aghast at his future prospects)—" I say, boss, ain't it about time I took my medicine 7" And then he coughed till the tears ran down his face. YOUNG MOTHER—" Doctor, there don't seem to be any indication yet of baby cutting her teeth. Do you know what is the matter 2" Young physician —" Well, I must confess I don't ma am, unless it is —er—that a good many children are cutting their teeth just now and perhaps there aren't enough teeth to go round." THE cheerful alacrity with which a young man will guide his sweetheart towards a milliner's shop window before they are married is equalled only by the marvellous skill with which he will steer hex away from it after she is his wife.

div.head: IS LIFE WORTH LIVING?
div.p: IS LIFE WORTH LIVING?

Most people from personal experience can appreciate the apt and witty mply that was given to the above question: "It all depends on the liver." There are but few realize the necessity of keeping that important organ in proper condition—if they will be free from biliousness, depression of spirits, headaches, indigestion and all the other disorders so common, yet so hard to bear. Especi- ally must the liver be looked after at this time of the year. Like the blood, it has become sluggish in its action during the long and cold winter, and it must be roused to perform its functions properly. There are no remedies that can comparewith Warner's " SAFE " Cure and Warner's " SAFE " Pills to regulate the Liver and Kidneys.

div.head: "CAPITAL, CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL, CHAT."
The mere statement that Mr. Lewes was George Flliot's heir and executor does not convey the full _

- significance of what Mr. Lewes obtained under the novelist's will. It is said that he received nearly £150,000 in cash, the copyright of her works and those of his father, Mr. G. H. Lewes, as well as the house in which- Mr. Lewes had lived.

After Monday's meeting at Cambridge it may be hoped that the days of the Spinning House are numbered. The Town Council have definitely re- solved that no settlement of the question will be satisfactoiy which does not deprive the University authorities of all jurisdiction over the people of the town, and on that basis a conference is to be ar- ranged with the University.

In view of the fact that the visit of the Empress Frederick to Paris has been taken advantage of by the remains of the Boulangist party, General Boulanger has gone to Brussels. He is said to be far from' well. He is confined to his hotel,and the place is watched by agents and the French police. He has re- ceived visits from some of his own agents in France, and is accompanied by the usual mysterious female.

Mr. George Kynoch, M.P., whose death was an- nounced on Monday morning, was the son of a Scotch village draper and tailor, and the only educa- tion he received was at the village. school. He commenced life as a clerk in the Midland Bank at Birmingham, but soon got into the gun and cart- ridge trade, running a large factory at Aston, near Birmingham, the place he represented in Parlia- ment from 1886 to the time of his death.

In these days the discovery of a new sandwich is socially quite as important as the discovery of a new country. The latest is composed of chopped celery and powdered parmesan cheese with an in- finitesimal addition of cayenne pepper. This pre- paration may be laid between thin slices of either white or brown bread and butter. The correct ac- companying fluid is dry champagne, and the combi- nation finds much in favour with gourmets of both sexes. The new sandwich will when milder tem- perature obtains be introduced as a savoury.

Before her last powerful ntivel, "The Wages of Sin," Mrs. Harrison ("Lucas Malet ") wrote "Mrs. Lorimer; a Study in Black and White," "Colonel Enderby's Wife," and "A Counsel of Perfection.' Her husband, the Rev. Wm. Harrison, is son of the late Wm. Harrison the celebrated tenor of the Pyne and Harrison English opera combination. His brother is Mr. Clifford Harrison, the reciter. An- other of Charles Kingsley's daughters, well known for her writings on French art, has just received the title of officer from the French Academy.

Grasse has been fixed upon as the temporary con- tinental residence of the Queen. Grasse is in the valley of the Var, and surrounded by over 115,000 Englist acres devoteff to the cultivation of flowers. Far as the eye can reach lie fields, groves, and hedges of jonquils, cassia, orange blossoms, roses, violets, tuberoses, jasmine,and lavender, perfuming the air with their fragrance. In the neighbourhood of Grasse are the factories of many patfumiers. The violets and jonquils will be in full bloom on the ar- rival of her Majesty, and the scent manufacturers will be gathering in their crops.

When the Czarewitch, on his Eastern "travels, touched at Aden, of course all the officials, civil and military, donned their full-dress uniform.; to re- ceive the future" Tsar of all the Russias." They were not a little surprised to find him :when he came on shore dressed in what looked like a cheap suit picked up for a few rupees at a ready-made clothes shop at Port Said. 116 shuffled off all pre- sentations as quickly as possible, and was soon on board his man-of-war again. Decidedly when a young" Bear " goes on his travels he ought to have an intelligent keeper with him to tell him how to behave.

Sir John Macdonald is known by his admirers in Canada as the "Grand Old Man." Ile is also dubbed the Canadian Dizzy, because of his resemblance to Disraeli—physically and politically. Sir John cul- tivates the resemblance, including a Jingo policy and a curl Ott his forehead. He has been altogether about thirty years a Cabinet Minister. Sir John.. is now in in his seventy-seventh year. Be is a native of Scaland, but the Land 'o Cakes did not afford him sufficient scope for the development of his energies, so he emigrated when he was a few years old, taking his Old parents and the rest of his family with him.

Mr. Gladstone is the patron of two livings at. Liverpool, one in the city itself, and the other at Seaforth, where the Bishop of Newcastle was at one time vicar; and the Gladstone family were formerly patrons of St. Andrew's, Renshaw-st. (about to be taken down by the Midland Railway), where Pre- bendary Forrest and the Dean of Norwich won their spurs. Mr. Gladstone has now, however, acquired the advowson of two parish churches in the city of his birth, presumably from Mr. Houldsworth vicar of St. Andrew's, Wells-st., and the event has caused great searchings of heart among the Orangemen and the ultra-Protestants.

The " Methodist Recorder's "special Wesley Cen- tenary Number contains a vast amount of interest- ing facts about the founder of Methodism. There are articles on Wesley and his native country, on Wesley at Oxford, Wesley with the Moravians, on his Publications, on Early Methodist Women, &c., and numerous pictorial reminiscences of Wesley. There is quite a museum of articles which belong to him, including illustrations of the room in which he died, his writing table, his clock, his bureau, his teapot, &c. Most of the contributions are signed. A fine engraving of Wesley, alter Roumer's portrait, accompanies the number.

Lord Ampthill, who has just been elected Presi- dent of the Oxford Union Deflating Society, is better known to the general public as rowing No. 6 in the 'Varsity boat than for his ability as a debater. It is a coincidence unique in the annals of the Uni- versity which vests the Presidency of the Boating Club and the Union in the same hands. Lord Ampthill, however, is as fully qualified for the one position as the other. He is lavishly endowed with that comparatively rare combination muscles, brains, and money. Tall, handsome, and of excel- lent physique, the young peer is at the same time the backbone of the Dark Blue crew and one of the most popular members of the University. Ile is a good speaker, above all cliquism, and certain to make an admirable president.

The Tory candidate for Ashton Manor, Captain Grice-Hutchinson, has been a fortunate man. His wife is the daughter of the late Vicar Orice, of Sherborne, in Worcestershire, and this lady not only gave him a double-barrelled surname, but brought him a substantial share of worldly goods. Captain Grice-Hutchinson,who is forty-two years of age, saw some fighting among the Zulus. He it was who had to mount guard over the Prince Imperial's corpse. The breed is a warlike one. His father was a colonel of Engineers, and among his ancestors was Colonel Hutchinson, one of Cromwell's sturdiest officers and a fearless religious zealot. His candi- dature will get more assistance from his wife being the grandniece of Thomas Attwood, one of the most notable figures of old Birmingham.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 7, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 7, 1891.
I am glad to hear that Lord Rosebery is deriving benefit from his tour, and that his spirits- are recovering from the terrible shock of his wife's death. He will stay abroad at least a month longer.

It is not generally known that a highly-interest- ing lawsuit is being tried at Zanzibar between Mr. H. M. Stanley, the African explorer,of the one part, and Tippoo Tib, the notorious African slave dealer, of the other part. The action is brought' by Mr. Stanley to recover £lO,OOO damages for Tib's breach of agreement in failing to supply carriers and other necessaries for the Rear-Guard of Stanley's expedi- tion. I have just beard of an extraordinary bit of luck that *has befallen Mr. Stanley in connection with the action. Tarya Topar, an Indian banker well known in Zanzibar, had incidentally but inju- diciously mentioned to a hiend of his that he had just received ten thousand pounds to Tippoo Tib's credit on ivory sales. This came to the ears of Mr. Stanley's representative, who promptly impounded the whole sum, pending the result of the trial. The court has sustained the impounding of the cash.

div.head: NOTES FROM MANXLAND.
div.p: NOTES FROM MANXLAND.
By F. R. R.

IV. WINTER IN THE ISLAND. Those of your readers who have come here only in the season can have but a very inadequate idea of what the Island is like in winter. I pitched my tent here last year when the abnormal activity and fevered life of the summer were beginning to die down into the normal. But Douglas was still thronged with visitors ; the piers were still scenes of bustle and excitement ; there was still a full service of boats ; innumerable vehicles, crowded with jovial, happy people, were flying about; the many places of entertainment in and around the town were daily the resorts of thousands; and by night Douglas was ablaze with countless lights. The little village in which it is my happy lot to reside—so beautiful in itself and its surroundings is it—lies on the' high road to Peel in one of the most picturesque valleys of the Island. We had but to stand at our doors to witness a procession of waggonettes filled with what might have been the . . _ _
inhabitants of a ..menagerie 'fudging. by their

queer antics and gestures and still queerer noises, especially on the return journey— whilst our village "pub' did a roaring and lucrative trade. But gradually the stream ceased to flow ; the " pub" no longer had its string of conveyances in front; the villagers removed the cards advertising" refreshme-its " from their win- dows ; the leaves fell rapidly from the trees, and winter was upon us. In Douglas the change was even more marked. The piers lost their thousands of excited people; the boats were moored in the harbour ; the pleasure resorts were closed ; the promenade was gradually abandoned to the gamins of the town ; the vehicles were stored, their drivers dismissed, and the cattle either sent " across the water" or hired to the farmers; and by night the bay ceased to be bordered by afringe of flame. Of course these outward and visible signs bespeak an inward and invisible change, which has important bearings on the moral, spiritual, and social life of Douglas, and indeed oh the whole island. For three brief months the Manxman (and woman) works like a slave and makes money. During the other nine he is idle and spends. The proportion of the population which thus hybernates is a very large one. The winter popula- tion of Douglas is about 20,000, and that of the whole island about 56,000. The vast mass of the people of Douglas derive their living from visitors, as will be seen when it is stated that in the season

there are as many as 60,000 visitors quartered in the town on the same day. Then there are many others scattered through the island, and a large number at Ramsey and at Peel and other towns. During the summer months, therefore, not only the lodging-house keepers but our farmers and our butchers, our bakers and grocers, must make their hay, and they do it. Now it follows from this state of things that the nine months of comparative idle- ness which so large a number of the people—l will net say enjoy, but endure—expose them to many temptations, and lead to many difficulties. The labouring classes, porters, carmen, boatmen, find themselves when the season closes with a fair sum of money in their pockets. Spent judiciously and eked out by occasional labour, it would suffice for the winter's need ; but unfortunately many of this class have been taught-ixtd-htt44te-in-thcir-vontact‘ with the English tripper, and are too prone to their indulgence when the trippers are no longer there to tempt. The consequence is that in far too many cases the little hoard soon disappears,and want and misery supervene. Work is hard to get in winter. This year certain public undertakings—the Marine Drive and the Eiffel Tower—have found work for some hundreds of men, and have been a real bless- ing to the town and the Island. I am informed that the police hare plenty to do here in winter in Douglas; and one officer told a friend of mine that they anticipated exceptional trouble this year on account of the shortness of the last season, but that the public works now in progress had staved it off.

I find there is a large amount of distress in the villages as well, much more indeed than the uninitiated imagine, for the Manx poor are wonderfully uncomplaining and patient. They will not ask an alms, sad will only accept aid if proffered in an unobtrusive and unpatronizing way. They are very sensitive in such matters. Besides those obviously and particularly poor, there are large numbers of lodging-house keepers who find it difficult to tide over the winter. A few wet weeks in the season make all the difference to them be- tween fair comfort and considerable distress for the rest of the year. The season of 1890 began badly, and as a result there is a good deal of real suffering among this large and growing class. But I must leave myself room to say a few words about our winter climate. Before I came here I was warned that I should find the climate intolerable in winter. lam convinced my friend had had no experience of the fact he stated. My own experience is simply this—l have been waiting until now for wintry weather and it has never come. March, it is true, has brought us " rude Boreas "for a visitor; but the whole of February was like an English June. One could sit in one's garden in one's shirt sleeves. The gorse is in bloom on the mountain sides. Last week I found a primrose in the meadow. Wall- flowers in bloom are to be seen everywhere, and I could enumerate many other flowers which I have never seen in England until May or June if I had not had the misfortune to spend so much of my life in a Lancashire town and to be so ignorant of floral nomenclature. It may seem almost incredible to your readers who have not long emerged from that terrible ten weeks' frost which held England in its iron grip, that we had nothing of it here. I will quote an indisputable authority, Dr. Haviland, of Douglas, who took careful note ot the insular temperature—" There were only three days at Douglas on which the mean temperature fell below freezing-point. Practically, we know that whilst we read of the south coast, London and the Riviera and other winter resorts being shrouded in snow and ice and darkened by fog, the residents and visitors in the Isle of Man were enjoying sun- shine, and weather that neither interfered with pleasure, business, nor health." We had snow on one day only, and it rapidly dis- appeared. Even thus, one old inhabitant assured me that this had been the severest winter for twenty years! However that may be, there is no doubt that owing to its broad surrounding belt of sea, warmed by a branch of the Gulf Stream, the Isle of Man enjoys a mildness of climate in winter which is not equalled in any part of England, or even in the Isle of Wight or the Channel Islands. I can heartily recommend it as a most desixable winter resort for the weakly, while at the same time its clear pure air adds vigour to those who are already strong.

div.head: SOME BOOKS ON GAMES.
div.p: SOME BOOKS ON GAMES.

Two is. volumes published in the " All -England Series" by Messrs. George Bell and Sons,of London, give some interesting and useful information about the great popular English game of football—one volume being devoted to Association football, and the other to the game as played under Rugby rules. The books give an ample account of the origin and development up to the present time of both systems of football, and several chapters are devoted in each book to an explanation of the duties of the different classes of players, and many useful hints are given as to what constitutes good play. All the laws and regulations of the games are also set forth in full. To the playing member these little volumes will be useful, as they will enlarge his knowledge of a favourite pastime, while a perusal of them will place the non-Playing spectator in full posses- sion of all the " points " involved and thus enable him to derive the fullest enjoyment from the game. It appears from the book on Rugby football, the writer of which is Mr. Harry Vassal', that the Rugby Union was organised in the early part of 1871 at the initiative of the Richmond and Blackheath clubs, and it is interesting to note that its first balance sheet showed an income of only £7 and an expenditure of £5. Some progress is shown when we say that the income of the Union is now something like twice as many hundreds as it was single pounds in 1871. In addition to this the growth in England, Scotland, Ireland, and Wales have, in the meantime, started separate Unions of their own, which are all in a flourishing condition. At first the entire committee was composed of London men, but from time to time other parts of the country in which Rugby football has taken root and flourished, have been admitted to a share in the management. The earlier matches were played with twenty a side, but this num- ber was reduced to fifteen, because of the difficulty of putting twenty men in the field. Soon after this change the number of threequarter-backs was increased from two to three with one full back. Against what he calls the "hydra of professionalism" in Rugby football, Mr. Vassall speaks out in pronounced language,and he highly commends the rulers of the Union for the firm, and, he thinks, successful, stand they have made against its in- troduction either in an open or a veiled form. At the same time, he admits that the Union authorities know that "a great deal of latent professionalism exists in the country," but he claims that they "also know that it is making no headway against them, and they feel that they are holding it in check and have it in their

grip." In the volume on "Association Football" Mr. C. W. Alcock gives a complete and interesting account of the formation and progress up to the present time of the Football Association. The history of football is a history of development, and in this little book we can follow the various phases the game has assumed before it reached the form it is now played by such teams as Preston North End, Blackburn Rovers, and Everton. People are sometimes curious to know how it is that Scotch professionals are in so much request amopgst leading association organisations, and in this book we find an explanation. It was the Scotch teams, such as Queen's Park and the Vale of Leven, which originally displayed the greatest boldness and judgment in im- proving, or, as we may say, systematising the game. It was the Scotch clubs who introduced the " new dispensation "under which, as the author says, " it was necessary that the eleven should work on a definite system, and with a mechanical precision which , had hitherto been unknown. Each player had his allotted station; he was, in fact, an integral part of a machine which could not work smoothly unless every section was fitted to a nicety and the gear • I properly adjusted." At the same time Mr. Alcock is just to English players,for it was to them,he says,that the" cre- dit of the introduction of the principle of combination, of which the third balf-bick was the keystone, belongs ;" and he writes with deserved praise of the " immense power for good " in the game possessed by that fine amateur organisation, the Corinthians. In addition to the two above-named books, we have received from Messrs. Bell and Sous, books published at a similar price, on "Skating "and on "Round Games with Cards," the former by Mr. Douglas Adams and the latter by Mr. Baxter-Wray. Besides initiating the reader into all the mysteries of skating, Mr. Adams gives a variety of useful hints as to dress, boots, and skates, and some particulars he gives of skating in Sweden, in Hol- land, and in the Fen-country of England will be found especially interesting. The book on "Round Games with Cards" is divided into no fewer than fifteen chapters, and each chapter deals with a particular game. The familiar " Nap" is the subject of the first chapter, and " Loto "that of the last, and between there are full des- criptions in every case of games, some of which are well- known, but of others most people will barely even be ac- quainted with the names.
LORD SALISBURY ON LABOUR QUESTIONS.

Lord Salisbury. speaking on Wednesday night at the dinner of the Associated Chambers of Commerce, rferred to the Protectionist tendency in France and Ainerica, and pointed out the impossibility of any re- monstrance from the English Government being ot use. Turning to the labour disputes in this country, he said that Trades Unions were in no way to be deprecated. He admitted the perfect liberty of working men to unite, but held that the co-relative of that was the right not to unite. He also alluded to the eight hours question, re- marking that if they gave up the present principle of non-interference with adult labour, if they went past the ' Rubicon which separated them from the domain of Socialism, they would part with their commercial and industrial supremacy. With regard to the proposed Labour Commission, he said that while it might supply some hints for future legislation, its principal utility would be found in the opportunity it would give for the ventilation of ideas.

NORTHERN COUNTIES ATH.ELETIC CHAMPIONSHIP. Manchester racecourse was the scene of the great cross country race for the championship of the North, and to everyone's satisfaction the genial sunshine and pleasant weather attracted an enormous attendance of spectators, fully twice as many being present as last year. Satur- day's race provided great excitemeht, although on all hands it was admitted that no team could hope to suc- cessfully compete with the holders, the Ashton Harriers being generally allotted the second place. Sixteen clubs had entered, but of this number the West Cheshire res- igned on Friday owing to the decision of the Cross- country Association in granting the appeal of the Wirral Club to run Leos and Mothersole. The Liverpool Gym- nasium Harriers were also absent, much to the disap- pointment of the spectators, whilst the Cheshire Tally-ho were not represented, fcr the first time since the institu- tion of the Championship in 1883, on which occasion they occupied the honourable position of second. On Saturday, after some little de ay, the competitors were all marshalled in line, to the Humber of 117, and the pistol was fired at 4.20. Away the men went, G. Parry (Liverpool) being the first over the hurdles, with E. W. Parry, Souch, and Morris at his heels. Round the bend the B'rchfield (Souch) raced tothe front, but this posi- tion he did not occupy long, as coming down the straight past the winning post for the first time Morris was leading by 20 yards. Ingham (Halifax) being second, with Parry, Souch, and Morton all together, whilst Nightman and Barlow, of Warrington were also well up. Later on in the race it was thought that Parry had the event entirely at his mercy, but Morton gradually crept up to him, and adopted his last year's tactics by conten- tedly jogging along in the National Champion's footsteps. A couple of hundred yards from the finish Parry was some three yards in front of Morton, and amid a wild scene of excitement the two men raced desperately for the winning-post. Inch by inch Morton gained on his rival, and it seemed as though he must win, but he was evidently in distress and only his marvellous courage kept him going, as his strides was quite broken and his progress the result of a kind of erratic gallop. Barely a yard, however, separated him from the leader when the post was reached, and both the victor and the van- quished came in for a magnificent ovation. The follow- ing are the scores for the first half-dozen clubs : Salford Harriers Ashton Harriers North Lonsdale Warrington Halifax 2ll Liverpool 244 Wirral • Cheetham 325 Oldham 337

The following was the order of the first twelve E. W. Parry, Salford Harriers W. H. Motion. Salford Harriers C. Souch, Ashton Harriers Ingham, Halifax Morris, Salford Harriers Johnson, Salford Harriers Bacon, Ashton Harrison, Ashton Cliffs, Salford Harrie-s Gontersall, Halifax Harriers Jones, Salford Harriers Wainwright, Salford Harriers The Warrington team finished as follows :—J. Barlow, 13; J. Wightman, 22; J. Whitfield, 25; A. J. May, 31; J. Jefferson, 35; P. W. Pair, 45.

div.head: PERCIVAL GORDON;
div.p: PERCIVAL GORDON;
OR, THE CHILD OF-THE REGIMENT. -- BY SYLVANUS COBS
CHAPTER I.
THE BATTLE-FIELD OF TALAVERA—THE DYINa

HUSSAR. Very near to midnight, on Friday, July 28th, 1809, two persons, one of them carrying a lighted antern, were earnestly engaged in searching among the dead and dying upon the broad and sanguinary battle-field at Ta.lavera, in Spain, where the Duke of Wellington had defeated Marshal Soult, one of Napoleon's ablest commanders. In personal appearance the twain afforded a striking contrast. He who led in the search was Sergeant John Coverly, of Maxwell's Hussars. He was of powerful frame, strong and vigorous, of Saxon type, his closely curling auburn hair tinged with the frosts of more than fifty years. A very woman in the depth and ardour of his strong affections, the din of battle and the roar aud smoke of burning powder transformed him into something very like

a (lemon. The old sergeant's companion was a bright, fair- aced boy, who had seen but a few months beyond his sixth year—a boy to be loved and trusted at sight. He, too, wore the uniform of a Hussar; and, strangely enough, bore upon his arm the chevron of a corporal. And this honourable distinction had _ _ .

been 'fairly won. Having been adopted as "The Child of the Regi- ment" while the force was being gathered and organised at Cork, during the spring of the pre- vious year, he was duly mustered in as an attaché of the commissariat. His father belonged to the regiment, with the rank of sergeant. His mother, only child of John Coverly, knowing no fear, had chosen to go with her husband and father, and had been engaged as hopital nurse, an office of tender mercy and good-will which she had performed aforetime in barracks, and in which she had won the love and chivalric devotion of the entire com- mand. But she was not to accompany her loved ones to the Peninsula. While in Cork she had been taken down with malignant fever, and death speedily robbed the reginient of its ministering angel. So we may see how natural it was that the the gallant hussars should have adopted the motherless child. John Coverly had lost a daugh- ter that had been for years the one bright thing of his life, while Robert Coverly had lost a wife whom he had loved with a love that was both devotion and worship. -

The regiment took ship at Cork for Mondego Bay on the coast of Portugal. During the voyage a gunner's mate, in an insane freak, in possession of a key to the door, made his way to the magazine, where he stuck a lighted candle into an open cask of gunpowder, and shortly afterwards he whisper- ingly chucked to little Percival of what he had done, bidding him hold his tongue and wait for the fun. He said he had locked the door and thrown away the key, and the grand show was soon to come off. As soon as the boy could calm himself and gather up his startled thoughts, he resolved upon his course of action. Without a word or a sign to any- body, he sped to the room of the gunner, where he found a duplicate key. The entrance to the maga- zine was on that self-same deck, so he was but a very short time in gaining the interior of the cop- per-lined depository, and there, sure enough, he found the lighted candle in the powder cask, its flickering flame within an inch of the awful black- ness that upheld it! With teeth firmly set, with- out the quiver of a nerve, he stepped forward, and steadily, carefully lifted the burning, dripping tallow from the powder, and in a moment more he was outside the magazine, with the candle in his hand. Presently he was aware of a wild commotion on the deck above. Frantic men were rushing wildly to and fro, and boats were being cast free from their lashings. The crazy mate had whispered to another of what he had done, and the alarm had been given. The little hero stood just without the door of the magazine, now weak and quivering from the unwonted shock and strain, when down came the commander of the ship, accompanied by Harry Maxwell, by courtesy Lord Clayburn, colonel of the —th Hussars. Brave though they were, and staunch and true, they could not hide the horror that paled their cheeks. The boy's story was quickly told, and when the colonel had seen the magazine safe and secure he took the little fellow on deck, where he very soon brought the terror-stricken men to a realising sense of safety. Thus our hero gained renewed love and blessing from his loyal comrades, and also grained the chevron of a corporal, the highest grade that Max- well felt empowered to bestow upon one of such tender years. And that was the boy, now on a ghostly search with his grandfather, known since the hour of his chrittening as Percival Coverly, though it was whispered among those most intimate with his father that he was entitled to another name. Wellesley had found Marshal Soult at Talavera with an army of 53,000 men, all soldiers of Napoleon's trained host. Against this force he could bring 22,000 British troops of all arms, together with 38,000 undisciplined Spanish levies commanded by the "superannuated, impracticable and ignorant Cuesta.," an old Castilian nabob, who had arisen to eminence through family influence, without capacity on his own part. Expecting, at least, something of assistance from his Spanish allies, Sir Arthur gave battle to the enemy, and in a series of terrible engagements—of fierce and bloody onsets—lasting two days (July 27th and 28th), defeated him, though with heavy loss. At the close of the second day's fighting, when the French had fled, entirely routed, the English commander found himself unable to reap the full fruit of his dearly-bought victory. His Spanish allies had scattered and disappeared, occupying," as Wellesley himself said, "every village and sheltering nook within fifty miles of the field of battle." To pursue the fleeing foe was impossible, and he plainly saw that he must fall back, and that &mit would re-occupy Talavera. The condition of the English army was at this time deplorable. The ministry at home refused or neglected to send the most necessary supplies, while the Spanish authorities, though they con- ferred upon Sir Arthur all honour of empty and high-sounding title, made not the faintest effort to save his soldiers from starvation. The horses of the cavalry perished by hundreds for want of food; sickness was in the camps, and within a brief period full five thousand men died in hospital. But enough of this. Let us back to the battle-field of Talavera. When the shades of night had fallen on the 28th of July, and the worn and weary remnant of Maxwell's Hussars had gathered together in a small hamlet on the right bank of the Tagus, Sergeant John Coverly sat within a shattered mule-shed, engaged in placing a bandage upon the upper part of his right leg, where he had received a lance wound, It was a clean cut, he thought, In the abundant flesh, and he felt himself competent to dress and care for it. In fact, he might have waited-for an army surgeon. He had just taken the last turn of the poor bandage, when to him came the boy, Percival, in search for his father. The old sergeant was on his feet in a moment, his wound forgotten, with not a thought of disa- bility. He had been happy in the belief that his son-in-law had come in safely, and had been detailed at headquarters. At least he had been so informed. "How, boy thy father missing ?" the old man cried in alarm. "Art sure he is not at headquar- ters ?" "0 ! .dear grandpa, he is on the field, wounded sore! Sergeant Crawford has just crawled in. He and papa were together—" "is your information all from Tom Crawford ?" broke in the old man, without waiting for the boy to finish. "Yes. I have only seen him." " Where is he ?" "In the old barn, right opposite." "Then come. Let us have his words direct." With a slight limp, but more from the tightly drawn bandage than from soreness of the wound, John Coverly strode forth from the shed, across the narrow cart-path, into a dilapidated old barn, where, with full two-score more in like situation, he found Sergeant Tom Crawford, stretched upon a bed of straw, with wounds of sabre and bullet, an assistant-surgeon having just taken him in hand as one of the most critical cases. Tom Crawford and Robert Coverly had been chums and dearest frends from the dty of the latter's enlistment. No two brothers ever loved one another more truly and fondly. They had been made corporals on the same day, and the same day had seen them both made sergeants ; snd since leaving Dublin on their present campaign they had given a mutual pledge that should one of theist be taken away the other would look to the care _of. his affairs with_ true. brotherly faith and

punctuality. Should Robert be the one to go nrst, and should his father-in-law be left, of course, the elder man would not be separated from his grand- son ; but, nevertheless, Tom should take the father's place. And John Coverly had freely given his assent to the compaot. Crawford was of middle-age; a heavily-framed, handsome man, with the physical development of an athlete. He was accounted the best boxer and best swordsman in the regiment. The heavy abre or broadsword was his favourite weapon. " Ah, Jack, old fellow 1" he cried, as the rays of a lighted candle in the hand of the surgeon's assistant revealed to him Sergeant Coverly. "I guess I'm done for this time. But never mind me. Have you found Robert ?" "No, Tom. I have come to learn what has befallen him, and where I shall look for him. Can you give me guidance? 0, tell me that he is not dead." The surgeon lifted the wounded man to a sitting posture, and suffered him to speak. "He was alive when I left him," Tom replied. "I'll tell you: It was the last charge of our division. The Spaniards, as you know, had cut and run—every man of them. Our squadron—only about a score of us left, with most of our horses shot under us—had got separated\ from the main body, when we came upon a bf igade of Jourdan's French infantry on the retreat, and were mixed up with them before we knew it. It was curious fighting, that—a score of our hussars in the midst of five hundred to a thousand of the enemy. But we fought as best we could. Robert and I stuck side by side, both on foot. He fell, shot through the body, and I stood over him, striking at all that I came within reach. I think I left six Frenchmen lying dead where I struck them down. But the work was quickly over. The French did not stop to claim a victory. They were on the retreat, and on the retreat they fought. Very soon they swept on, leaving Robert and myself among the dead and dying. As I saw the last of the fleeing column I heard the bugle of our division sounding the recall; and Robert heard it, too, and he struggled to his feet, and said we would join our comrades; and he started as though he would walk. "Really and truly, until that moment I had not thought of my own wounds, but when my chum came to lean on me for support I discovered that I was weak and faint from loss of blood. However, I upheld Robert and started to answer the recall, but we were not to go far. I bore up while I could, and as long as my mate had strength to help himself at all I managed to move on. At length he failed entirely, and sank down. I tried to lift him in my arms, and while doing so the blood gushed in a stream from my shoulder, and Rob saw it, and he begged of me to leave him and

save myself. "For a moment the thought of leaving him there alone was like a crime to me but I quickly saw that only in that way could I hope to help him, and having seen him as comfortable as I could make him, with a knapsack under his head and a blanket over him, I crawled away. Yes —I crawled. I could not walk, I could not stand; but I got in after a terrible pull, as you see. ",Jack, old fellow, you know the route our division took. Just beyond the little brook, where we let our horses wet their noses, you will turn to the right and follow the bank of the stream until you come to a spur of the wood that makes out in a point towards the water-course. There you will find death in all shapes—dead horses and dead men—and there you will find Robert Coverly, if he is where I left him. If you bring him safely in and I should never see him again, you will tell him that I did all I could. 0 ! the Lord knows I could do no more." The old sergeant promised the wounded man that Robert should know the truth, and having spoken a few fervent words of cheer and blessing, he took the hand of the boy and hurried away. The night was dark, the moon having gone down within the hour last past; so Coverly per- suaded one of the surgeons to lend him a lantern with a section of waxen taper sufficient to last the night out with fair usage. The lantern and a flask of brandy, together with a few strips of linen-rag, were quickly gathered up, after which two horses were procured and caparisoned, and the train set forth. As the old man lifted himself somewhat clumsily to the saddle, his grandson asked him tenderly if his wound hurt him. "Pooh! pooh! not a bit of it," was the ready response. "I got the bandage a little tight, that's all. Don't you fear for me, young man. It must be more than a prick like this in my leg to knock your old grandfather up." But a close observer, could he have seen the boy's expressive face, would have detected that his grandfather's assurance had not satisfied him. However, he offered no further remark on the subject, and, moreover, he had something else to occupy his thoughts. He was eager to find his father—more eager than he could tell. • On their way to the brook of which Tom had spoken, they left the battle-field far to the right; but they could see in the distance the ghostly specks of light where lanterns were being carried to and fro by those who sought the wounded. And there, on the ensanguined field, those only a few short hours before striving in fierce and deadly conflict with the hate and enmity of demons, now met as friends, ready and willing to give and to receive the kind offices of friendship and brotherly goodwill. After a passage of between three and four miles our two adventurers found the s---ur of forest flank- ing the little stream, and found the ghastly relies of battle on every hand. By far the larger portion of the dead and dying there were French, and a relief party of Jourdan's Cha.sseurs appeared upon the scene, whose greetings were respectful and kindly. With the slide of his lantern open and the gleam thrown in advance, the old sergeant guided his horse until he believed he had come near to the spot indicated.by Tom where Robert had been left and here they dismounted and secured their beasts while they should make the search on foot. They had searched a long and weary time, ever 1 and anon calling the name of the man they sought, when as they took a turn down by the margin of the brook, the boy's quick ear caught a familiar sound. He bent low down and listened, and presently he heard a hoarse, faint voice begging for

mercy. "0 1 take all else, but do not take THAT! It is not money! it can he of no value to you !" These words Percival heard distinctly, and it was the voice of his father! And he knew on the instant that the robbers of the battle-field had found a packet of papers in an envelpe of oiled silk, closely sealed, which his father carried in his bosom sewed into an inner-garrnent. "Percy ! what is it 1" asked the old man, as an exclamation of wrathful indignation burst from the boy's lips. "it is papa! Tt is papa! Come quickly! 0, come !" And with this the lad leaped forward towards the point whence the sound had come, his grand- father following close behind. At the distance of a dozen rods Percival came upon a scene that gave his heart a tremendous throb. Two men, evidently of the lowest class of the country, with a small lantern, were bending over a prostrate soldier in the uniform of an English Hussar, one of them on his knees pulling at something in the soldier's bosom. "If you have mercy, spare that," the prostrate man implored. The answer was a coarse Spanish oath, as the ruffian tore open the shammy-skin vest. The boy's pistol had been in his hand and cocked from the moment of the first alarm; but one thought occupied his mind—the saving of the father whom he so dearly loved. "Ha, boy I didst hear? It was thy father's—" The closing word of the old man's exclamation was drowned by the sharp report of Percival's pistol. The boy had sprung forward and shot the kneeling robber through the head. As his corn- panion fell backward, killed on the instant, the tiecond ruffian would have leaped upon the intruder had not the old sergeant's sabre at that moment fallen upon his head with a force that sent him to earth instanter. As Percival knelt by the side of his father, ten- derly lifting his head, two French chasseurs came up, attracted to the spot by the discharge of the pistol. The matter was quickly explained to them —for Coverly spoke French fluently—after which one of them, a sergeant, bent over and began to overhaul the pockets of the robber whom the old man had struck down; and his search was well rewarded; for he found, stowed away in the rascal's bosom, a gold watch, and several valuable diamonds, which had been robbed from the body of his colonel. The watch was a repeater, the case elaborately carved, and set with rubies and diamonds. He examined the treasure, by the light of one of the lanterns, and then turned to where Percival was holding his father's head upon his bosom while be made sure that the packet of papers was safe. "Faith !—thou art a brave boy," he said, warmly, "and though shalt keep this in token of the deed thou haat done."

And he gave the lad a gold ring in which was set a diamond of purest water; and be told him he should keep it as the free-will-offering of the Countess de Noyan. Then, in few words, he explained that the colonel of his regiment, from whom these things had been stolen, had been Philip Count de Noyan ; the watch was an heirloom, having been given to the count's grandfather' by Louis XV. Also a heavy ring—a signet—had been an heirloom through several generations. The count's wife, in treasuring these for her son, would bless the boy who had been instrumental in saving them to her, and he—Percival—might keep the ring with perfect assurance that the countess would gladly recognize the gift as her own. "My colonel, as 1 have said," the Frenchman concluded, "was the Count Philip de Noyan; and I, Sergeant Max Savernay, have servedhim well and truly, as I served his father before him." At first our hero objected to accepting the gift; but his grandfather decided for him, and he finally said he would take it, and endeavour to keep it while his life was spared, whereat Max Savernay returned thanks which were truly deep and sincere. The feelings of Robert Coverly, when he found himself in the arms of his brave little son, with the old sergeant at his side, can be better imagined than described. As soon as the matter of the ring had been settled, the grandfather took Percival's place, and having given to the sorely wounded man a generous draught from his flask the latter was able to sit up, and to speak quite clearly; but he was too weak to stand. The French sergeant helped Coverly to lift the patient, and bear him to where the horses had been secured; and there he gave his assistance in getting him upon the saddle, and fixing him in a position as easy as could be contrived. "God grant we may never meet again as foemen !" said Coverly, as he held the hand of Sergeant Max at parting. And the Frenchman made answer: "Something whispers to me that we never shall." Percival mounted behind his father, giving his whole attention to his care while the old man, in the other saddle, guided both horses. It was between one and two o'clock in the morning when they reached the hamlet where their regiment was encamped, and a surgeon was quickly found to attend to the needs of the wounded

man. Sergeant Robert Coverly was a brave and hand- some man, tall and strong. and far, very far, above the average British soldier in intelligence. Be was six-and-thirty years of age, and his life had been one of stirring incident and adventure. Ile was beloved by his comrades of the rank and file, and his superiors respected him for his sterling manhood, and admired him for his unswzrving and always reliable intrepidity. As quickly as possible he was placed upon a con- venient cot, and the clothing stripped from the wounded parts. While they were removing the shammy vest, he asked his father-in-law to take charge of the packet of papers, which he had carried in that same place for a long time. It was a small parcel, not larger than an ordinary pocket- book, secured in a tightly-sealed cover of oiled silk. A hush fell upon the party while the surgeon examined the wounds. "Well, Doctor, what is the verdict ?" the suf- ferer asked, as the surgeon arose from his examin-

ation. "You are a brave man, Sergeant, and want the truth ?" "Yes,—exactly that." "Your hours are numbered! It is doubtful if you can see the light of another day." "Give me two hours,—can you ?" "Yes, I can warrant you that." "And you can help me to talk," "Yes. Stimulants cannot harm you." "Then, father," turning to the old sergeaetz "I wish you would go to our colonel. Tell him I am dying; that I have an important revelation t° make which may deeply affect my son in the time to come. I wish, I humbly beseech—that he will hear it. Will you do this for me ?" "Yes,—but Percival shall accompany me.'' "You will go, my son?" "0, yes. But, papa,—you shall not die. cannot - cannot let you go yet." "Fear not, my blessed boy. God is good. kle will surely do all things well. Trust Him, my —trust Him with all your heart,—and bow W will. There,—your grandpa N, •Aits." (To be continued).

1100'S TWO YEAR OWD TO-MORN. Aw've bin eawr Nelly's slave so long,
Aw dorti'd want to be free; Aw'in t' doctor, too; when dolly's ill,

It's awlus brow', to me. An' mony a ugly wcawnd aw've stitched Wheer t' skin's bin badly torn, Who' hoo's set like a little queen— Hoo's two year owd to-morn. Yet when ho's eawt care snidges reawnd, Then steyls in like a thief ; When hoo comes back hoo brings in mirth, An' leaves no room for grief. Then hope an' love con grow an' spread, _
Like scented flowers, ''Mongst corn; Aw wish hoo'd come : hoo doesn'd know Hoo's two year owd to-morn. It's strikin' eit.T.ht ; hoo'll nod be long
Afoor hoo show's her face— - So little an' so young, an' yet, Beawt hor ther's not i th' place. Beawt hor this life wer bleak an' bare--
0' th' choicest pleasures shorn Hoo's tek her doll an' ride on th' tram—

Hoo's two year owd to-morn. Though t' fire's bin bet aboon an heawr, Id hesn'd burnt so breet ; Whol boo geds up, though th' sun may shine, Id corn'd come gradely leet. Nell, bring thy smiles, an' let's leet up Life's derkest nooks adorn; Hoo's here! Cum, led me tell tha t' fost-- Tha'rt two year owd to-morn. Last neet tha'd two times to gcd up, But neaw tha's nobbut one; Here, mammy, reych them clogs of hors, But led me put 'ern on. Ther little neaw, an' eawt at th' tooas, An' th' heels is badly worn; Tha's hey o pair wi' brass o reawnd— Tha'rt two year owa to-morn. Thy steps aw'll guide whole'er aw live, An' even when aw dee ; Aw feels as Ivy should turn i' th' grave If owt wer burtin' thee. To thee aw sing this simple song; Let critics laugh to scorn ; My happiest liars are spent wi' thee— Tha rt two year owd to-morn. JOHN RA.WCIO4I.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Harrison, Wright, and Sutton; Councillors Blackhurst, Fairclough, Flem- ing, Taylor, Shaw-Green, Voi soy, Hepherd, Gree n all, Heaton, Walker, Hill, Garner, Muir, Browne, Bea- man, H. Robert% Bolton, Hutchinson,Monks, Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Chorley (borough treasurer), and Longdin (borough surveyor.) ELECTIVE AND MAYOR'S AUDITORS.

The MAYOR announced that Mr. J. Harrison and Mr. James Bolton had been re-elected elective auditors of the borough and that he had re-appointed Councillor Muir to be the Mayor's auditor for the ensuing year. WATCH COMMITTER.—SIINDAY NIGHT CONCERTS.—ALLEGED
INDECENT POSTERS.

1 This Committee -recommended that the tender of Messrs. James Smith and Company, of Derby, to supply clothing for police officers should be accepted. In addition to the scale of pay for the police force which we published last week, the committee, on the recommenda- tion of a sub-committee, proposed that the following officers who have been recommended by the Chief Con- stable, and who have become entitled to an increase of pay on the present scale, should take such advance. viz.: —P.C's. Bell, Turner, Smith, Corbett, Corcoran, Holling- worth, and P.S. Cheney. Also that the pay of Detective- Sergeant Monaghan be increased from 31s. to 335. 6d. per week, and that Sergeant Bowen, who holds the post of Vehicular Traffic Inspector, take the rank of Inspector in the force. The MAYOR moved and Alderman HARRISON seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor BROWNE, referring to the new scale of pay of inspectors, said that the provision that, when the new scale of pay came into force on the 25th March, the rate of pay of the officers should be increased to the rate of pay in the new scale next above their present rate of pay, and that the qualifying periods of service should be reckoned as from the date named, would operate un- faily with regard to the older inspectors, such as inspec- tors James and Spinks. He thought the years of serviee these inspectors had already given ought to go towards the qualifying period. Councillor FLEMING said that on Sunday night he was going along Sankey-st. when he heard music in the Theatre of Varieties, and he was told by a person stand- ing at the door that there was a concert being held in aid of the charities of the town. He had nothing to say against that but he should like to know if that Council had any authority over these places of entertainment. There was another objectionable thing in Sankey-st. and that was some of the bills that were posted up. His attention had again and again been called.to them, and he should like to know if the Council could deal with them. Alderman HARRISON: In what respect are they ob- jectionable? Councillor FLEMING said there were indecent pesters on the walls. The MAYOR, in answer to Councillor Browne, said the new scale lf pay was not intended to affect officers for past services, but simply a guide for the future. He did not doubt, however, that the point raised by Councillor Browne would be brought up at the next meeting of the Watch Committee. In answer to Councillor Fleming he thought the only thing they could do about the Theatre of Varieties was to bring the matter before the Watch Committee. He had never heard about any of these concerts on Sunday evenings. As to the posters, he was informed by the Town Clerk that the Council could not interfere unless there was something indecent put upon the walls, when they could either deface the posters, or take other steps. The minutes were then adopted.

STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended approval of the following plans :—Seven houses in Longford-st. for Mr. A.Worrall ; stables in Norman -st. for Mr. James Newton ; alterations to Scotland Bank Ironworks for Messrs. Greening and Company Limited; alterations to premises in Bridge-st. for Mr. John Mynekyne ; house and stable off Thelwall- lane for Mr. W. Williams; fireproof mill for the Long ford Wire Works Company, Limited. It was further re- commended that the Corporation purchase from Mr. Jas. Gandy a strip of land in Longford-st., containing 11 square yards, at the price of a 15s. The minutes were adopted OR the motion of Alderman Surrow, seconded by Councilior BLACIEHIIEST.
THE SANITARY COMMITTEE.-CCHINCILLOR DIXON CENSURED BY THE contutrrgE,

The Sanitary EO-mmittee recommended that the Town Clerk be instructed to close a house behind 43, King-st., as unsanitary. The Committee's minutes also contained the following :—" Report of the Foreman of the Inter- cepting Depots, relative to the visits paid by Councillor Dixon to the depots, at which he, Councillor Dixon, had endeavoured to predjudice the workman against their employment. The Committee record their strong dis- approval of Mr. Dixon's conduct." Alderman BURGESS moved and Alderman Surrox seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor MUIR asked by what authority the Sanitary Committee lodged several tons of concentrated manure in the stables at the Town Hall. (Laughter.) It was a rather serious matter bringing an, intercepting depot under the very noses of the Corporation. (Laughter.) He hoped it would not be repeated. Councillor GREENALL, referring to the " censure " on Councillor Dixon, asked what was Councillor Dixon's conduct, and whether any evidence or correspondence could be produced in reference to it. Alderman BURGESS thought that the best reply he could give to Councillor Greenall would, perhaps, be to read the document sent by the foreman of the works to the Sanitary Committee. He then read this document, dated Feb. 4th, 'which stated that about ten o'clock on Wednes- day morning, Councillor Dixon came to Lythgoe's- lane depot, and walked up to the gas engine and back to where the men were working. He (the foreman) followed him, and said, "Good morning, Mr. Dixon, have you any complaints to make ?" and Councillor Dixon replied, "It is all complaints." (Laughter.) One of the men was working the dolly and Mr. Dixon asked him what he was doing there, and the foreman having explained, Mr. Dixon said, "How would your masters like to get up there and do it themselves?" (Laughter.) Mr. Dixon next turned to a workman and said, "Do you call that a man's job? The masters treat you as a lot of fools (or tools) ; there is many a beast treated better than you." The foreman then asked Mr. Dixon if he thought the place was clean, and he replied that it was. Mr. Dixon added that the work ought to have been done by machinery, and added that "Mr. Longdin and the Chairman must think they had a lot of fools to deal with." Mr. Dixen visited Howley depot on another occasion and he (the foreman) told him that it was "one of the healthiest jobs in town," to which Mr. Dixon said "Nonsense man, I will have them closed." (Laughter.) Alderman Burgess added that he had another report •of the foreman, dated 6th February. This report stated that Mr. Dixon came to Howley depot and asked the foreman where the boiler was for hot water. He was told that there was no boiler. He then asked what they scrubbed the vans and pails out with, and the foreman replied" with carbolic and water, and then disinfected the tubs with powder." Mr. Dixon said there ought to be a boiler. The foreman asked if Mr. Dixon was aware he would re- port all to the Committee, and Mr Dixon replied, " Yes, by all means ; and tell them from me I do not believe a word they say as regards cleaning the vans and tubs with cold water and carbolic, nor yet the fan to clear the place from smelling,"—(laughter)—and also" If I had them at the depot with a rope I would hang every one of them." 'Langhter.) The report then went on to say that about half an hour after Mr. Dixon,Councillor Fair- dough came to the depot and inspected the place, and in reply to the foreman said he had no complaint to make and that there was no smell. Alderman BURGESS said ,he had no remarks to make upon the documents jusetead. Alderman HARRISON: I was in hopes you had. • Alderman BURGESS: I have never made any observa- tions upon the remarks of Councillor Dixon, nor do I intend to do SQ. (Laughter.) Ahlerinan HARRISON: Pay hi & a compliment. (Re- hewed laughter.) Alderman BURGESS said that with reference to Conn- • cillor Muir's observatiens it was, he admitted, impertin- ent on the part of the Sanitary Committee not to consult some other superior Committee as to what should be done at the Town Hall. It was, in fact, very much like the Committee to do so. (Laughter.) The MAYOR said that Coincillor Dixon called upon him that morning and said he was sorry he should not be able to be here to-night as he had to attend a meeting in Manchester, and he was expecting every minute a tele- gram summoning him to London. He informed the Mayor that had he been able to attend the meeting he should have been prepared to repeat everything he said at the depots. -He thought there were many blunders there. (Laughter.) The minutes were then passed. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.—THE COST OF
STREET MAR ING.

The above-narned Committee had-passed the following resolutions :--" That the following apportionment of the cost; of forming and paving Garibaldi-st. be approved, and that the- Town Clerk be instructed to recover the camp :—Executors of the late J. B. Edelsten, per Mr. A. Bennett, Market Grate, £62 4s. 3d.; Mr. Stephen Dale, £72 I3s. 2d. ; the Whitecross Co., Limited, £65 6s. 5d.; Mr. illobert Proud, £3sli. 2d.; total, £237 155." It had also been resolved that the Town Clerk take the necessary steps Tor the forming and paving of Dickenson-St. Alderman WRIGHT proposed the adoption of the minutes. Councilloriltszon,seconded. Councillor HILL asked whether the proposition made by Councillor Roberts at a previous meeting as to the ex- tension of the period for the re-payrnent of the cost of street improvements had been carried out. Alderman HOLMES said that question would come before the Finance Committee. Councillor HILL said he understood from Mr. Ratcliffe, Earlestown, that there 30 years were allowed, and they all knew that in Ireland 49 years were given. Surely Warrington,would have the same privilege as that which Ireland or a village like Earlestown enjoyed. The minutes were adopted. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. From the report of the Inspoctor to the School Attend- ance Committee it appeared that 53 cases had been enquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 48 cases for 108 children. That 41 cases had been taken before the magistrates, and fines inflicted in 38 cases, 2 boys sent to the Industrial School, and one boy ordered to 'Ae whipped. 38 cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with. The Clerk reported that he had received the examination schedules, giving the results of the examination held at the Town Hall, on the 30th January last, from which it appeared that—Of 22 boys presented in the IV. standard 10 passed and 12 failed; of 16 boys presented in the V. standard 12 passed and 4 failed; of 1 boy presented in the 111. stan- dard 1 passed and none failed; of 12 girls presented in the IV. standard 6 passed and 6 failed; of 18 girls presented in the V. standard 8 passed and 10 failed. 'The minutes were passed, on the motion of Councillor FLtursai, seconded by Councillor SHAW GREEN. MUSEUM COMMITTEE. From the return for the month of January it appeared that there had been a decrease of 23 per cent. in the number of visitors to the Museutn as compared with the same month last year; a .decrease of 28 per cent. on the books issued in the reading-room; and an increase of 4 per cent. on the books issued from the lending depart- ment. Report of the following gifts, for which the thanks of the Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors : Long-tailed fieldmouse, from Mr. G. Mountfield ; eggs of Budgerigar, from Councillor H. Roberts ; M.S. Account Book of the Trustees of the poor of Lynam, 1763-76, from the same ; " Marylebone and St. Pancras," by Clinch. from Mr. P. Pearce; "Fourth report on Puffin Island Biological Station," from Councillor F. W. Monks; " Bubastis," by Naville from the Egypt Exploration Fund; " Phonographic instructor," by Sloan, from Mr. W. H. Woodcock. Report of the Curator :—(1) That en- larged models of a grain of wheat had been lent by the Science and Art Department,in order that they might be used by the Field Club. (2) That the bust of Mr. Rigby presented to the Corporation by Mrs. Rigby, has been received. Councillor H. ROBERTS moved the confirmation. Councillor HILL seconded, and the minutes were adopted.

THE CEMETERY. From the report of the Registrar to the Cemetery Com- mittee, it appeared that the interments during the past four weeks were : Adults, 45 ; minors, 44 ; stillborn and premature, 12; corresponding period last year, adults, 44, minors, 85 ; stillborn and premature 5. The receipts for the past four weeks were £9O 12s. 3d., corresponding period last year, £77. The Committee had resolved that the sum allowed to the Registrar of the Cemetery for an assistant be increased from £2O to £3O per annum. The minutes were adopted, on the motion of Alderman HARRISON, seconded by Councillor TAYLOR. TOWN HALL PARK AND BATHS COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that the sum of £25 be voted for providing music inthe park during the ensuing summer, that the money be entrusted to Mr. Coun- cillor Monks for the purpose ; and that the thanks of the Committee be given to Mr. F. Muir for his gift of birds for the park Aviary. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Councillor BOLTON, seconded by Councillor HEATON. THE GAS COMMITTEE. This Committee reported that the average illuminating power of the gas for the present four weeks was equal to 18.39 candles at both works. They also recommended that the contract of Messrs. J. and R. Stone for the supply of coal be increased by 1,000 tons. Alderman HOLMES proposed the adoption of the minu- tes. He mentioned that the Committee would bring for- ward a resolution at the next meeting for the extension of the gas to Penketh and Sankey, and also another reso- lution to lend gas stoves out on the hire system in addi- tion to letting them out on hire on the purchase system as at present. Alderman Holmes asked the nipmbers of the Council what they thought of the gas as im- proved by the new burners, as it was now exhibited in the Council room. (A chorus of voices here expressed approval.) The MAYOR: I think Mr. Dixon must have been about. Alderman HOLMES : I put the burners on one chande- lier to see if the Council liked it. Councillor FLEMING : I have never found anything so satisfactory in all my life. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor FLEMING : If we only have a light like this in our houses, I don't know where we shall be. The minutes were adopted. THE RIVERS COMMITTEE. This Committee's minutes contained several conditions which the Committee thought necessary in the event of the Corporation of Liverpool laying a temporary pipe

TWO VESSELS CAPSIZED. GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. NEW YORK,TIIESDAY.—A terrible disaster has occurred on James River, in Virginia, during the prevalence of strong gales. Two vessels were capsized, and those on board thrown into the water. Other craft went at once to their assistance, but, in spite of all efforts to save them, twenty-three persons were drowned.
ANIERICAN PROTECTION VERSUS ENGLISH FREE TRADE.
LECTURE BY MR. F. MONKS.

On Monday evening a lecture on "American Pro- tection v. English Free Trade" was given by Mr. F. Monks, J.P., in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-st. Warrington. There was a very large attendance. The chair was taken by Mr. R. Davies, and others on the platform were the Rev. F. K. Freeston, Coun- cillor J. Shaw Green, Messrs. T. Birchall, 3. Hough- ton, and A. Rathbone. "SITTING ON A VOLCANO." I

The CHAIRMAN, in the course of a few introductory remarks, referred to the visit paid by the Bishop of Liverpool to Warrington to consecrate the new Church of St. Peter. The Bishop, he said, preached e, sermon—a very serious sermon, in fact, quite a lugubrious 'sermon —in which he drew attention to strikes. as an instance of selfishness. He reminded the congregation that working- men had the voting power in their own hands, and he finally told them that they were on the brink of a vol- cano. He (the Chairman) hoped he would not be consi- dered presumptuous when he said that he thought he knew as much about working-men as did the Bishop of Liverpool. (Hear, hear.) With reference to strikes, he was of the Bishop's opinion that a more barbarous, anti- quated, rough-and-ready way of settling disputes was neverinvented, for the end of a strike was that both par- ties came out in the position of a certain king of whom they might have heard, when he said "Another such victory-and I shall be undone." (Laughter.) But he (Mr. Davies) believed the world had been advancing ever since he was born at all events, and he believed it would advance. He believed that more sensible means of settling disputes between masters and workmen were already to be seen. (Applause.) He did not despair of the future, and as to being on the brink of a volcano he confessed he had been sitting on the edge of one all his life. (Laughter.) If they believed the papers and what pessimists said, they would never be encouraged to do anything. He did not think the working classes were fonder of a volcano than he was, but that they had plenty of good sense to manage affairs, and that they would be welded together into a far more harmonious whole, than the empire had ever known. (Applause.)
A PROMISE FULFILLED.

Mr. MONKS' who was received with applause, said that on his return from the United States and Canada he was asked to give the results of his experience in a lecture to to the working-men of the town, and he made a promise to do so. He was there to redeem that promise, and he only hoped that what he had to say might not only in- terest them but might add some little knowledge of a grand country, so nearly related to them by ties of blood and race and the mane aspirations for the intellec- tual and moral and religious-welfare of its people. When he began to think of what he should say, considering the character of the audience he was likely to have, it oc- curred to him that the subject he had chosen would pos- sibly have as much interest as any other in more ways than one, for we in Warrington ars already feeling the first effects of the McKinley Tariff Bill by the absence of orders for iron which has been supplied in large quanti- ties for many years past for packing American cotton.

div.head: HOSPITABLE RECEPTION.
div.p: A HOSPITABLE RECEPTION.

Mr. MONKS then briefly referred to the voyage to America and the reception there of the party who repre- sented the Iron and Steel Institute of Great Britain. They were most hospitably received and everything was done by their American friends to make their visit as pleasant and profitable as possible. To begin with, there had been subscribed about £30,000 to enter- tain them, and many of their American friends gave what money could not purchase, namely, personal supervision and thoughtfulness to all the details of railway travelling by night and day over a distance of some 5,000 miles without any accident to a single member of the party, which numbered over 500 gentlemen and 100 ladies. The ladies of the party were suitably entertained and taken charge of by a ladies' committee. Receptions and dances, as they might imagine„ took up a great deal of time, and of course, there was a dinner for the gentlemen, and it was one of the most pleasant and agreeable public dinners he had ever attended. The dinner itself was excellent, and the speeches afterwards were exceptionally good. Witty, humourous, and generous in sentiment to the old country, which, after all, he thought they loved best next to their own—whatever they might say. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: GENERAL SHERMAN'S SENTIMENT,
div.p: GENERAL SHERMAN'S SENTIMENT,

One speaker,whose name he mentioned with reverence and respect, and the death of whom the American people now mourned, General Sherman, spoke most kindly of the Queen and Prince of Wales,and the way he had been treated by our fellow-countrymen when on a visit to England, and in reference to a remark of the President of the Institute, that in the event of our liberties ever being threatened, we might count upon the support of the United States, he said, "If ever there should be a shindy going on, I doe't know but what we might take a hand in It." (Applause.) Such a remark from one of their best and most representative men, brought a response from the hearts of the Englishmen which would not be soon forgotten by those who heard it. (Hear, hear.)
