div.head: TWO BROTHERS DROWNED.
div.p: TWO BROTHERS DROWNED.

Two brothers, named Nathaniel and Robert Wilcox, were drowned at Lever, near Bolton on Sunday. Nathaniel went on a raft on the river Irwell, and fell in the water. Robert the younger brother, 'aged 14, jumped in to his assistance, but had himself to be rescued, and died from exhaustion. Nathaniel was drowned.

div.head: ......-40--....... THE BUENOS AYRES SIEGE.
div.p: ......-40--....... THE BUENOS AYRES SIEGE.

The "Times " special correspondent telegraphing from Buenos Ayres says the state of the siege continues, and 2,000 troops are in garrison, but a settlement of all diffi- culties is hoped for through General Mitre's intervention. Business is at a standstill and discounts are curtailed. A semi-official report has reached Buenos Ayres that three battalions of the 4th Regiment of the Chilian Government troops shot their officers near Pisagua, and declared for the revolution.

div.head: SIR EDGAR BOEHM'S WILL. SINGELAR MISTAKE.
div.p: SIR EDGAR BOEHM'S WILL. SINGELAR MISTAKE.

In the Probate Court, on Tuesday, a curious applica- tion was made rto Mr. Justice Jeune, relative to the will of the late eminent sculptor, Sir Edgar Boehm. It was admitted to have been his intention to bequeath a life interest in -.C10,000 to each of his two unmarried daugh- ters, Georgiana and Florence. By some mistake Georgiana's name was inserted instead of her sister's, giving the former £20,000 and the latter nothing. His lordship reserved his decision.

div.head: .....-4, THE RUPTURE IN IRELAND.
div.p: .....-4, THE RUPTURE IN IRELAND.

Mr. Parnell, addressing a meeting at Navan, on Sun- day, asked at what moment or hour during his sixteen years of publie life he had ever been unfaithful to the principle to which he pledged himself. He never pledged himself to do much in the Imperial Parliament, but they , had put the snaffle in the mouths of the landlords, and he promised them that by-and-bye, with a parliament in College Green, they would fit these same mouths with bit and bridle. An Anti-Parneilite meeting was held at the Town Hall, Maryborough, on Tuesday night, and a branch of the Irish National Federation was formed. The Parnellites did not attempt tb interfere with the meeting. The "Dublin Express," referring to Mr. Parnell's seizure of the League funds and the books at Belfast, on Monday, says :—Mr. Parnell and his colleagues are ad- ministering the unwritten laws of the National League with a firmness and a vigour which would do credit to a constitutional government. MR. PARNELL ON HIS DEFENCE. A meeting, called by the London Parnell Leadership Committee, was held on Wednesday evening at the Foresters' Hall, Clerkenwell, to hear an address from Mr. Parnell. There were some opponents present, as was apparent when Mr. McCarthy's name was mentioned. Replying to a resolution expressing confidence in him as , "leader of the Itish race," Mr. Parnell said he believed the English people would eventually see that the Irish people must be allowed to settle the present political difficulty for themselves. He had been charged both by the Liberals and the Conservatives with being a separatist. (A voice: Lord Salisbury will back you.") Well, Lord Salisbury was just as likely to back him as Sir William Harcourt was likely to put him on a plank bed at the first opportunity. Proceeding with his defence, Mr. Parnell said the Constabulary force stood in the way of a settlement; but the Irish people did not want an armed force of this kinds in their country. With regard to the land question, he declared that no agrarian question was ever settled. It would always require attention and alteration from season to season.

The cost of getting the coal and de- livering it into trucks it was expected would not exceed is. per ton by negro labour. On the other side they had the hill filled with iron ore,and here all that was required was a pick and a spade with some blasting powder, for the ore lay close to the surface, a solid block in such quantities as to be practically inexhaustible. One of the mines was opened with a face of ore in sight some 135 yards wide and 100 yards high. No man knew how ' far it extended or to what depth it might go. Their travelling companion, who was the state geologist of Kentucky, said he knew the same ore cropped out on the otber side some miles away, indicating some hundreds of millions of tons of ore in that one mine alone.- (Hear, hear.) PROTECTION AND AGRICULTURE AND WORICING-3IEN'S WAGES.

I ..-. . Dealing with Protection in America, Mi. MONKS said the advocates of Protection claimed that by fostering the growth of manufactures they required for home con- sumption they were creating industries that brought .a population as consumers of agricultural produce to their doors, and, consequently, secured better prices, and that they were able to pay better wages to those employed in manufacturing than were paid in England and on the Continent, and so enable the population to sustain life on a higher plane of comfort wit kless labour. If that theory was true, America had certainly had Protection long enough to test its truthfulness,but what were the facts ? At one time agriculture was a successful business. Most of the emigrants went on to the land and did well; they grew corn and other products, and sent them in exchange for iron and other manufactures, and the trade between the two countries grew rapidly,to the benefit of both. At that time America was looked upon by our skilled arti- zans as a plaee where they could earn higher wages, and where the cost of living, on the whole, was as cheap as in England. With the growth of Protection things, had, however, gradually changed, until at the present time agriculture was a decaying industry in the States; • and the farmers complained of the cost of disposing of their produce at a profit. The great bulk of unskilled labour received very little more than in England in actual wages, and the men had to work harder and make longer hours for the money they received. To estimate accu- rately whether the skilled workman was doing better, they had to ascertain whether he was working by day, piece,or job, and whether he had any men working under him. But whether he had or not, it was the unanimous opinion of the Lancashire contingent, who numtered from 24 to 30, that the system of driving their men was far beyond anything practised in this country. He knew that in his own branch of business from in- quiries made on the spot, the same class of men were not earning any higher wages than their own for the same hours of labour, and in some of the branches nothing like so much.
LONG HOURS AND IRREGULAR EMPLOYMENT.

What was the condition of the man earning his weekly wages ? Many of them did fairly well, and lived in their own wooden cottages, and lived very comfortably, but they had to work hard and make long hours. They usually started at seven o'clock in the morning and worked till six, with half an hour or three-quarters of an hour for dinner, and they worked till four, five, and six o'clock on a Saturday evening. The great bulk of them rented their cottages or rooms in a cottage, but if a man was only earning a dollar a day, and that was the usual wage,and had to pay from Bs. to 12s. a week rent, with clothing double the price it was here and with food no ()beeper, he left the audience to judge whether he was as well off as an ordinary labourer in this country working the same hours. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Every man in that room knew the difference it made to him whether he was regularly employed or not. The system of Protection in America made them dependent entirely upon their own demand, and when things got overdone, work fell short, and the wages, if they did not cease altogether, were very much reduced in consequence. He could imagine that in their* times of depression there was much the same con- dition of things which he could remember as a boy at the fag end of the days of our own Protectionist sys- tem. A new generation had sprung up since then, who knew nothing of the hardship i and poverty which pre- vailed in consequence of the rregula9ty and want of employment, and he was almost certain that the same condition of things prevailed over there at such times, and that they in England heard nothing of the inarticu- late moan of poverty, which found its relief in this coun- try through the channels of the poor law. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: EXTREME LIMITS OF PROTECTION.
div.p: THE EXTREME LIMITS OF PROTECTION.

There was a limit in this world to everything, and he believed that the Protectionist of America had pushed their selfish creed to the extreme of endurance,until it had begun to open the eyes of the farmer, an.lhe had revolted. Others wGuld follow in his wake, but it remained to be seen whether the manufacturers and others interested in the maintenance of things as they were would be suffi- ciently strong to overcome the advocates of Free Trade and purity of Government. (Applause.)
A COMPARISON.

Continuing, Mr. MOn-k-s—Saia--t-lia-t when he reViewed his visit and compared the condition of the great bulk of the people as he saw them in the various towns they visited, when he saw the wooden cottages in which they lived and their surroundings, even if wages and the cost of living were the same he should not hesitate to say that our own people were better off. He had been on the Continent, and now he had visited Canada and America, and with the result that he believed the condition of the working people in any country he had visited where Protection existed would not compare with our own for comfort, prosperity, and real freedom of its people. (Applause.) He went over to America quite prepared to admit that perhaps in a new country. with such resources, Protec- tion was economically the soundest policy, but he re- turned with the conviction that it had been a huge mis- take ; that America, as a whole, would have been better in every way, morally and materially, without it, and that Protection had sown the seeds of corruption, frcm which the people would find it most difficult to free them- selves. (Hear, hear.) BRITISH STAMINA. '

Having alluded to the immense and as yet undeveloped rescources of America, Mr. Monks said it must not be supposed that he was in any way an alarmist. He thought we should be able to hold our own for some time to come, and hoped we should be able to do well. (Hear, hear.) But there were two ways of meet- ing difficulties. You could recklessly close your eves and mind against them and live as though they did not exist; but the day came when you had to face them whether you liked it or not. The other way was to recognise their existence, and, by thought, pru- dence, and perseverance grapple with them until you overcome them. The latter course, he thought, was the wisest, as well as the most manly—(applause) but it required the exercise of self-denial, courage, and common-sense. (Hear, hear.) Those were qualities which existed in old England. and toa greater degree in Great Britain, than in any other country of which he knew. (Hear, hear). He had no wish to be unjust to our neighbours or to our American cousins, but his con- viction was that they had not the high organizing pow- er, the resourcefulness, or the stamina that Britishers had. (Applause.) The Anglo-American was superior to those about him ; the mixture was not equal to the orig- inal and, fortunately for us, it would be the mixture that our working, people would have to compete with. On equal terms, he should have no fear of their compet- ition, but we could not afford to overlook the enormous advantages they had in their cheap labour, coal, and ironstone; and they would not be slow to use them. Neither could we afford to overlook the great tempta- tions which such advantages offered to European capital, Even ,pow, Englishmen and Scotchrnen were to the frontialid three of the best and most favourably situated properties he visited were owned and being developed by English capital, controlled by Englishmen and Scotchmen. THOUGHT OF ESTABLISHING BRANCH WORKS. He confessed that he went out to therStates with the idea that it might be desirable to establish branch works out there in the newly settled districts ; but after carefully considering the subject on the spot, and view- ing and reviewing the whole question from many stand- points, and after completing his visit to Canada, he had a big think on his way home, and decided that so long as working-men were reasonable he should,on the whole prefer to develop his business at home, and live the remainder of his days amongst his own people, doing the best he could for them and for himself also. (Applause.) Mr. Monks next spoke in favour of technical education, and concluded by saying that courage, self-reliance, and steady perseverance had given John Bull a character of his own which had enabled him to win many a well- fought battle against odds that seemed to be overwhelm- ing but which he had faced with a clear head and un- swerving courage. He had faith that the same qualities would manifest themselves in the future as in the past, that by skill and judgment we should be able to maintain the lead in excellence of workmanship and the quality of our productions. which would give to us a continuance of that prosperity we now enjoyed. (Applause.) The race was not always to the swift, nor the battle to the strong. It was not the virtues but the vices of a nation which killed the national life and brought its just retribution. (Hear, hear.) With all our shortcomings and national faults, he could not return to the old country without a feeling of pride in being one of her sons—(applause)—and he honestly believed that Eng- land was the foremost nation in the world to-day for that love of jystice, truth, and freedom which alone exalteth a nation. (Loud applause.) On the motion of Mr. JOHN HOUGHTON, seconded by MT. ANDREW RATHBONE, andsupported by MT. BIRCHALL, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Monks for his able and interesting lecture. A vote of thanks to Mr. Davies for presiding concluded the meeting.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. ARCH 7, 1891.

THE Tories have not taken Lord " One Man One Vote." R. CHURCHILL'S advice, and had the sense to give wq on the ques" tion of reforming the registration laws by adopting the principle of "one 'man one vote." The question was before the House of Commons on Tuesday evening, upon a motion introduced bY Mr. STANSFELD, who seeks not only to get rid Of thd plural voter but to reduce the qualifying period to three months, and make special provision for putting every person on the lists wh° is entitled to have a place there. At present it is left to political agents to make objection, and it i 5 notorious that these' objections sometimes result in wholesale disfranchisement. Mr. STANSFELDI speaking on behalf of the Liberal party, would remedy this grievance by appointing registration superintendents "who shall be officially responsible for superintending the preparation of accurate lists of vocers." With regar4 to the qualifying period, as Ulla w stands at present, it is possible for two years and a half to elapse before the householder can secure what should be an almost immediate right to vote. Who will venture to say, be be Tory or Liberal, that this is fair to the citizen? A three months' qualification is quite long enough to establish household suffrage; and we would go further and say that justice will not be done until manhood suffrage is adopted as the basis of the title to.vote.

Coming to the main issue—the "one man one vote "principle—it is indicative of the old Teri leaven that Mr. HOWORTH should have sneered, in the style of fifty years ago, at "a mere count of heads." He said:—" He recognised the fact that a man might have some other claim to the posses' sion of a vote than the mere fact that he was s householder, and he could not think that a man who held a fiduciary position to his neighbours or workpeople should not have the power and privi" loge of representing his own opinions in the plazas where his influence was exerted." The plain Eng- lish of this round-about statement is that woe who have money should have more votes than those who have none. It ought to be too late in the day to discuss nonsense of this kind; but Toryism is like- an ill weed in a garden. There is no getting rid of it, for, if it be up-rooted in one place, it crops up at another. Rich men have on overpowering influence through their riches with- out giving them extra votes ; while, as to the lay/ itself, thepoor are as much interested as the rich in seeing that it is just. The absurdity of the plural vote was ruthlessly exposed by Mr. G 1.09" STONE who said :—" It depends on whether Ynti happen to have chambers or lodgings within s privileged precinct; whether you happen to have taken your name off the books of a university or tgt have kept it on.; whether your property, such as i may be, happens to be in one county or in more than one County. It is a pure lottery, and it has no connection with wisdom, rank, traditional res- pect, excellence of character, distinguished talent?, or public service." The Tories, of course, know all this as well as Mr. GLADSTONE ; but they possess 3 hold them, defensible or indefensible, voltnes large proportion of these plural votes, and moan tf. as long ithey can. There was an attempt to show tghar. the bone of contention was a small one; but by G. people to learn that there are still over two millions of square miles that are classed as "Unappropri- ated." The area includes Morocco, Bornu with Kanem, Wadai, and Bagirmi. Turning to another important part of the world—the United States— we get the results of the census taken in June last. Details are given as to each State, but there is to lie a special census of the population of Indian Territory, of Indian Reservations, and of Alaska. When these aie added, it is estimated that the population (now taken at 62,622,250) will amount to 63 millions, as compared with 50,155,783 in 1880. The total area of the United , States is 3,499,027 square miles, with a population per square mile, in 1890, of 21.5. The Roman Catholics claim a total of 8,277,039 adherents in 1890; and it is estimated that the adherents to Protestantism number 30,000,000. With regard to our own "tight little island," the population for 1890 is given as 37,823,215. The area is 121,481 square miles, and the population per square mile for England and Wales in 1881 was 446. The population of the earth in 1890 and the lands of the globe available for occupation is given as follows

The index has been most carefully pre- pared, and occupies no fewer than 26 pages. div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
"Reader."—Rabbits are not classed as game under the Game Laws; but they are sometimes referred to by sportsmen as "ground game."

Mr. Seton-Karr says he is" entirely in favour of perfectly religious toleration and equality." But he must tell that to the marines, for he voted against the Catholic Disabilities Bill. The Catholic electors of St. Helens will know how to estimate the professions of the man who mis-represents the borough. "Actions speak louder than words."

There was a time when Mr. Chamberlain stumped the country with a" Radical programme," and had a good deal to say against the plural vote. On Tuesday evening he both spoke and voted against Mr. Stansf9ld's motion condemnatory of the plar- al vote. Alas poor Joseph!

Mr. Gladstone the same evening smartly ex- posed the hollowness of the plea for doing nothing because Ireland is over-represented. In effect, he observed, it was to say to the English :—" We won't put you upon the register, because, owing to the excessive representation of Ireland, you are al- reaßy suffering from being under-represented." This reduction to absurdity of the Ministerial posi- tion was greeted, a correspondent says, with loud cheers and laughter from the delighted Opposition.

It is rumoured thatthe Government are in a state of perplexity on the question of Free Educa- tion—" letting I dare not 'wait upon I would.'" They would like to• do something for the masses but they are afraid of offending the classes. There will probably be great cry and little wool. The policy they pursue is the policy of the jumping cat ; and there is no certainty as yet as to how the animal will jump.

The Warrington Parish Church Branch of the Church of England Ttmperance Society sets a good example by its frequent meetings, and the excel- lent speakers which it provides. What are the other churches doing? It is usual for minor churches to take the cue in good works from the major. Can it be that some of the vicars have doubts as to whether the promotion of temperance is a good work? If not, it is time they were up and doing.

Newton Improvement Commissioners have again been considering the question of a Public Hall. It would seem to be a hardy annual which survives the severest winter. Nothing was done of course, for, if the Commissioners begun to do something in the matter, there might some day or other be an end of it. That would never do; like Tenny- son's brook, it has a character to preserve.
Men may come, and men may go, But I go on for ever.

The old song says that "The Pope he leads a happy life" because "he has no care of child or wife," but the present holder of the office tells a different tale. Leo XIII. has just passed his 81st birthday, and, responding on Monday to a con- gratulatory address,he referred to the past year as one of" anxiety and vexations due to attacks made upon the church" It is to be hoped that his Holi- ness will have an easier time of it as he declines in the vale of years.

The jerry builder is here, there, and everywhere. He has been at work in Russia building fortresses, above all other things, of the veriest rubbish. In- deed, so bad have some of the walls been found that they have been "razed to their foundations and rebuilt." One contractor has been tried by court martial and dismissed the service; and another has blown his brains out rather than face an inquiry into his misdeeds. Moral for the Jerry builders: Honesty in building as in other matters is the best policy.

There was a lecture at the Warrington Training College, on Tuesday, on "William Wilberforce" of anti-slavery fame. He did a noble work, and he was admired in his day as a pattern of virtue. A funny story couples his name with that of Sheridan. The lively anther of the "School for Scandal" had imbibed too much on one occasion, and was picked up in the street. Asked for his name, he said it was "William Wilberforce." Sheridan could not help being witty even when he was drunk.

The poet Cowper was justly credited with doing good work in the movement, and his "Slaves can- not breathe in England" was effectively quoted by the lecturer. In another poem on slavery, Cow- per beautifully says— Fleecy locks and black complexion Cannot forfeit Nature's claim; Skins may differ, but affection Dwells in black and white the same. We have not yet done with slavery. "Darkest Africa " is still a prey to this "sum of all vil- lanies." Major Wissman is reported to be doing good work in freeing African slaves; but what is he amongst so many?

The lecture which Mr. Monks gave in Warring- ton, on Monday evening, on "American Protec- tion versus English Free Trade," was in the nature of a staggerer to those who hoped he would have something to say in favour of the American system. And yet there was no evidence of special pleading;, it was a case withhim, when in America, of keeping eyes and ears open, with a view to the guidance of himself and his townsmen. The sum of his obser- vation is that Protection is a huge mistake, and that America would have been better in every way without it.

Mr. Monks had two suggestions to make which ihe people of tins country would do well to act upon. The first has reference to developing the resources of India by increasing railway facilities. This would mean a demand for English rails, and general in- crease of trade with the teeming millions of our great Dependency. The second hint is to prepare for the further pressure of competition by the tech- nical training of the youth of to-day. Something i is being done, but the pace s slow, and if it be not

Manchester there were 12,000 voters, of whom 4,340 were non-resident. In Central Birmingham there were 1,970, and in Central Bradford 1,981. In the counties the grievance took a more acute form, for in the county of Chester here were 5,400 non- resident voters, of whom more than 1,000 were in one constituency. The condition of householders under existing conditions was such that it was no exaggeration to say that fully 30 per cent. of the genuite citizens of this county were living in a state of disfranchisement.

Yet despite this overwhelming evidence of the serious character of the grievance, the Tories, true to their traditions,rej ected [the Motion which sought to provide a remedy. They are determined, it would seem, notwithstanding Lord CHURCHILL'S warning, to sustain their title to be called "the stupid party " ; and they will have to pay for their stupidity at the next election.
MONDAY last was the centenary The Wesley of the death of JOHN WESLEY; Centenary. and the week may be said to have

been dedicated to memorial services and confer- ences. Not that there is any special need of keep- ing green the memory of the great revivalist preacher ; that is being done every year all the World over by the erection of Wesleyan chapels. Still, it is fitting when a hundred years have gone by that there should be a stock-taking, so to speak, of the results of the movement which was corn- commenced in the eighteenth century by the brothers JOHN and CHARLES WESLEY. And what a stock-taking it is! Great indeed was the work which WESLEY accomplished in his life-time; but the seed sown has brought forth a thousandfold. When the good man died, in 1791, he left behind him in Great Britain and Ireland 312 preachers and 79,000 of "the people called Methodists." To-day there are over 40,000 ministers and lay preachers in Great Britain alone, while there are over 16,000,000 of people receiving instruc- tion, in various parts of the world, in the principles of Methodism. There are some who still argue that JOHN WESLEY ought to have re- mained a strict and obedient member of the Church of England. Even Canon MAsoN expressed himself in London, on Sunday, as "sighing to think how different would have been the history of Methodism if WESLEY, atong with his other vir- tues, had possessed the virtue of patience, and been willing to wait until God set doors open to him' instead of kicking them down." • Patience for- sooth! There are times when patience is a crime rather than a virtue. We shall be told next that Christ should have been patient with the money- , changers in the Temple. Canon MASON i of the Class who wait, and wait, and get nothing done. EUERSON somewhere finely says that "the soul's emphasis is always right." The soul of JOHN WESLEY said it was his duty to go forth into the highways and byeways and preach the Gospel to every creature that he could reach. He went, and that he went at the right time, and did his work in the right way, is shown by the extraordin- ary hold which he laid upon the hearts of men. He did wait in some cases for church doors to be opened to him, but they Were frequently Closed. The Church did not help; 1

it hindered him; and sometimes persecuted him and his followers—just as it does to-day. Persecu- tion is hard to bear, but it makes men strong, and it brings in converts who are not easily shaken. Granted that perseverance under persecution is no
test of the truth of doctrines, it is at any rate a

testimony to sincerity and to an exalted faith. One clergyman who .was taken to task by his bishop for - Preaching in the open air, at uncanomcal hours, pleaded that he only preached in two seasons—"in
season and out of season." That was the token of
the earnestness of the Wesleya.ns ; and it
Was this preaching in season and out of
season which at fast touched the hearts of
the people.
And they needed touching when
John WESLEY commenced his labours. The Church
as described by Archbishop LEIGHTON, was "A fair carcase without a spirit." " Society" set an example of gambling, drunkenness, and immorality which was too readily followed by the humbler
classes. There was need of a change, and the revival which followed upon WESLEY'S preaching
effected that change. Since then We-sleyanism has thriven rapidly ; and if it keeps in touch with the masses it will continue to thrive. But it must
recognise that there are bodies to be saved as well as souls ; that, with the schoolmaster astir, doubtful dogma must give way to a catholic spirit
411 d elevation of vision. Th 3 world moves, and Wesleyanism must move with it.

BOOKS of reference in these days Statesman's of express speed and sub-division 'Year Book, of labour and knowledge are be- coming more and more valuable. GOLDSMITH'S schoolmaster was such a prodigy that it was a 'wonder to the villagers "that one small head could carry all he knew " ; but not even he could carry all that a busy man requires when he is try- ing to keep Dace with these busy times. Hence the need of reference books, and textbooks, so that, 'without burdening the brain, information of the latest and most reliable kind may be obtained in the quickest way. Taking front rank amongst 'works of this class, we have the "Statesman's Year Book," which has now been issued for twenty- eight years. It is a "Statistical and historical 'annual of the States of the World" published by Messrs. MACMILLAN and Co., price 10s. 6d., and comprises no less than 1,132 closely printed pages, over 300 of which are devoted to the British tnapire. Details as to government, population, teligion, commerce, education, finance, &c., are given as to every country in the world; and, as the statistics are brought up to date every year, it is Obvious that the editor Mr. J. S. KELTIE is at all t.imes burdened with a serious task. "Superhuman effort of reluctant will" is, as old " Polonius " would say, a good set phrase; but— let us whisper the question—what does it mean? We recollect a reporter of the high fainting type who, getting intoxicated during an important en- gagement, turned out some most extraordinary copy." His own account of the matter was that, when he was sober, he couldn't urkderstancl. what he had written; but, he insisted, "it sounded well," Can it be that the facile pressman has wandered to Japan and giver: Sir Edwin a lesson?

A Ship Canal navvy named Jacks, seems to have had an idea of going "on the spree" with a "wax-work -.lady, in a Warrington show, on Satur- day night. Be kissed the figure, danced it round, and finally threw it on the floor. Perhaps he thou..ll the lady of wax would have a melting heart, wlilst he himself was in the humour of the clown who said he could embrace a lamp-post—with a'petticoat on. The adventure ended in the police court, in an order to pay for the damage done, besides ss. and costs for being drunk.

It needs to be better understood that the Knights and Dames of Primrose Leagues assemble to be entertained not to be enlightened. This was demonstrated at Toxteth the other evening when Mr. W. J. Burgess, formerly of Warrington, pre- sided over a compound meeting and entertainment, and found that he was in the 'position of a Ruling Councillor who couldn't rule. Musicians enjoy a rest in due season, but to rest whilst four speeches were being made was more than they could endure; so they began their programme at the end by sing- ing the National Anthem in the ante-room.

And still the speeches went on. Colonel Morri7 son was the last on his legs. Alter a long speech, he said he would tell them an Indian story about the Goram case; but that story remains untold. The audience got impatient and then the speaker got impatient, and oh "picture it! think of it ! " he actually said "-- the Goram ! "After this he made " a palpable hit "—he sat down. It was found then that some of the artistes had left the place, and one of them, Who had "totted" the thing up, declared in the street that he wouldn't sing for £1,780. The programme was of course curtailed, for it was a case of "-- the Goram " and "-- everything." And all this conies of trying to edu- cate the Primrosers. Oh, the pity of it!

FOOTBALL AT RETS(XAM.
At Runcorn on Wednesday the local half-holiday club defeated a similar organisation from Swinton by one goal, three tries, and four minors to nil.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, the macbdstratcs granted the following transfers of licenses :—Red Lion, from Henry Urmson to Sarah Ann Urmson ; Volunteer Inn, from Joshua Thompson to Margaret Thompson ; Royal Oak from Alfred Crowther to Thomas Pendlebury; Cornwall and Devonshire from David Williams to Mary A. ST. JOHN'S AMBULANCE ASSOCIATION RUNCORN CENTRE.

This association has ace-c7M-p-h-sled a good work in Run- corn during the past two winters. A few weeks ago over 40 members succeeded in passing an examination on "How to render first aid to the injured," Dr. McDougall having ably fulfilled the duties of lecturer. On Wednesday next a tea and entertainment is to be held with theobject of raising funds for carrying on the good work, and Lady Brooke has consented to grace the pro- ceedings with her presence and present the certificates. At a meeting of the General Committee, held at the Town Hall, on Monday night, it was resolved to close this fund. The disposal of the balance in hand, amount- ing to £6l 4s. 4d., was discussed. It was eventually re- solved that in the event of a Cottage Hospital being opened in Runcorn within the next twelve months the treasurer be authorised to transfer the balance to such object. A balance sheet is lying at Mr. Marshall's office at the Town Hall, for the perusal of anyone who has been interested in the movement. Oa, YES!'" Cough Mixture, Chiretta Balsam. Relief in three minutes. Cures Bronchitis. Hope. late Methuen, Deansgate, Manchester, and all Dealers.—Advt.
SONS OF TEMPERANCE, RUNCORN

At a well attended meeting of the above order on Satur- day; an interesting discussion on the United Kingdom Alliance and the direct veto, took place. The subject was introduced by Mr. Thomas Heesom. The United Kingdom Alliance is an association of temperance and social reformers, and was formed in Manchester on June Ist, 1853. At the first g( ,tern meeting'of the Council a number of resolutions were passed, as a basis for the agi- tation, and as ii.dicating the character and scope of the movement. The 7th resolution was "That rising above class, sectarian, or party considerations,all good citizens should combine to procure an enactment for prohibiting the sale of intoxicating beverages, as affording most efficient aid in removing the appalling evils of intemper- ance. Mr. Heesom spoke of the necessity of making the direct veto a vital issue at elections—a vote for a vote and nothing for nothing. Messrs. Edward Key, S. M. Temperley, Thomas Whyte, J. Jones. Thomas Clarke, Thomas Cooke, James Johnson, and D. Bisbrown took part in the meeting. The discussion was adjourned for a fortnight. Mr. John Taylor occupied the chair. Lsww 3lowEws.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington, and at Earlestown.—Advt.
CARPENTERS' STRIKE AT RUNCORN.

The carpenters employed by the -11f;tiChester Ship Canal Company at Runcorn came out on strike on Satur- day. A fortnight ago they gave notice to their em- ployers for an increase of wages, but their terms have not been acceded to. It is now sixteen years since a similar strike took place at Runcorn, and the men, after having been out for seven months, gained their point, having their wages increased from 30s. to 325. per week. Since that time, however, a return has been made to the old rate of wages, and the men, considering that they are entitled to an increase have now asked to be paid at the rate of 71-d. per hour. The Ship Canal Company, how- ever, have offered to meet their demands by paying 7d. per hour, which the carpenters have declined to accept on the ground that they will not be any better off than at present, as they can only _work from daylight till dark, and consequently would only be employed some portion of the year a few hours a day, and would have to work longer hours during the summer months for the same money. There are at present about 100 men out strike, and they assert that the joiners have received an advance in wages, and they, therefore, consider them- selves entitled to an increase. Sir Edwin Arnold, who resides in Japan, thus describes the Mikado :—" It is a typical Japanese man's face, in many points. You shall see a thou- sand such in a week's travelling hereabouts, but this one stands apart in character as in elevation, touched in its most ordinary lines and lineaments with an almost marble reticence and an ironclad refusal to be common, even if nature stamped it common, in so much that the slightest bend of the brow in salutation appears to be the result of a superhuman effort of reluctant will."
ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court on Monday Thomas Cruise,of Water-st., was charged with having on the 14th Feb., unlawfully wounded Samuel Byes, lodging-house keeper, Lugsdale-road.—P.C. Hargreaves, deposed to seeing the prisoner kick Eyes several times on the legs,and Dr. Mc- Lennan said that Eyes was in a dangerous state,suffering from erysipelas in the legs caused by being kicked.—The prisoner was remanded for a week. REV. PETER MACKENZIE AT WIDNES.

Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel, Widnes, was crowded on Sunday morning and evening last, when the 'Rev. Peter MacKenzie, the well-known preacher and lecturer ' occuyied the pulpit. On Monday evening Mr. Mac- Kenzie delivered a lecture on ' Nehemiah, his patriotism and his piety," the subject proving a deeply interesting one, illumined by the lecturer's humour an powers of description. Mr. Thomas Robinson presided. LECTURE ON THE PASSION PLAY AT WIDNES.

In Wkintt Volunteer Hall on Monday evening,Professor Gatley delivered a lecture on the Passion Play of Ober- ammergau to a very good audience. The lecturer's graphic description was aided by a series of magic lantern views. The chcir of St. Mary's Catholic Church sang " 0 Salutaris " and the " Tantum Ergo." While, the children of the school rendered several choruses. Miss Leatherbarrow sang "There is a green hill far away." BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The annual tea party in connection with this Church was held in the schoolroom on Wednesday evening. About 200 persons sat down to an excel:ent tea, and a still larger number was present at the meeting after- wards held under the presidency of the Rev. John Simp- son, the pastor. The Chairman opened the proceedings with a suitable address, and during the evening speeches were delivered by the Rev. John Morgan, the Rev. R. G. Hughes, Mr. W. H. Chadwick, and Mr. Hollinshead. The choir rendered several anthems and glees in a manner that called forth much applause, and Mr. and Masters Outhwaite performed several instrumental selections in capital style. Miss Smith,gave a violin solo with good effect, and Mr. W. Cook contributed a pianoforte solo. The usual votes of thanks were passed. ENTERTA INMENT.

n connection with the Independent Order of Recha- ites, a miscellaneous entertainment was given in the National Schoolroom, Kingsley. on Tuesday evening. The Vicar, the Rev. A. P. Reynolds, M.A., presided, and there was a large audience present. The programme was a somewhat lengthy one and the various items were well received. Mr. Hicks contributed a cornet solo in good style, whilst Master and Miss Timperley, of Runcorn, were encored for their excellent playing of the duet, violin, and piano. Miss Hall sane with much sweet- ness and expression, "Happy be thy dreams," and earned a well-merited encore. Mr. A. Fox, of Runcorn, sang " The Skipper," and met with quite an ovation, and Mr. Clegg. of Runcorn, delivered a humorous speech, which convulsed the audience with laughter. , EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets Qowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Guion, American, and other lines.— john Walker. agent, "Examiner' Office, Bewsey-st., Warrington.—Advt, THE FALLS OF NIAGARA. Visitors to Manchester who can enjoy a genuine realistic and artistic treat should make a point of seeing the colossal cyclorama of the Falls of Niagara which is now on view in the Panorama Buildings, Deansgate. It is truly a wonderful representation of "the wonder of America"; and so perfect is the illusion that it grows on the spectator the longer he gazes on it. The painting is by a great scene artist, Mr. William Telbin, who has cer- tainly surpassed himself in this extraordinary work. A descriptive lecture, given at intervals, enables the visitor to thoroughly understand every point of in- terest in interesting scene. CRITCHLEY'S Tailoring meets the times.—Advt. AN OVER-SHARP GIRL. On Thursday, at the St. Helens Police Court, Alice Maud Milner, 14, of Westfield-st., was charged with stealing two sums of sixpence by means of a trick from Elir,beth Whittle, provision dealer, and Robt. Roberts, ...atcher. The prisoner went into the shops of prosecutors, and having tendered sixpence for meat and provigions, which wereof less value than sixpence,. received change, and subsequently re- turned stating she had paid a shilling. Mrs. Whittle believed her statement,handed her the sixpence, and the prisoner afterwards proceeded to Robert's shop and was also successful there. She ackbowledged her guilt, and was fined ss. and costs in each case, with the alternative of seven days' imprisonment. CRITCHLEY, High Class Tailor, Bold-st.iVnrrington.—Advt. COLLIERY FATALITY AT HAYDOOK.

An inquest was held at the Wagon and Horses Hotel, Haydock, on Tuesday morning, by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, on the body of Michael Knight, a day wageman, in the employ ,of Messrs. R. Evans and. Co. The evidence showed that deceased, who was 39 years of age; was employed in the Queen pit on Friday morning, and was preparing to erect a prop in the mine, when tbe roof without warning gate way. Deceased was buried in the debris, but it was found that a large stone had struck him on the head, and smashed his skull. He was taken out unconscious, and removed to the hospital, but he died about half past four hi the afthnoon. He had been working at that particular job a few seconds when the accident happened. A verdict of "Acci- dental death " was returned. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st. Warrington.—Adrt.

GOOD TEMPLARY. , At the annual session of the South-West Lanca- shire. District Lodge, which was held on Saturday, in the Lecture Hall of Trinity Presbyterian Church, Trinity-road, Bootle, there was a good attendance of representatives, amongst them being Templars from Golborne, Earlestown, Ashton, Wigan, and other districts. The D. Secretary (Bro. R. D. Petterson), reported an addition of one new lodge, and after allowing for all removals, &c., from the district, a total financial membership of 2,358 in 55 lodges. The returns from all the lodges were very ; encouraging, and pointed to a large increase in the coming official year. Amongst the officers elected for the next six mOnths were D. Co. Brother George Clarke, Earlestown, who was re-elected; and •E. D. ; Guard, Bro. T. Charnock, Wigan. UN BRELLIS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W, BUTTON'S Sankey-at.. Warrington.—Advt. THE WELSH DISESTABLISHMENT Sionox. The Executive Committee of the Liberation Society have adopted the following resolution in reference to the ,Welsh Disestablishment motion, which was discussed in the House of Commons on February 20th.—" Th. Committee regard with great satisfaction the result of the recent motion in the House of Commons in favour of disestablishment of the Church of England in Wales; the motion having received the official support of the Liberal party, and a hostile majority of 53 being reduced to 32. They confidently 'anticipate that at the next general election the majority of English representa- tives will be in accord with those of Wales,Scotland and Ireland, who are already in favour of disesta- blishing a church which meels the religious wants of only a small minority of the Welsh people. The Committee will spare no efforts to ensure such a result; and will look for a hearty co-operation of the Society's supporters in the constituencies." BessiNgTTEs.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., garrington.—Advt.

CHAMBERS OF COMMERCE MEETINGS. At the meeting of the Associated Chamber of Commerce on Wednesday in London an interesting discussion arose on the motion of Mr. Leicester from North Stafford, that the Government ought to take over the canals and make them national pro- perty. Reference was made to the Manchester Ship Canal, Mr. Atkinson, M.P., expressing the opinion that the shareholders would be glad to sell at a loss. Mr. Platt, of Oldham, one of the Ship Canal direc- tors, looked upoa the undertaking as a great national •enterprise, and said as time went on the shareholders would get much better percentage than any Government could give. He emphatically denied that the shareholders would be glad to sell at a loss. The motion was rejected by a large majority. Mr. W. Pierpoint attended the meetings, as representative of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce. Resolutions were adopted recommend- ing a uniform penny postage throughout the British Empire, and recommending that the profits of the post office beyond three millions annually should be expended in the improvement of the postal service.

Now OPEN FOR THE SEASON—Smart and Co.'s private Writing and Commercial Academy for ladies and gentle- men. at Mr. Chantry's, 13, Sankey-st., Warrington. Open every Tuesday from 3to 9 p.m. Writing: Gentle- men are taught a .fine bold, rapid business hand, and ladies an elegant and flowing style. Terms for the com- plete course, One Guinea. Bookkeeping: Pupils are taught how to open, keep, balance, and close a complete set of books by double entry ; and our certificate for pro- ficiency is given to each pupil. Arithmetic and mental calculation taught practically. Shorthand; Pitman's system. Pupils will be received on Tuesday next, at any hour from 3to 9 p.m. No classes, the instruction is individual. Card of terms and full particulars may be had at Mr. Chantry's,l3, Sankey-at., Warrington, or post free from our Head Academy, 2, BroWn-st., the Market, Manchester.—Advt.

RUNeORN BOWLING CLUB. The annual meeting was held at the Bridge Hotel, Ash- ridge-st., on Wednesday evening. Arrangements were made for the coming season. The subscription was raised from 2s. 6d. to 3s. 6d.; and Mr. Thomas Cooper was relelected president, Mx. S. Yarwood vice-president, and Mr. Thomas Wood secretary. The selection of captains was deferred until the first games were played.

Johnson), received on Monday, a cheque for £l,OOO from the periodical" Answers "to be invested for the benefit of Mrs. Crick, wido iv of the late William Crick, insurance agent, and his children, Eccleston-villa, Thatto Heath, who was recently killed on the Lon- don and North-Western Railway at St. Helens Station, having in his possession copies of the cur- rent issues of " Answers " and "Tit-bits." The £lOO insurance has already been paid by "Tit-bits." UMBRELLAS RE COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. E.; W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. • •
MR. BRUNNER, M.P., ON SUNDAY OPENING 011 LIBRARIES.

There is a proposition before the Brunner Free Library, Northwich, to open the reading-room cn Sundays from two to five o'clock, and from half-past seven to nine in the evening, Mr. Brunner to whose , generosity Northwich mainly owes the library, ! writing to express a hope that the motion may be carried, says :—"A public library which is closed on Sundays mocks at the efforts of poor men and women to obtain intellectual culture, and Sunday is the very day on which those who are fo*unate enough to possess libraries of their own enjoy them most."

div.head: CONGREGATIONAL UNION.
div.p: CONGREGATIONAL UNION.

The annual. conference of the Lancashire Congre- gational Union was opened in Liverpool on Wednes- day,under the presidency of the Rev.A. Foster. In the afternoon a dinner at, the Adelphi Hotel was atten- ,ded by about 400 antlemen, and in the evening Mr. William IVoodall, M.P.' presided over a large meeting in Great George-st. Congregational Church. Mr. Woodall stated that in Lancashire there were now 305 places of worship, with accommodation for 156,480 persons. On Thursday the annual meetings were concluded. Preston was fixed upon as the place for next year's meetings, and it was resolved to ask Professor A. S. Wilkins, of Owens College, to accept the office of Chairman of the Union for that year.

div.head: HOMB IRON TRADE.
div.p: THE HOMB IRON TRADE.

The English iron market pursues the even tenour of its way; that is to say, it remains quiet with a very slender prospect of matters improving at an early date. The warrant market has again been inanimate, and the business done in pig-iron of moderate scope. Crude iron remains steady in the North of England and Scotland, but weak in Lancashire and the midlands. Bessemer pig is ex- ceptionally quiet, and Is. a ton lower in the north- west; trade in steel being slow, and the orders I placed of small dimensions. There is not much life I in the finished iron business, and prices are weaker. Black sheets, probably owing to the disorganisation of the trade,have dropped another 2s. 6d. Tinplates are quiet, but strong. In the shipbuilding trade it is observable that the new orders received do not nearly reach the tonnage launched. There is greater competition for engineering vt ork.—lron. EARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT LIBERAL CLUB. With the closing of the Liberal club, a few months ago,many people expressed the opinion that Liberalism in the Newton Division was dead, at least so far as its centre was concerned. This, how- ever, proves not to be the fact,and from the inform- ation below, it will be seen that it is very much alive, and in a fair way to again become one of the chief institutions of the district. After settling the landlord's claim, and paying other incidental expenses the Committee found themselves with £ll Is. sd. to their credit. There were, however, other claims to meet,amounting in all to £39 16s. 5d., and to clear off this incubus, the Committee, with the assistance of their secretary (Mr. H. Ball), have worked very persistently. With the arrears in sub- scriptions from members, and the following dona- tions from gentlemen interested in Liberalism, all debts have been cleared off, and the Committee now stand with a sheet. Mr. W. Mitchell, gener- ously subscribed £lO ; Mr. G. W. Rawlins, C.C., £5; Mr. J. Vicar, jun., ..£1 is., and Mr. C. Pilkington, £l. It is intended to organise a new club, and with this object a meeting will be held next week, when it is hoped that every assistance will be given by a Liberals.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hal on Tuesday night. Mr. J. Pritchard presided and there were present Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Rkv. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. MacDougall, Messrs. S. Taylor, A. Salkeld and G. Moss (clerk.)—The _School Atten- dance committee reported that during the month 76 parents were summoned to appear before the Com- mittee for infringement of the Education Act and 63 attended. Proceedings were ordered to be taken up before the magistrates against 24 parents. A gratifying improvement had takdn place in the attendance of children at school. The number on the rolls was 3,422, an increase of 119 on February last year and the percentage of attendance was 82,as against '7B last year The lack of accomodation in Newtown district continued to manifest itself. A parent strongly objected to send her child from the top end of Surrey-st. into the lower part of the town —The minutes were passed on the motion of Dr. Gastaldi seconded by Mr. Salkeld.—Tha Clerk reported that Mr. Brunner, M.P., had provided a number of pictures for the Board Schools. They represented various subjects— natural history, geology, botany, mechanics, &c.—Dr. Gastaldi proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Brunner for his present. The pictures would be greatly appreciated by the children who would be able to learn a great deal from them.—Mr. Salkeld seconded the motion which was carried, the Chairman remarking that it was a very useful present to the school, and would be of consider- , able advantage in lectures and lessons.
RUNCORN POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. Brundrit ana Major Flazie- burst.

RhFUSING TO QUlT.—Joseph Williams was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and refusing to quit the Man at the Wheel when requested te do SO. TUESDAY.—Before Major Ilazlehurst and Dr. Steele. DRUNIE.—WiII. Parker and Samuel Steele, were each fined ss. and costs for drunkenness.

A STAND UP FIGHT.—A navvy named Charles Hill was charged with assaulting Wm. Neild,a walking ganger,on the Ship Canal at Runcorn. It was stated that Neild had had occasion to discharge Hill for neglecting his work, and on Sunday when the two •men met on the highway at Halton Brook, Hill cursed Neild and struck him. eild returned the blow.—Mr. Burton, .who defended, called two witnesses to prove that it was a fair stand up fight." The case was dismissed. WEDNESDAY.—Before Major Hazlehurst and Dr, Steele. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed upon Benjamin French, John French, John Duff, and John Iliddock. A LUCKY CAPTAIN. Overize Ned, captain of a schooner, was charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Wheatsheaf Inn Bridge-st., on the previous evening. Superintendent said it was fortunate for the man that he got into the hands of the police, as he bad £3O in his possession. A fine of 10s. and costs was inflicted.

DISHONEST WHEN Dux.—Jehn Duggan, a navvy,was brought up on remand, charged with stealing a pair of boots from the shop of Thomas Whinyates, Church-street. Tin prisoner said he was drunk at the time, and he should have taken the shoes back when he was sober. As this was his first offence, he was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. H. Gastaldi.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. H. Gastaldi.

MISCELLANEOUS.—Henry Swell, was fined ss. and costs for being 'drunk and disorderly.—For sleeping in Hutchinson's Chemical Works, William Shannon, a tramp, was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. THEFT OF CoAL.—Martha Johnson, of Pear-st., was convicted of stealing 561bs of coal the property of the trustees of the late John Hutchinson, and she was fined 10s. or 14 days' hard labour.

SHOP ROBiERY.—Mary Stewart, 35, Elizabeth-st., was charged with stealing three flannel singlets, value ss. 3d. from the shop door of Edward Wareham, draper, Albert- roal The prisoner, who •was caught in the act, had been'three times previously convicted of felony, and she was sentenced to six weeks' hard labour.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Major Hazle- burst.

POOR RATE DEFAULTER-E-.----Nir. W. Sutton, the assist- ant overseer, had issued 43 summonses for non-payment of poor rates. The amounts due had been paid with the exception of in seven cases, in which the usual orders were made.

WANTED A SEPARATION.—Mary Ushan, a young woman, summoned Patrick Ushan her husband forassaulting her. She alleged that on Menday morning, the defendant commenced to ill-use her, but his brother stopped him. In the evening he " clouted " and kicked her, because she had no money for drink for him. The defendant sold up the furniture on Tuesday. She did not want to punish him, but a sepuation. She had been married two years.—Mr. Lake for the defence, denied the offence ia tote and said the husband had remcnstrated with her be4use of her " gadding" about with other girls.— The Bench bound the defendant over to keep the peace for:six months, in his own recognizances of £5 and one surety of £5.
SCHOOL BOARD CAsEs.—A number of parents were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in eabh case.
DISORDERLY CHARecrEns.—Margaret Hancock pleaded guilty to behaving indecently in Alcock-st., and George
Mundy, a navvy, pleaded guilty to having unlawfully counselled and procured her to connimit the offence. Each prisoner was sentenced to three weeks' hard labour.
DRUNIC.-Murphy Flannigan and John Sefton Ball were each lined ss. and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly.

BEG-GING. —Owen Daley, a young man, was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging. A YOUNG THIEF. —Ellen Walker, 12 years of age, pleaded guilty to stealing from a clothes-line in Vicar-st., a sheet and an apron, the property of Mary Kilcullan. The girl had pawned the articles for is. and spent the money.—The Bench ordered her to come up for judgment when called upon; and Mr. Reynolds advised the mother to deal more strictly with her in future.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS,
THURSDAY. —Before Mr._ H. Gaskell, jun., and Lieut-.
Col. Gaskell.

iDRUNKENNESS.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Thomas Mulloy, James Smith, Nicholas Walsh, Thomas Fallon, Margaret Cannon, Honora Can- non, and Patrick McLoughlin. A fine of 7s. 6d. and costs was imposed upon John Reynolds and Mary Daley. CHIMNEY ON FIRE.—John Bird. Cromwell-st., was fined Is. and costs for this offence. SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted a number of parents for not sending their children regularly to school, and a fine of ss. was inflicted in each case. , DOGS WITHOUT LICENSES.—WiIIiam Butler, Ditton, and James Forbes were each fined 7s. 6d. and costs for 1 keeping a dog without license. Wm. Wilson,Crow Wood, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing his dog at _large without a muzzle.

THE THEFT 1:-R-0-3-1 A CAPTAIN.—Mary Treacy, Nelson- St., was brought up on remand charged with stealing 325. from the person of Roger Powell, captain of . the schooner Richard Cobden, under circumstances already reported. The prisoner pleaded guilty and was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

CRUELTY TO A HORSE.—William Parker, of Eclelsten's- yard, Warrington, was summoned for cruelty to a horse by working it in an unfit state, on the 23rd February. P.C. Almond said the defendant's pony,which ,was draw- in.' a spring cart, had a large raw wound on the left shoulder, and three other wounds in various parts of the body. The prisoner said he did not know they were so bad. He was fined 10s. and costs.

THEFT OF A WArcH.—Thomas Daley, aged 14 years, pleaded guilty to having stolen a silver watch, worth 65., belonging to Ann Needham, from the bedroom of a house in Warrington-road, where he lodged. He was severely reprimanded and fined 10s. Joseph Jones, sen., 60, Ox- ford-st., was charred with receiving the watch, knowing it to be stolen. His son had purchased the watch from Daley for 6d., and handed it to the prisoner, who pledged it for 4s. 6d. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and was fined 20s. and costs, or a fortnight's hard labour.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting Was held at the Town Hall on Thursday. Mr. S. Taylor niesided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speaknian, C.C.,J. Pritchard, H. J. Grice, J. White, J. W. Lightburn, E. Iroison, W. Hankinson, F. Wiswall, B. W. Humphreys, F, A. Lake (law clerk), C. Marshall (secretary) and M. Barker (surveyor).

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN
div.p: THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN

The Medical Officer (Dr. McDougall) reported thatdur- ing February there were 44 deaths, of which 7 were due to whooping cough, 3to mesenteric disease, 5 to bron- chitis, 2to scarlet fever, 4 to premature birth, 3 to phthisis, 3 to convulsions, 3 to senile decay, 2 to inflam- mation of the lungs and one each to inflammation of kidneys, rheumatism, inflammation of bowels, diabetes, exhaustion, ulceration of windpipe, cancer of the liver, ctumia, and cardiac dropsy.—ln answer to questions,the Doctor said the town was very healthly indeed, except for a wave of whooping cough.
MISCELLANEOUS.

The Highways and Buildings Committee recommended: —That notices be issued on persons having rings fixed in the streets to remove them. Thatthe following tenders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company be accepted, for , the construction of an arch with retaining wall and pil- lars at the Victoria-road Viaduct, for the sum of £567 ; for the construction of a sewer at the same place,at prices set out. That Major J. C. Orred's offer to give the sum of £35 towards the ouilding and retaining walls in lieu of wing walls at the Victoria-read Viaduct be accepted. That the tender of Mr. H. Coward to take down and re- build the Bowling Greenwall, in Thomas-st., for the sum of £3O be accepted. That the offer of the Runcorn 'Soap and Alkali Company to give £5 forthe weighing machine at Waterloo Bridge, beacce,pted. These minutes were passed on the proposition of Mr. Speakman. -

div.head: WATERLOO BRIDGE.
div.p: WATERLOO BRIDGE.

The Waterloo Bridge Committee recommended that the sum of £6OO be paid on account to Messrs. Morrison and Son.—Mr. Pritchard, in moving the adoption of this minute, said Messrs. Morrison had completed the altera- tion of the bridge with the exception of a trifling matter of recasting two yards of the handrail. This payment was og account. the Board had still in hanT,a balance of £.300, and had the right to retain it Until the work was certified complete.—Mr. White seconded the motion, which was carried. FINANCE COMMITTEE. _

This Committee reported that during the month the treasurer had received the following sums :—General district rate, £6Ol 7s. 3d. ; market rents and tolls, £3O 10s. 3d. ; slaughter-houses, &c., £4 6s. lid.; School Board rent, £2O ; nightsoil sales, £ll 12s 4d. ' • total, £667 16s. 9d. Accounts amounting to £351 4s. 2cl. were passed for payment. There was a balance of £584 Bs.7d. of the general district rate still to be collected.

div.head: ' THE FIRST BOON.
div.p: ' THE FIRST BOON.

On the recommendation of the Highways Committee it was resolved that application be made to the Cheshire County Council to have the road leading from the East- ern Boundary Railway Station, and comprising Halton- road, Bridge-st., High-st., Waterloo bridge, and Station- road, declared a main road, and also to have the road leading from the station to the boundary beyond the hosoital, and comprising the Holloway part of Highland. read, and Weston-road, declared a main road.—Mr. Speakman remarked that a committee had been appointed to make formal applications. He pointed out that be- fore the County Council would adopt the road, it would have to be put in such order that the County Surveyor would pass it. If the Council did adopt the road it would be an everlasting boon to Runcorn, and one of the first things where the Council would have been of service to the town. He had interested himself very much in the question, and it was in such a way that it would be ac- accepted by the Council.—Mr. Lake remarked that the Countil would repay about one half of the cost of maintaining the road.—Mr. Speakman said it would be more. It would certainly be three-fourths and perhaps more.

UNDER CONSIDERATION. Mr. Hankinson mentioned that during the past month the General Purposes Committee had had a discussion with respect to better lighting of the town, and the mat- ter would be brought. before the Board in due course. The Committee had also considered the more efficient equipment of the fire brigade.

INFECTIOUS DISEASE. In accordance with the notice he had given, Mr. Lightburn moved "That the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners' being the Urban Sanitary Authority for the district of Runcorn, hereby adopt The Infectious Disease (Prevention) Act, 1890," and declare that the provisions thereof shall be in force within the said Urban Sanitary District on and after the 13th day of April, 1891."—Mr. Lightburn said the first of the leading fea- tures of this Act, was that it gave_the Board increased power in the inspection of dairies. At the present time the Board had only power to inspect dairies within the boundaries, but under this Act if they had reason to sus- pect a dairy outside, they could inspect it, and this was most important as Runcorn was supplied with milk from dairies at Halton, Weston, &c. Thenv.tain with respectto the disinfection of bedding and premises, if the occupants failed to do it, the Board had to bring them before the magistrrtes. Under this act the Board could do the work themselves and charge the occupants. A person ceasing to occupy a house wherein there had been a per-ion suf- ering from infeetious disease, was subject to penalties if he did not disinfect the premises or give the owner in- formation in respect to it. Persons dying of infectious disease must not be keptlonger than 48 hours in a dwell- ing or workshop without sanction in writing of the local authority. Any person removing the body of another per- son that had died from infectious disease in a vehicle other than a hearse must give notice to the owner of the vehicle, and if the vehicle was not disinfected immedi- ately the owner was subject to a penalty. A very im- portant clause was one providing for the disinfection of all matter coming from a person suffering from infectious disease under pain of a penalty of £5. Mr. Wiswall seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.
TRADESMEN AND OBSTRUCTION.

The Secretary said Mr. Fisher, -t-h-e—ch—air-m. an of the Highways Committee had intended, had he been pre- sent to appeal to the tradesmen of the town to assist the Board and the Police in pre- venting obstruction of footways. The custom was prevailent now of encroaching on footpaths by placing goods before shops, which tradespeople had no right to do, and the Committee, through the Press, wished to appeal to the tradesmen to • assist them in this matter.—Mr. Grice said the Board did not wish to harass any tradesman—they were all tradesmen them- selves—and they did not wish to interfere unduly with their business. Many tradesmen had expressed them- selves strongly on this obstruction, but it was out of the province of the Board to deal with it;. it rested entirely rin the hands of the police, and if the police took the matter up, they were simply doing their duty.—Mr. Speakman said this was a subject which would need to be delicately dealt with. He saw more obstruction in Liverpool thaia they had in Runcorn.—Mr. Humphreys said there were a certain number ef trades- men who carried out the bye-laws in the letter and the spirit, and it was unjust to those to allow obstruction.— Wiswall said the footpaths were rather narrow, and there was not much room for obstruction. It was some- times a difficult matter to walk along the footpath.—The i Chairman said the police knew their duty ; t was

not within the province of the Board to inter.. fere in this matter. If they laid down rules as to the duties of the police they would very likely get their fingers rapped.—Mr. Lightburn said they simply wished to assist the police in their duties in preventing - obstruction.—Mr. Grice : That is it.—The subject then dropped.

div.head: TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
div.p: TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

! The Board then- went into Committee to consider a communication from the County Council with reference- to the application of the Board for a grant towards build- ing a technical school in Runcorn.—On resuming, a depu- tation was appointed to interview the sub-committee of the County Council on the subject.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, Szc.
BY "AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.°

The idea of establishing a cottage hospital in Runcorn,which has emanated from the Relief Fund Committee is one that ought to meet with univer- sal approval. Accidents are continually occurring at our local manufactories, and the necessity of a hospital has been demonstrated on many occasions during the past month. About eight years since Dr. Steele, the then chairman of the Board attempted to found a similar institution, but his efforts were unfortunately unsuccessful. May Dr. Taylor's scheme share a better fate. The subscribers to the relief fund will no doubt be only too glad for the balance of £6l to be appropriated to such a purpose as benefitting the maimed. Another fatal accident on the Ship Canal at Runcorn is recorded this week being the second within a fortnight. The death list is a very heavy one up to the present, but it is only to be expected on a stupendous and dangerous work like that in progress. Davies placed his foot on a greasy plank, was precipated into a dam 24ft. deep, and injured his spine. The jury at the inquest expressed their sympathy in a practical manner by giving the widow their fees, and the chief witness added his contribution.

The letter of the correspondent in the "Exam. iner " as to the inefficient lighting of the streets of the town has apparently had an effect. The General Purposes Committee have considered how the light- ing may be improved, and Mr. llankinson promises that a proposal shall be made to the Board of Com- missioners.

, Mr. Neil Mathieson, of the firm of Mathieson and Co.. has signalised his retirement from business by a very graceful and generous act. The otter day he called into his office a few of the oldest employes of the firm, which is now merged into the Chemical Union, and informed them that he had invested £l,OOO as a nucleus of a sick and benefit fund for the workmen when incapacitated for working by 'sickness or accident. May his example be followed by other manufacturers!

I -One of the chief topics of conversation in Widnes is the proposed incorporation of the town. The Government inauiry into the application for the charter will be held at the Town Hall on March 25th, and Mr. Allen, the clerk to the Local Board is collecting a number of facts and figures to lay before the Inspector. It is not anticipated that there will be any opposition to the scheme, and there is no doubt entertained that the .town will be a full- fledged borough in the course of a month or two. . The Local Board election takes place early next month,and efforts are being made to avoid a contest, which . would be a useless expenditure of public money. Of the five retiring members it is under- stood that Messrs. Taylor and Liddell will not seek re-election and the Ratepayers' Association propose to fill their places by Mr. James Tilley and Mr. John Beech, who figured prominently at the last election. Should this course meet with the approval of the Owners' and Occupiers' Association,a contest, it is expected, will be avoided,as no outsider would risk the odium of causing an election under the circumstances in which the town is now placed. The real struggle will come when the members of the_. Council have to be chosen by the ratepayers.

PENKETH. THE WESLEY CENTENARY. In connection with the celebration of the Wesley Centenary, a special service was held on Sunday afternoon, in the Wesleyan Sunday School. The usual monthly address was first given by Mr. W. Moores, and afterwards several interesting addresses; descriptive of the life and character of John Wesley, were given by Aferssrs. C. E. Parker, D. Garnett, and It. E. Garnett, and attentively listened to by the scholars.

div.head: ESSAY ON "ETHNOLOGY."
div.p: ESSAY ON "ETHNOLOGY."

On Wednesday evening, in connection with the Mutual Improvement Association, an essay on "Ethnology "written by Mr. J. Simpson, was read by Mr. Philip Hughes, Mr. Simpson being unable to be present. In a clear and lucid manner, the essay- ist gate some of the causes by which the different races of the earth have been developed. He urged that it was mainly owing to climatic effects added to other natural influences working through long periods of time that had produced the many dif- ferent tribes that inhabit the globe. The paper was most interesting, and at its conclusion Messrs. Peers, Parker, and Gandy commented upon it. SCHOOL ENTERTAINMENT. Last evening week in connection with the Wes- leyan day school, a juvenile musical sketch,entitled " Kinderspiel, or old friends with new faces," in aid of the chapel enlargement fund was given in the schoolroom. There was a large attendance, the room being crowded. The first part of the pro- gramme consisted of musical drill, recitations, dia- logues, and action songs, cleverly and correctly gone through by the children under the direction of Mrs. Wilson. After a short interval, the children all arranged and dressed in pretty costumes, pre- pared by the teachers and friends for the musical sketch" Kinderspiel," were exposed to view, pre- senting a most pleasing picture. The musical accompaniments to the various songs were played by Mrs. Watson. During the evening the children were provided with refreshments, the expense of - which was generously borne by Mr. Cross. Finan- cially the entertainment was a great success, a very handsome amolnt being raised to present to-the. treasurer of the chapel extension fund,

div.head: WA.RRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WA.RRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

TRIMSDAY.—Before His Honour Judge Ffoulkes. THE CAUSE LIST comprised 3 adjourned plaints, 4 default summonses, 131 original plaints, and 50 judg- ment summonses. BURTONWOOD FARMERS IN COURT.—Richard Kilshall, farmer, Burtonwood, claimed £l6 from Thomas Perks also a farmer of Burtonwood, as damages for injuries to, a cow in October last. Mr. Horridge, barrister, (in- structed by Mr. H. B. White) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. nrshaw, of Warrington, defended. From the statements made and evidence given it appeared that an occupation road, named Moss-lane, was in connection with the farms of the plaintiff and defendant, and on the evening of the 10th October, a man employed by the plaintiff was driving some cows along it. The defen- dant's cart laden with potatoes, was being driven along at the sime time, and it was said that the driver had no reins to the horse. The cart passed one of the cows suc- cessfully but went against the hind quarters of another, and the wheel passed over one of the cow's feet. It was stated that the cow at the sametime wasin full milk and was giving 12 quarts a day. Since then it had, however, deteriorated very much, and had been attended by a veterinary surgeon. For the defence it was contended that the injury to the cow had not resulted from any negligence for which the defendant was responsible. His Honour, however, gave a verthet for the plaintiff for £l3.

A CLAIM ron MANURE DELIVERED.—In this case Mr. Joseph• Gordon, manure merchant, of Liverpool, claimed £lO from Mr. John Warburton, farmer, Burtonwood, for a load of manure, delivered in June last. Mr. Browne was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Forshaw for the defendant. The plaintiff's manager (Mr. William Bartley), stated that a load of manure, about 70 tons in weight, was de- livered to Mr. Warburton, in June, 1890, the amount agreed upon in payment being £lO. A labourer in the plaintiff's employ said he delivered 70 tons at Sankey Bridges on the date in question. Mr. Warburton said that the contract was that he should pay the plaintiff 3s. per ton. When he woighed the manure he found that the weight was 44 tons 3 quarters.—Cross-examined by Mr. Browne: The defendant admitted that he did not weigh the manure until a month or six weeks after delivery. In the meantime it had been kept in a field and might have got lighten—His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed.
It is announced that the Maryport Hematite and Steel Company have suspended payment.
