div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
ASSOCIATION.

The Bla.ckburn Rovers have won their way into the final for the Football Association Cup once more. This was achieved by their success over their old rivals, West Bromwich Alhion,on Saturday. The clubs met at Stoke in the presence of some 15,000 spectators and a finer game for a Cup tie is not often seen. The match was very exciting throughout, and whereas the Albion were wonderfully aggressive tor the greater part of the first half, the Rovers afterwards took up the running and were seen at their best. Just at the last the West7Brom- wich forwards werenerribly in earnest, but were knocked out by three goals to two,although they were the first to score. There was some splendid play on both sides. Gow, the Rovers' goalke.ver, was too unwell to appear, but Pennington made a capital substitute. He found a rare helper in Brandon. John Southworth gave a grand exhi- bition at centre forward, and Lofthouse also did well. He was far too cute for Dyer, the Albion half-back. Groves and Horns were about the best of the West Brom- wich forwards, whilst Perry at half-back and Reader in goal were very conspizuous.

There was- a tremendous gathering at Sheffield to see the semi-final between Sunderland and Notts. The crowd was estimated at 25,000. The Northerners were the favourites, but they met their match in Notts, although the latter were without M‘Lean, one of their backs. The vacancy was filled by Harry Cursham, who some seasons ago was one of the finest forwards in the kingdom. Sun• - derland were the mcre scientific of the two, but this was counterbalacced by the dash and vigour of their antago- nists, and the final verdict was three goals each. The- tie will be replayed, by order of the F.A. Council, on the • same ground on Wednesday next.

Out of the two teams that are to oppose Wales and Irelandito-day will doubtless be selected that which wilt face Scotland at Blackburn on the 4th April. The team that is to meet Wales is strong in every department, but hardly good enough for Scotland. In this a place will perhaps, be made for Holmes, of Preston, who has ren- • dered yeoman service for the North End this season. He is a Preston youth, and a steadier and smarter back no club could desire. Oliver, of Sunderland, will perhaps be his colleague.

div.head: FOOTBALL.- RUGBY.
div.p: FOOTBALL.- RUGBY.

. Cumberland were not expected to have much of a chance at Whalley Range on Saturday, nor had they. From the first it was easy to see that the most the visit- orscould hope for was to keep down the score, and to- wards the accomplishment of this end they set to work with a will. That they were only partially successful is shown by the extent of their defeat, which was Pretty decisive. Three goals and three tries to a try testify to the superiority of the Lancastrians. Another goal ought to have been kicked from the try by Craven, but Coop missed the opportunity badly. Valentine led the way in the matter of scoring, which was maintained with some- thing like regularity to the end, two goals and two tries having been registered up to thc interval. The back play of the winners was all that could be desired, and if their present form is kept up, the appearance of Gloucestershire at Whalley Range need not be dreaded. The passing of the whole back division won rounds of cheers, and individually there was little to choose. M'Cutcheon has fallen, into the style of the other backs,. and the whole lot now work together like machinery. Whilst the forwards hardly came up to recent perform- ances, they did well at times, the most noticeable beingPyke, Kent, Whittaker, and Craven. It is to be hoped, that Kent will sooa have fully recovered from his injury.

In certain townsin Yorkshire football is anything but- a game of pleasuce. The referee in the match at Otley versus Saltaire lard such stiong complaints against the conduct of some of the speetators that the Rugby Union, saw fit to suspend Otley and ordered them not to play on, their own ground on Saturday last. A number of play— ers of other clubs were also suspended for misconduct.

The championship of the West Lancashire League is. not to be another walk over forWigan. Last season they were unbeaten in the competition, but they are not far- ing so well this year. • Indeed, Walkden have triumphed over them an two occasions, beating them again on the. village enclosure last Saturday. From this it would ap- pear that Walkden have a much stronger team than the. outside world are aware of, and they may look far a higher class of fixtures.

div.head: WINTERS' TRIALS.

During this season also the germs of consumption—that scourge which annually sweeps away so many of our youths and maidens—are often ' implanted in the system, originated by an apparently slight cold or cough, which is too frequently ne aected till it assumes alarming proportions. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
STEALING CASKS FROM A CHEMIST'S.

Walter Warburton, a married man, aged 30, who re- sides with his mother,at 289, Winwick-road,was charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, with "steal- ing from a yard behind the premises of Septimus Ken- yon', chemist, Winwick-road, three empty casks his pro- perty. Chief Constable Hunt said the prisoner had occa- sionally gone errands for Mr. Kenyon, and had been call- ing on people for the purpose of disposing of the casks, representing that he was selling them on commission for Mr. Kenyon. The casks were found on his mother's pre- mises. He was fined 20s. and costs, in default one month's hard labour.

div.head: SHAMEFUL ILL-TREATMENT OF A MARE
div.p: SHAMEFUL ILL-TREATMENT OF A MARE

At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, Thomas Jacks, employed by the Ship Canal Company, was charged with cruelly ill-treating a mare in Wilson Patten-st. on the 20th ult. P.C. Corbett deposed that he saw the defendant in charge of a horse which was draw- ing a lorry loaded with what was called Chinese clay. He was beating the mare with a whip stock and also kicking it abou'i the fore legs.—The defendant: The, mare was kicking.—Alderman Harrison said the defend- ant had no right to follow her example; and denounced his inhumanity in severe language, and asked the Chief Constable whether he would not report the man's con- duct to his employers. Mr. Hunt said that would be causing him to be twice punished for the same offence, and his employers knew about the prosecution. Alder- man Harrison said the loan deserved to be punished twice, and he himself would communicate with his em- ployers rather than they should not know.—The defend- ant was ordered to pay. 20s. and costs or go to prison for two months hard labour. A STRANGE FROLIC WITH A. WAXEN LADY. ,

At the Borough Police Court on Monday, Samuel Robertson was charged with being drunk on Saturday night in Bridge-st., and doing wilful damage to a wax figure at an exhibition, the property of Mrs. Elizabeth Adams. Mrs. Adams said the defendant came into the exhibition, and got inside the barrier behind which there was a "lady figure," and danced it reund the room,then th.rew it on the floor. She did not see him touch the figure, but she saw him inside the barrier. A young lady saw him do the damage. He "cursed something 'orrid " all the time, and witness tried to stop him. She called for a constable, and the defendant made his way through, the house and got out by a side door. He was carrying a pair of new boots, and threw them away, and squared out to "fight at her." The young lady who had witnessed the whole affair and who had not kept a pro- mise to come, was sent for, and testified that he came in drunk to the show, went behind the barrier, tumbled over the waxwork figure,and knocked it down,damaging it. He kissed it, and said if she could not get up her- self she must lie there. The Mayor said the defendant must evidently have taken it for a live young lady— (laughter)—and addressing him said "Did you think it was alive ? "—The defendant • I don't know. Mr. Chair- man. (Renewed laughter.)—He was fined ss. and costs for being drunk, and ordered to pay the damage, or go to prison for a month's hard labour. CHARGE OF ASSAULT WITH AN AXE. At the Botough Police Court, on Tuesday, William Henry Sheldon, aged 16, living in a street off Golborne- st., was brought up in custody charged with inflicting grievous bodily harm upon Thomas Rathbone, aged 20, who' lives in Flag-lane, by striking him on the head with in axe, on the previous afternoon. It appeared from the statement of Chief Constable Hunt, that the follow- ing were the circumstances. Angry words were ex- changed between the complainant and the prisoner, and they. ultimately bad a fight. It was alleged that the prisoner went to an outbuilding near to the house he lives in, and brought out an axe, with which he struck the /omplainant three times on the head, with the result that'he became immediately unconscious, and had to be conveyed to the Infirmary. The prisoner was subse- quently apprehended. Mr. Hunt applied ior a remand for a week, as he thought it would be that time before the prosecutor could appear. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor for the prisoner, said some of the facts as stated by Mr. Hunt, were according to his (Mr. Browne's) instructions. But the complainant did not become at once unconscious: he walked a distance of 60 or 70 yards, and then walked arm-in-arm with a friend to the Infirmary. Mr. Browne consented to a remand,but applied for his client's release on bail, stating that he could prove that the complainant had been following him about for three days, and as- saulting him. The prisoner was remandecUtill Tuesday, and was released on two sureties of £25. each being found for hisre-appearance. THEFT OF £6 FROM A PUBLIC-FIOUSE BAR.

Jag. Paul Antrobus,a black-smith, and a married man, residing at No. 4, Naylor-st., and who has latterly been employed at Mr. Fletcher's, gas engineer's, Warrington, was 'Charged with stealing on Saturday afternoon, from a cab box at the Ring-o-Bells public-house, Church-st., the win of £6 the property of George Littlewood, the landlord of that house.---Chief Constable Hunt stated that ,the prisoner Went into the house about half-past 11 a.m.;;and had a glass of beer and about 12 o'clock had anot.lier supplied to him. About one o'clock Mrs. Little,Wood went out of the bar, leaving £22 in an un- IrcCkos.l cash box on the counter in the bar, and Mr. Littood went into the cellar, the prisoner being left alonmear the bar. She came back and found the pri- sonegone ; end wanting change for half a sovereign out of the, cash box, from the appearance of the money thoUght her husband had been giving a deal of change, and .fsma.rked to him " My word, man, you have been doing,sqrne business while I have been upstairs." He asked her whatshe meant, and she said " Well, you have been.siving some change." He replied that he had not, and yad never touched the cash box. The theft was then;plisawered, and as the result the prisoner was ap- prehghidgd. Efe said he had been working short time or he vinutifinpt have Stolen the. inoney.—Mrs. Littlewood de wised to the circumstances of the case, and said she had qiilpected the prisoner meant robbery, and told her hnslird tolOok after the bar in her absence, but he did not 4056. be had missed money before.—Mr. Little- wood ',having given evidence, the Chief Constable in- formed the Bench that the prosecutor had got £4 17s. of the Money and a pair of bats which the prisoner had bout with part of it. lie was sentenced to two months' imp4sonment with hard labour.

d , AN ARTFUL ADVENTURER. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Saturday, before Mr. Alderman Burgess (chairman) and Mr. Coun- -cillor. YaseA.Arthur Edward Hulse, a cripple, and a respectable-looking man, was charged with obtaining money by false pretences at Orford Barracks, the pre- flay. Chief-Constable Bunt said the complainants in this case were Sergeant-Major Bailey and Sergeagt Craythorne. The defendant, on August 14th, under the name of Edward Harker and the false pretence of baying been robbed at a Warrington lodging-house of £9 obtained 2s. 6d. from the court poor box.. the police bad consequently been on the look out forrhim ever since until last night when they were informed of his visit to the barracks. He had represented there that he was spensioner, and had been in the 28th regiment of foot and in the Ashantee. War where he had received a sun- stroke, and that his name was Arthur Curton. Sergeant- Major Bailey and Sergeant Craythorne and others sub- scribed £1 18s. sd. for him, out of which they were on the point of paying his railway fare to London, but.first communicated with the police, the result being the pri- soner's apprehension at the railway station.—Sergeant- Major Bailey and Sergeant Craythorne corroborated,and Inspector Spmks deposed to the apprehension, and said Hulse admitted never having been in the army or had a

sunstroke. He had been convicted two or three times of felony. He stated that he had a pension which was given to him because he dashed aside a revolver which a man presented at the Queen.—The prisoner : That is quite correct. The prisoner from his incessant ex- traordinary and convulsive motions' appeared to be suffering from St. Vitus's dance, and there was some doubt as to whether he was shamming, but Police-Ser- geant Chantler deposed to having known him as a crip- ple when a child at Kingsley near Frodsham. He was sent to prison for seven days.

div.head: MINOR CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: MINOR CASES. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MONDAY. —Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb), Aldermen Harrison and Sutton, and Major Litton.

DRUNK AND BEGGING.—James Butler, of Wrexham, drunk in Liverpool-rd. on Saturday night was dismissed, having been locked up since that night.—George Williams, drunk and begging in Bridge-st. the same night, was sent to jail for 14 days.—Patrick Jennings was charged with begging in Buttermarket-st. on Satur- day night. A constable said the man begged a penny from him, and then seeing what he was, wanted to get away, but witness took him into custody.—The prisoner said he only asked for a match.—The Chief Constable: And you got your match.—The prisoner was fined 10s. and costs.—John Patten drunk in Bridge-st. while in charge of two horses and a beer dray on the 21st inst, was fined ss. and costs.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—There were the following convictions for being drunk and disorderly :—William Monagan, in Bridge-st.,on Saturday night, 10s. and costs —Michael Starley, in Horsemarket-st on the same night, ss. including costs.—Martin Morgan, canal worker, at Bridge Foot-,\on Sunday night. div.head: RUGBY_
div.p: RUGBY_

RuNcogs A v. TRANMERE.—This fixture was played off on Saturday, at Tranmere. Play was very hard and fast, the Runcorn forwards rushing tioe ball down to the home 25, where some tight scrimmaging ensued, and from a bit of scrambling play Evans popped over, T. Woods missing zn easy place. Runcorn continued to press, Tranmere making only a brief incursion before Runcorn once more gained ground. Clare and Lynch got off with.a good dribble, and play was located in the Runcorn "25." A bold rush to the line resulted in C. Lumgair getting over. P. Little got away, and with a good rush gained a lot of ground, throwing to Shaw, who got over between the ' posts, T. Little gaining a magnificent goal. Final result—Tranmere,l goal, 2 tries, 1 minor; Runcorn A, 1 try, 2 minors., _

, - WIDNES V. BARROW.—The return match between these two clubs was played on Saturday at Widnes before about 3,000 spectators. Widnes immediately attacked, and the home backs were conspicuous with some good passing. Barrow now pressed, but Hartles relieved to centre. Here Kenyon got possession, and put in an ex- cellent run to the visitors lines, where failing to get through, he passed to Barber, and the latter to Brennan, who in playing the ball threw it forward. Barrow de- fended well, and a moment later A. Harley got away, and crossed the Widnes line, butthe kick at goal failed. From the drop out Barrow forced two minors, when Drummond relieved, and his efforts were supplemented by Evans and Barber, who transferred play to the visi- tors',quarter. Here Barber received a pass and got over close to the posts, but the ball being thrown forward,the point was not allowed. Widnes' continued to press for a few minutes, when A. Harley again cleared, and placed Widnes on the defensive, Harley saving grandly. Widnes again carried the ball to the centre, where Gordon put in his kick and Brennan following up prevented its return, and evcoatually Evans for Widnes got over. Brennan however, failed at goal. On changing ends, Barrow were called upon to defend, and Widnes keeping up the attack, a minor resulted. From a throw in near the visitors' line, Holt scored, but Brennan again failed at goal. Widnes now having the wind to their backs, commenced a number of rushes which completely broke up the ;visitors' defence, and Barber, after a very tricky run,evaded all his opponents, and grounded the ball in an easy position for a goal. Smith converted. Widnes again forced the game, and Smith after playing the ball over theline, lost posses- sion, but Holt being near did the needful. This point was also converted into a goal. Play now became very even for a time, when Leak for Barrow got away and scored, but the kick at goal failed. No further point was scored, and when the game ended Widnes had achieved a brilliant victory by two goals, two tries, and two minors to Barrow's two tries and two minors.

RUNCORN v. BURTON.—.This match, which has been looked forward to with more than usual interest, was brought off at Runcorn on Saturday, in the presence of a large body of spectators. Both teams were not fully represented, five of the home team being absent, their places being taken by members of the second string. Play was opened ny W. Hughes, and the visitors had to touch down. From a scrimmage which afterwards ensued, Robinson obtained possession of the ball, and some neat passing was observed between that player, Crompton, and Abrams. Burton were thus put on thc defensive. Samboul cleared the !ine, and H. Hughes and Crompton put in some eommendable play, whilst Faulkner passed to Hampson, the latter getting over at the corner flag. A fine but unsuccessful attempt at goal was made by I Houghton. Gorton then made a grand run, but owing

div.head: EXAMINER, SATtTRDAX, MARCH 7, 1891
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATtTRDAX, MARCH 7, 1891

to the tactics of Boughton, the visitors were again put on the defensive. Then followed some superb passing by H. Hughes, Faulkner, and Crompton, the latter essaying a drop at goal, the ball striking the post. Relief was given to Burton by scrimmages, and atthe centre flag Hughes, Crompton, and Faulkner treated the spectators to a series of fine passes. Faulkner got over at the corner flag, and a magnificent goal was scored by Houghton. A little later the home team broke through nearly the whole of the home team's hands, and Abrams succeeded in get- ting over after a long run; but the attempt at goal failed. Then followed some fine play on the part of Evershed, Ward; and Gorton, but Houghton was equal to the occasion, and tackled superbly. Robinson passed to H. Hughes, who got over, and Houghton placed a magnificent goal. The result at half-time was: Run- corn, two goals, two tries, two minors ; Burton, one try. On the resumption of play, Frank Evershed put the ball again into motion; but Crompton returned into touch, and W. Hughes dribbled to the visitors' quarters. W. Hughes,Faulkner,and Crompton gave a repetition of their previous passing tactics, and Crompton getting over, an attempt at goal was essayed, but failed. Riley led the home forwards on, and Gorton put in the saving clause at the right moment; but Robinson again broke away, and Cronipton, who received the ball, raced over; but unfortunately no goal resulted. Final score.; Runcorn, 3 goals, 5 tries, and 8 minors; Burton; 1 try, and 2 minor. The teams were as follows: Burton: Samboul, back; Lowe, Ward, and Gorton, three-quarter backs; Fordham and Marsden, half-backs; Evershed, Magher, Yeoman, Greswell, Weston, Beck, Beamount, Gorton, and Wear, forwards. Runcorn : Horton, back ; Faulkrer, Crompton, and Abrahams, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes and George Robinson, halftbacks ; Antrobus, 0. Hughes, Williams, Hampson, Gayter, W. Hughes, P. Riley, Broady, and Davies, forwards. WARRINGTON " A " V. TYLDESLEY "A."—The return match between these two teams was played on SaturdaY at Wilderspool. The home team differed slightly from that which inflicted defeat on Widnes "A " the previous Saturday, Lalley taking Mather's place at half back, whilst Potts made his debut at three-quarter. Fine weather prevailed, and Tyldesley started towards the pavilion goal, offside play ruling a scriinm'age at half way. The visitors' forwards broke away and play was taken to the home lines. Thorniley and Creaghan dribbled to half way, but a smart kick by Miller and a short rush by his forwards again took the oval to the Warrington territory. Huge kicks by Jolley and Webster forced the visitors back, and a neat pass from Potts to P. Lawless saw Warrington attacking. J. Lawless ran away from a pack, and Jolley was prominent with some more tall kicking. Crippen tried hard to relieve his side, but his kick fell into the hands of Potts, who ran and passed in style to P. Lawless, that player having no diffi- culty in crossing the line, but no goal resulted. The home team still attacked, and although the visiting for- wards, headed by Schofield, did a rush down the field, the effort was easily staved off by Webster. Pretty passing by J. Lawless, Laney, Potts, and P. Lawless deserved a better fate, and Jolley had hard lines in fall- ing when scoring seemed a certainty. Miller and Allen removed the danger, but only for the moment, for J. Lawless got clear away, but spoiled the effort by hold- ing the oval too long. However, from some loose play P. Lawless secured, and dodging his opponents, he suc- ceeded in dropping a neat goal, amid cheers. Webster responded to the restart by a strong run, and Potts was applauded for a clever kick to touch near the line. Miller cleared slightly, and the Tyldesiey forwards broke away to the half-way, only t& see grand combined play by Potts, P. Lawless,Jolleyrand Webster taking the oval again to the line. Molyneux tackled Miller under the posts and a minute later another pretty pass from Potts saw P. Lawless cantering over for his second try. The interval was reached with no further additions to the score, Warrington leading by the substantial majority of egoal and two tries. Tricky play by the home for- wards on the restart forced Tyldesley at once to defend, and Webster ree.eiving from Jolley was only pulled down on the line. Gibbons got the oval away, Webster making his, mark. A tall kick to the line was well followed up by the same player, and he secured the oval again and scored. Jolley met Miller's drop out by a huge punt,and Lawless and Lally were to the fore with smart runs. A grand burst of passing by I. Lawless, Jolley, P. R. Lawless, Webster, and Lally saw the latter being tackled on the line, and the next minute a dodgy run by Lally and smart pass to Thorniley- ended in the latter crossing the line. Exchange kicking by both sets of backs was next witnessed. and Lally and Webster had hard lines in not scoring. Potts and Davies showed up hereabouts, and Jolley made a grand run half the length of the field, but nothing resulted, and at the end of a pleasant but one-sided game, the home team ran out easy winners,the final score reading as follows :—Warrington, 1—.4---4; Tyldesl'ey, nil. Teams :—Warrington : Hamlet,, full back; P. R. Lawless, Potts, Jolley, and Websterthree- quarters ; J. Lawless and Lally half backs; Davies, Isherwood, A. Barnes, Creaghan. Mblyneux. Teare, Knowles, and Thorniley,forwards. Tyldesley : Gibbons. full back ; Taylor. Miller, and Allen, three quarters; Evans and Crippin, half backs ;. Smith, Mahon, Tinker, Wilson, Worthington, Duckworth .Roberts, Schofield, and Phillips, forwards.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
EASTE/AM TO RUNCORN. • A correspondent of the" Sunday Chronicle" thus re- ports:-

- With regard to the condition of the work at Eastham, some hundreds of men and any amount of steam, power are actually engaged in putting in the machinery to work the three sets of lock gates. Of these the storm gates of 80ft. and 30ft. locks are already swinging upon their hinges; the gates of the 50ft. loilks are now being fixed into place, and presently a handsome accumulator tower for the hydraulic machinery will rise above the structiver and be a feature in the landscape- The men tell me that the Eastham work will be finished for certain by May. Thus ends one of the mightiest mid most troublesome tasks on tin- undertaking. The Ellesmere Port, Pool Hall,. and Ince embankments are now having their inner slopes faced in, and begin to look a; neat as if they had beerepatted into shape with a gigantic butter-slice. The great syphons by which the river Gowy is made to pass below the bed of the canal have been bedded in puddle-wallS, and are now reported watertight, and sound as a bell. This, again, has been a fearsome task, no less than the diversion of a consider- able stream to a depth of torty feet into," the bowels of the land," and causing it to emerge again beyond the outer wall of the canal into the estuary of the Mersey. Through the Ince section almost to the centre of the Weaver Junction, the canal may be called complete, with the exception of the removal of contractor's plant and railway lines, and some little blasting of• red sandstone in one or two of the " boniest " parts of the bottom. With a few finishing touches in the shape of "dressing down," my informant, a ganger on the section, holds that the section will be completed. From the information I can gather, and from what I have seen, everything is going on well on nearly every part of the scheme. Floods and fog, the natural conco- mitants of wintry weather, have caused some little in- terruption in the work, but nothing more than might have been, expected, and there is no reason now to take a more despondent view of matters than at any previous period in the Ship Canal's history. Thereis a great deal of work to be done on the river wall extending across the junction of the Weaver, where enormous quantities of "spoil" will yet have to be dumped down before this link is completed. The same remark applies to the con- nections with the Bridgewater system and the concrete wall which passes under Runcorn Bridge. Liverpool has not yet syphoned its Vyrnwy water under the track of the canal and the river; in that notable scheme, in- deed, the Mersey city seems to have acquired a full-sized white elephant. The flood waters on the Latchford sec- tion have been got rid of,. and the great locks. with their fall of 16t. 6in., are fast approaching completion. A WORKMAN'S VIEW.
Recording the opinion of various workmen, the writer says:—

kr. Brown and his friends hold, then, that the Canal shares need never have fallen from their issue price if the company and the late contractor had not undertaken to do too mach all at once. Instead of breaking ground from one end of the track to the other, and "trying to do everything at once," they consider that the engineers would have been well advised to have limited their efforts in the first place to making that portion of the big ditch which extends from Warrington to the estuary. As everybody is aware, from the Latchford Locks, just above where the twenty-three acres of new Warrington docks are to be provided, there will be a clear run of a lockless canal to Eastham, up which at high tides the water from the estuary can flow without interruption. The 'Bridgewater Navigation joins the Ship Canal just below Runcorn ; and at the magnificent sluices now be- ing erected at the mouth of the Weaver the whole of the traffic from that'river will be tapped. Supposing, for argument's sake,that the Warrington docks had been first completed, turning that town into a great inland port, and that the whole energies and capital of the company had been directed to linking Warrington with the sea. by this time, my friends argue, the proprietors would have had some fourteen miles or so of a paying water- way, the income from the tolls on which would have been subsequently used in constructing the remaining portion of the great cutting to Manchester. No extra capital would have been needed, and the developement of trade and industry all along the lower portion of the waterway would be steadily going on while the upper half of the canal was a-making. So much for the work- men's theory, which, if it possesses the drawback of be- ing to some extent wisdom after the event, might yet be worth while considering at headquarters.

div.head: MANCHESTER AND SALFORD END
div.p: MANCHESTER AND SALFORD END

The Manchester and Salford Docks together include a water space of 114 acres, and this is altogether too much of a surface of Irwell liquor to be allowed to fester under a midsummer day. Dirty as the water is, the Salford Docks have a majestic appearance as they now -stand. Walking along the I,looft. of quay side to the far end of dock No. 1, we find there is no longer occasion to cross the stream to the next section by boat. Another light bridge links the Salford territory to the Irwell side of the cutting that has been made along the margin of Sir Humphrey de Trafford's park. We traverse this struc- ture, and.pass the sheds in which steam-saws and steam- hammers have been busy for the past ten months, in fashioning the great gates of greenheart laurel for the Mode Wheel Locks.

Over railway lines, vast aggregations of waste tubing, scrap iron, and mounds of wood chips and shavings enough to start the final conflagration withal, we stumble until we reach the dizzy verge of this grand ex- cavation. It is the westward apex of the great trian- gular basin that will confront the open ends of the Salford docks. A mass of earth and rocks still keeps out the spumey river, whose white foam looks so lusci- ous and smelts so loud. The cutting, which stretches away into misty perspective to our right, has been flooded, and pat contains some mud at the bottom, for the draining of which a giant pumping engine is kept going. The work is complete, however, and the recoil.- structed railway below us resembles nothing so much as a child's toy line dropped down upon a great billiard table.

A quarter of a mile to the right of us are the two Made Wheel Locks. The larger one, nearly completed, is 600 feet in length by 65 feet in width; the smaller, 450 feet by 45 feet. There are beyond them, on the further side, four sluices, each 30 feet wide, and the fall below this mass of masonry is to be 13 feet in depth of water. Over the whole business there swarms a clinging cloud of men and boys with spades and wheelbarrows, wrapped fitfully in the steam of various vaporous appliances, of cranes and concrete grinders and locomotives, from which there rims a drowsy hum as of a distant , hive of bees.

The rock wall on the left now borders the diverted stream. An immense earth-bank across the bed of the late unlamented Irwell still shuts in the Eccles cutting and joins another artificial dam that runs parallel with the water-course. But beneath Brind- ley's aqueduct for half a mile the old river has gone ; its bed is dry. It has been excavated to the full depth of the coming canal, an I is another crowded scene of busy labour.

Be it understood that the Ship Canal hereabout is by no means in the right line with the late river. It takes a path to the left, and as becomes the modern and im- proved notions of bringing down a stream in the way it should go, discards all the natural windings of the un- educated old Irwell. The new aqueduct will be about ten yards nearer Manchester than its predecessor, and it will have to be in working order before the old one can be removed, so that the cutting may go bravely forward. The swing bridge that shall replace the present roadway beyond the aqueduct has also to be built, and for this, again, the side work has already been commenced. Peo- ple who wish to see the last of the fatherof British meal aqueducts at Barton will do well to go.now,.for the day cometh, and that right soon, when it will be demolished, and tourists will be taking away bits of- its weather- beaten stones as relics of the engineering past.

div.head: MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND, THE
div.p: THE MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND, THE
LOAN.

The special Sub-Committee, consisting of the chair- men of the various committees of the City Council, ap- pointed to suggest a course of action to he taken by the Council with reference to the Ship Canal, met on Monday to prepare a plan to be submitted to the directors of the waterway. The deliberations lasted several hours.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

A youth named Thomas Wilson, of Bold-st., who was employed on the Ship Canal Works at Runcorn,,met with •a serious accident on Saturday afternoon. He was working at a crane, when he slipped and in endeavour- ing to save himself he placed his hand on a cogwheel. The limbwas terribly mutilated, and it is feared that a part of it will have to be amputated. THE CANAL AND THE MANCHESTER CORPORA- TION COMMITTEE'S REPORT.

The Special Committee appointed by the Manchester City Council on the 4th ult, to consider the application made by the Ship Canal Company for financial assist- ance, having completed their investigations, ?sued their report on Wednesday. It will be considered by the Council at a special meeting which has been called for Monday next. The recommendation of the Committee, briefly stated, is that the Council should consent to ren- der the Company the pecuniary assistance requisite to complete its undertaking (in accordance with the plan set forth in the report), and that a committee be ap- pointed to confer with the Company and arrange for a joint bill in Parliament. The Committee have been led to the conclusion that the Company's estimate of the cost of the works required to complete the canal is too low, and that it would not be prudent to estimate it at a less than £3,579,878, being an excess of £350,981 over the estimate made on behalf of the Company. The canal will probably take two years to complete, and therefore the estimate of general expenditure ought to be made to Ist March, 1893, in- stead of to 30th June, 1892. This makes it necessary to add to the amount under this head a sum of £97,120 for interest on debentures and general expenses. Further, it will be necessary to provide for the interest down to Ist March,lB93, upon sums which will have to be found to enable the Company to complete its works. One hun- dred thousand pounds may be taken as a fair estimate

for this purpose. The total effect of these corrections is to increase the previous estimate of the cost by £548,101, making the total amount necessary to be provided £2,457,491. Whilst expressing their belief that two and a half millions will he adequate, the Company are ad- vised that it would be prudent that the borrowing pow- ers to be sought by the C orporation in Parliament should be stated at the sum of three millions. The details of the arrangement by which this amount is to be raised will be found in the report. All sums advanced by the Cor- poration are to rank as a charge upon the undertaking next after the debentures at present authorised, but of course in priority to all the shares. The Committee ex- pressed their belief that the Company's difficulties are due to causes of a financial character, and not to any- thing which affects either the public utility of the under- taking or its probable earning capacity. This does not lessen the imperative need of the assistance asked for if the undertaking is to be saved from failure, but it leads the Committee to the belief that the required assistance can be given without serious risk of throwing any burden upon the ratepayers of Manchester. The Committee, however,take the opportunity of saying that" the Man- chester Corporation would be willing to receive intima- tions from other municipal corporationsor local authori- ties who desire to participate with Manchester in the financial assistance proposed to be rendered to the Ship Canal undertaking upon the basis of this report."

div.head: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.

Sir Henry Lawrence, of Belgard, county Dublin, has been selected as the Unionist candidate for the Heywood Division of Lancashire, and the Hon. Edward George Villiers Stanley, eldest son of Lord Stanley of Preston, as the Conservative candidate for the West Howhton Divisiou of Lancashire at the next general election.
SHIPPING DISA:STERS.
STRANDING OF A STEAMER.

A telegram from Lloyd's agent at Dunnet states that a steamer has gone ashore at Skarfskerry, Pentland Firth. There is no trace of her crew. The:vessel sank in deep water. The name washed ashore is Victoria. Nothing has been seen but spars, the ,cargo :washing ashore consisting of hides, 'hales, featheis, locust beans, partridges, &c. COLLISION BETWEEN TRAWLERS.—LOSS OF FIVE LIVES. _ _
Two Brixham trawlers collided off Start Point on Tues- day night. Both sank, and five of their crew were drowned.

div.head: MAYBRICK CASE.
div.p: THE MAYBRICK CASE.

There is reported to be every prospect of a re-opening of the Maybrick case, which caused such an agitation at the time of the trial 18 months ago. The Baroness von Rogues, Mrs. Maybrick's mother, who is in London, on Saturday had an interview in regard to the case with an influential personage. The baroness, who was accom- panied at the interview by her private solicitor, Mr. E. Pooley, of Sloane-st., is understood to be thoroughly satisfied with the reception which in this case was accorded to her advances on behalf of her daughter. She says that she has new evidence touching the use by Mrs. Maybrick of arsenic for her complexion. On Tuesday the Baroness visited Mrs. Maybrick at Woking, where she is a prisoner. Mrs. Maybrick, it is under- stood,is in moderately good healtn, and hopeful of being released, and emphatic in her declarations of innocence.

div.head: TH_E WHITECHAPEL MURDER. RELEASE OF SADLER.
div.p: TH_E WHITECHAPEL MURDER. RELEASE OF SADLER.

At the Thames Police Court on Tuesday, John Thomas. Sadler, who was charged with the murder of Frances Coles, at Swallow Gardens on the 13th ult., was, on the application of the Treasury, discharged from custody. THE SUDDEN DEATH OF A WITNESS.

At an inquest in London on Monday on the body of Charles Guiver, aged 34 years, lately acting as night watchman at a common lodging-house in White's-rovr,. Spitalfields, who died suddenly on Wednesday last, it was shown that death was due to apoplexy, accelerated' by excitement. The deceased was one of the principal witnesses in the inquiry into the circumstances attend- ing the murder of Frances Coles in Swallow-gardens,and' had suffered from pains in his head since he identified the body.
THE QUEEN AND THE EMPRESS -._ FREDERICK, _ _ _ _

The Queen held the first Drawing Reem of the season at Buckingham Palace on Wednesday, the Einpress Frederick, the Prince and Princess of Wales, and other members of the Royal Family being present. There were over 170 presentations. The Queen left Buckingham Palace on Thursday morn- ing with the Empress Frederick, Princess Beatrice, Ptin- cess Margaret of Prussia. and a limited suite, and drove to the Agricultural Hall, Islington, to visit the Worse Show. Crowds cheered her Majesty on the route. The Royal visitors were received at the Agricultural Hall by the Prince of Wales, the Duke of Portland, the Duke of Richmond, Lord Tredegar, and the Earl of Ravenswortit. Their Imperial and Royal Majesties occupied the Royal box, and witnessed the special entertainment.

div.head: SCOTCH DIVORCE ACTION.
div.p: THE SCOTCH DIVORCE ACTION.
JUDGMENT.
WARRINGTON- v.. TYLDES.L.

With three short of their regular back players, the Warringtonians made the journey to Tyldesley on Satur- day, with anything but a bright prospect of lowering the colours of the ex-holders of the West Lancashire Cup. Singular to state, the Warringtonians- have been, placed in the same predicament before, as witness their matches against Kendal Hornets and Barrow, when, with appar- ently weak teams, they made sorry examples of their opponents. Such was the case on Saturday, and al- though the score was but a goal and four minors to one minor in favour of Warrington, it hardly formsa proper idea as to the state of the game. Tyliesley were. with- out Berry, their champion half back,. who was, assisting Lancashire to defeat Cumberland,

Shaw kicked off, and the preliminaries resting between Sampson and the home centre, play at the conclusion of the exchange was found at half way. From. the first iscrimmage formed Bate and Mather passed well, and the loyal being kept travelliug, the homesters failed in their efforts to stave off the attack, and. Daniels being the final recipient, he made a dart for the line, and after a fine run grounded near the posts, Evans placing a goal. The game was not yet two minutes old ;, and this unex- pected success inspired the visitors with every confidence and their combined play again placed them on the ag- gressive. Cook, the ex-Salford-Swinton three-quarters, was at fault with a couple of kicks, and Daniels, Evans, and Jolley each had narrow shaves for scores in very short time. Tyldesley defended well,. but failed to pass their quarter flag, and a neat kick by Bate was well res- ponded to by Derbyshire. Woodward and Hampson rushed the leather to neutral ground,. but a movement startedby Randles and Ashton soon had the oval back. Sanipson took play under the posts,, but Tyldesley re- sorting to heavy forward work,, of which they were no mean exponents, soon had the leather out of dan- ger, Boscow speedily directing them back to their original position. Loose play on the home line resulted in Fearnley kicking dead. The brothers Turner, Jolley, and Donohue were prominent in the drop out, and although a penalty kick fell to the credit of the Tyldesley men,, Boscow was safe as usual, and the attempt to invade was frustrated. A second effort was made by the homesters, this time with success, and for the first time they reached the Warring- ton 25, but Evans getting the better of Shaw, raced awayat top speed,though being. hemmed in near the cor- ner flag, he effected a long pass,fully thirty yards,which was unfortunately knocked on, and a comparatively easy chance missed. This was certainly hard luck for the visitors, but, nothing daunted, they played with Burl prising vigour, till, Tyldesley,. being favoured with a slice of luck, got the oval to Boscow, who replied in masterly style. Play was at the home quarters, and Berry, Fair. Turner, Jolley, and Sampson shared in a bout of passing, the ball falling into the hands of Derby- shire, who was safely held under the posts. A pass tc Sampson afforded him a chance to show his dropping capabilities, but his kick was touched in its transit, and Mather gained an apparently fair try, but it did not meet with the favour of Mr. Williamson. Again lyldes- ley rushed the oval out of danger, and Berry, Ashton, and Lloyd, by hard work in the pack, and the Turners, Jolley, Daniels, and Evans in the loose, soon had the ball again on the home lines, Sampson forcing a second minor. Daniels met the drop out in fine style, but Shaw with a fine kick, and Battersby and Smith, raised the hopes of their supporters, but these calculations were soon upset when Evans, taking a pass intended for Shaw, ran and kicked well into the home 25. Tyldesley would not be denied, and another rush took play near the Warrington line, when half time was called with the score as—Warrington, 1-0-2; Tyldesley, 0-0-0. Daniels was awarded a free kick for obstruction. A grand spell Of exchange kicking was here witnessed, and at its con- clusion Shaw endeavoured to force his way through the opposing defence without success, and Evans again in- tercepting a passing movement, punted finely to Fearn- lev, who mulled, but Bandies failed to utilize the fine chance offered him. Frank Turner put in a fine dribble, and collared Derbyshire under the posts. Shaw and the home half backs kicked judiciously, and although Sam- son was called upon lieplayed with every confidence, and rounded his men finely,pu nti ng to near the halfway. Shaw and Evans next exchanged kicks, and some smart play by Mather, Bate, and Daniels once more found Tyldesley being pressed. A fine run by Jolley was the next item, but a kick by Fearnley was taken up by Hanson and a minor scored. Hanson again put in a fine run, but the tackling was safe, and although play was close to the line, Mather, Evans, and Boscow defended admirably. The attack was only of short duration, for a fine combi- nation of the visiting forwards led up to Daniels and Evans, taking play beyond the half way flag. Fully a dozen exchanges were next witnessed, and play was Con- fined to the home 25. Randles made his mark, and War- ' rington now put on the pressure in earnest. Evans was responsible for at least half a dozen fine runs which were wanting in their final essays. Donohue was to the fore a few minutes from the closet, whilst Randles dropped at goal when a try was at his mercy. Cook made a fine run on behalf of the homesters, but BOSCOW pulled him up, and the game terminated as Warrington, 1-0-4; Tyldesley, 0-0-1. Teams :—Warrington : Boscow, back ; Sampson,

Lord Wellwood. in the Court of Session, Edinburgh, on Wednesday, delivered judgment in the action brought by Mr. A. L. Brown, M.P., for the Border Burghs, against his wife and William Shiels, a traveller. for divorce... is Lordship, after reviewing the evidence, granted' a divorce, with expenses against the co-respondent,„and giving the petitioner the custody of the children. Efis 14orsishin aid, he did not entertain any, doubt that peti- boner had proved his case. He had arrived at this con- clusion somewhat reluctantly, because from the evidence of the respondent and her manner in the box he was, in- clined to believe that she now regretted the misconduct of which she had been guilty. The conduct of them- respondent had been dishonourable and heartless in the extreme, and his evidence, which his lordship disbelieved had added to his offence by his insinuations that peti- tioner was guilty of cruelty to his wife, for whieh charge there was not the slightest ground in the evidence.

div.head: CABINET AND THE LABOUR COMMISSION.
div.p: THE CABINET AND THE LABOUR COMMISSION.

The Cabinet has aPpointed a Committee of its body to study the question of the reference to the ROyal Com- mission on Labour. The Committee, consisting of Mr. W. H. Smith, Mr Goschen, Mr. Ritchie, and, Mr: Mat- thews, held a long sitting on Monday in Downing-st.,and will report immediately to the Cabinet upon the terms of reference and the formation of the Royal Commission. It is rumoured that in case Mr. Goschen's duties should pre- vent his accepting the chairmanship, Mr. Ritchie. would take the post, Lord Dunraven being vice-chairman. Mr. W. H. Smith, replying on Thursday to a,deputa- tion from the Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress, said he thought the claim for one-half of the membership was excessive. He admitted, how- ever, that there should be a, strong representation of labour, not altogether excluding what might be regarded as extreme views.
In a letter to the secretary, of a London labour organi- Ation, Sir John Gorst says he hopes that the Ruyal Com- mission on Capital and Labour will report within a year.

div.head: ASTON MANOR ELECTION.
div.p: THE ASTON MANOR ELECTION.

Mr. George Kynoek, M.P.. the Conservative member for Aston Manor, died at Johannesburg on. Saturday. Mr. Kvnoch, who was fifty-seven, years of age, was returned in 1886 in opposition to Mr.. Hugh Gilzean Reid by a majority of 782, and was at one time one of the largest manufacturers of ammunition, in the world, and fulfilled contracts for the home and nearly the whole of the foreign Governments. The Conservatives and 'Unionists are run ninz Captain Grice Hutchinson' of Upton-on-Severn, as their candidate in opposition to Mr. W. Phipson Beale, Q.C., the Liberal nominee. Captain Hutchinson issued his address to the electors on Monday night. He calls himself a progressive Conservative, a warm supporter of Lord Salisbury's Government and of Mr. Balfour's Irish policy, and while anxious to redress all Irish grievances, he is for maintaining the Union at all hazards.

The election campaign commenced in earnest on ,Thursday. Mr. Beale, the Gladstonian candidate, ad- dressed a meeting of workers- on Thursday night, and Captain Grice Hutchinson, the Unionist candidate, was also on the spot.

div.head: SHIPPING', TRADE AGITATION.
div.p: THE SHIPPING', TRADE AGITATION.

A circular has been issued to Liverpool dock labourers by Mr. J. H. Wilson, secretary of the Sailors and Fire- men's Union, instructing the officers of branches to take a ballot upon the question whether the men are prepared to vote for a general strike at an early date if the Ship- pidg Federation refuse to withdraw their mandate that all labourers employed by them, whether union men or not, must take the Federation ticket. The London Dock Labourers' Union has withdrawn from the Federation of Trade and Labour Unions, the dockers' leaders not concurring in the proposal to order a general strike. They consider that the points in dis- pute between the Shipping Federation and the Seamen and Firemen'b Union are so small that there is no reason for orderino,e a general cessation of work, and that a gen- eral resumption of work will pave the way to an ami- cable understanding being arrived at with the Federation. The points left for settlement are considered so trivial that a few minutes discussion would settle the matter. The Shipping Federation officers at Aberdeen had ob- tained 50 men from the South; but the Union have in- duced tialf to return home.

According to a Cardiff telegram, the negotiations be- tween Mr. Wilson, of the Seaman's Union,,and the local members of the Shipping Federation came to an abrupt conclusion on Thursday, without anything being ar- ranged.

div.head: TR:E. GAS APPLIANCE INDUSTRY IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: TR:E. GAS APPLIANCE INDUSTRY IN WARRINGTON.

Some time ago we gave an account of the forma- tion of the company of M essrs Unsworth and Richmond. Limited, to carry on and develop the business of gas engineers and appliance manufac- turers, established in Warrington by Mr. Unsworth (formerly with Messrs. T. Fletcher and Co.) The Company have now transferred their works from Scotland-road to much larger and more suitable premises•in Academy-street, formerly occupied by Messrs Collin and Son, builders. Entering these works through the large gateway—which, by the way. is lighted at night by an ornamental specimen. of Webb' s- high power lamps, for which the com- pany are the sole agents—we find that they com- prise a large square plot of land. A portion of the frontage to Academy-street is taken up with large and handsomely furnished offices and showrooms, and in the immediate background are various sheds for • blacksmiths' and tinning work. In the centre •is erected a large three-storied building, which is well-lighted and in every way suitable for the carrying on of the gas- stove business. The ground floor is divided into stockrooms for castings and a packing-room, where a platform is erected for the delivery of the goods straight on to the lurries in connection with the hoists-from the stock-room. Another portion is utilised for grinding and glazing castings, and for stocking same when finished. A portion of this floor is also partitioned off as a pattern shop, there being at the time of our visit a number of most in- teresting patterns in hand, of various kinds of stoves, and, in particular, of a large range suitable for hotel work, into which many real improvements have been introduced, both Mr. Unsworth and Mr. Richmond having given considerable thought to perfecting it. The first floor is a sight well worth seeing, full as it is with machinery in motion and busy workmen. On this floor light boiling burners and small stoves are put together, and tin goods, copper water heaters, and various wrought goods are manufactured. All these floors are heated ' throughout with steam, and this also applies to the splendid stockroom at the top of the building, in which some hundreds of stoves are being put in stock ready for the coming season. This stove room is connected with the packing room by a powerful hoist, and thus the necessity for ascending and descending stairs is obviated. At the far end of the works, we come to the foundry which extends on both sides of a very powerful cupola. The floor of the foundry is built upon iron girders, with cross pieces of iron filled in with concrete. Underneath are extensive store places for packing boxes, and then next follow sheds and ovens for japanning, and two large engines and boilers. An experimental room is being fitted up adjoining the show room and both of these places, it may be added, are got up in fine taste and with every convenience. What will, perhaps, interest the public of War- rington even more than a description of the works and buildings is the fact that Mr. Richmond a short time ago attended a meeting of the Warrington Gas Committee and laid before them various statistics from Carlisle, Blackburn, Morecambe, and other places, in favour of hiring out gas cooking and other stoves, and as a result of this the Committee have decided to let out cooking stoves on hire. This arrangement will be a great boon to gas con- sumers in the town, as the various pattern cookers, which are somewhat expensive, varying from £3 10s. to .E 9 each, can now be had on hire, as will be seen from our advertising columns for small sums per half year, costing just over 14. to 4d. per week, according to size. The summer days are now approaching,and as coal tires are often at such times a nuisance in the kitchen, no doubt many people would flint it desirable to take advantage of this arrangement between the Gas Committee and Messrs. Unsworth and Richmond for the hiring out of gas stoves. We also understand that there is an economy not only in fuel but also in the food cooked by gas,. The heat in the gas ranges being so uniform there is not so much loss of weight in cooking. Thia is amply proved by the fact that joints cooked by gas require no basting. Taking as an illustratikm a 101 b, joint of meat, it is said that cooked by coal' this loses 41bs. or 40dgs., leaving the joint when cooked Gibs., whereas the same joint cooked by gas would only lose 211bs. the gas cooked joint weighing 7flbs., the saving thus being 'Vbs. on a 10ib. joint. Taking this saving of meat alone into consideration, it would seem not to be unwise to at any rate try one of these cookers on hire.

div.head: BOOTLE- ROMANCE.
div.p: A BOOTLE- ROMANCE.
FOUND BY A PHOTOGRAPH.

The following article appeared in the" Liverpool Express" of Monday. Considerable stir was caused in aristocratic Bootle some eighteen or twenty months-ago. by the disappearance of a lady who is the daughter of a Warrington magistrate, and who at the time mentioned had been married for some years to a gentleman holding a responsible position in a Bootle banking concern. The lady in question is said to have possessed considerable personal at,. tractions,. and during her residence in the borough she managed to run rather heavily into debt. All remonstrances on the part of her husband were un- availing, and ultimately a notice appeared in a local paper to the effect that the gentleman would no longer be responsible for any debts incurred by his wife. Very soon after the lady disappeared, and 'every effort to trace her failed. The other day, how- ever, a Warrington gentleman, who had been ac- quainted with the missing lady, whilst gazing into the shop window of a Chester photographer saw in- side what he believed to be her photo. Ile made inquiries, and he was informed that the original of the photo was residing at a farm not far from,Ches- ter. The facts of the case are now in the, hands of the parties interested, and it is said that divorce proceedings are pending."
THE O'SHEA AND -WOOD WILL. CASE.

In the Probate and Divorce Divsion on Tuesday, Mr. Justice Jenne gave judgment in the application made to him in this suit It will be recollected that the will in dispute was that of Miss Anna Maria, Wood, late of Milani, under which Mrs. O'Shea,,the respondent in the case of O'Shea v. O'Shea and Parnell,. was benefited to the extent of nearly £200,000. The will was opposed by the brothers of the lady, Mr. Charles Wood and Sir Evelyn Wood, V.C.' on the ground that the will was not properly executed, that tffe deceased' was not of sound mind at the time of its execution, and that she did not know and approve of its contents. His Lordship, in giv- ing his judgment, pointed out that there were actually two applications to dispose of. The first was whether the plaintiff could produce the books, Szc.,,in question, they not being in her possession, but in the possession of Mr. Pvm. He was of opinion that the books were not under the control of Mrs. O'Shea, and therefore she could not produce them. The other application was that the alministrator pendente lite should have power to inspect the books. No precedent had been cited for such an order, and he therefore declined to make one. He there- fore refused both applications. As to costs, he thought the costs of both motions should be reserved, excepting the costs of the administrator.

div.p: GATHERING OF LIPTON'S EMPLOYES.

The annual social gathering of the employes of Mr. T. J. Lipton, the well-known provision merchant and tea planter, was held on February 24, in the Grand National Halls, Glasgow, over 2,000 being present. Mr. Lipton presided, and in his address gave several interesting par- ticulars of his extensive business. At the outset,he stated that the amount of business that was now being done was eight times more than it was four years ago, and to further indicate the rapid increase, recalled the fact that about fifteen years ago there was only one small shop in Stobcross-st., Glasgow, in which he discharged the duties of clerk, window dresser, salesman, and—when occasion required—light porter as well,and many a night he slept in the back shop. The staff numbered two, and he was one of them. Now they have above 100 establishments, and employ at home and abroad, over 5,000 hands. Hav- ing got shops in all the most important centres in Scot- land and England, they have recently increased their es- tablishments across the Channel, and have opened in the leading towns in Ireland with most conspicuous success; and he,as a native Irishman, mentioned this as the most gratifying circumstance in his whole business career. In regard to shortening the hours of employes, he said it had his very cordial support. His opinion of the remedy was to have a compulsory early closing law, including a weekly half-holiday, which is observed by many of his branches. He concluded a happy speech by giving some advice to his assistants. Thereafter a most enjoyable evening was spent.
THE TANNERS AND TRADES UNIONISM.

On Saturday night, a meeting .of the tanners of Warrington and district was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Sankey-st., for the purpose of hearing addresses from Mr. H. Preece, of London, secretary of the Amalgamated Leather Trades Union and - others, in support of the principles of trades union- ism. There was only a moderate attendance. Mr. W. Bullock, secretary of the Warrington United Trades Council presided. The CHAIRMAN opened the proceedings with some re- marks, and expressed his disappointment at the discour- aging smallness of the meeting.
-MI7. PREECE then delivered Ms address. He said when
be considered that there were a number of trades in Warrington that had felt the benefit of trades unionism, it was the more surprising to him, and it wasyeally.sad,

to see that the tanners of the town' were not alive tO their own interests, because if they had been they would have mustered that night a thousand strong. He hoped that the few present would act as missionaries to the absen- tees. The union in connection with the leather trades in Bermondsey, though it had existed only 16 months had accomplished a revolution there. The meeting would have a grand result if the men would only be true to them- selves. When the Manchester Ship Canal Was completed Warrington would occupy a position far greater than at present : it would grow apace, and the land ot Warring- ton would increase in value; and unless the tanners took steps to increase likewise their wages, they would find they were called upon to pay more for rent, and would be in a worse position than to-day. (Hear, hear.) He understood that they were at present working for 20 per cent, less wages than were paid in the trade at Bermondsey—and for 10 per cent, under the rate paid 10 miles away. That proved to him that the tanners of Warrington had been unmind- ful of tlieir own interests. In Warrington fines were in- ficted by the master tanners on the men for they knew not what, and if a man was away from his employment for a week he was fined 3s. 6d. per day for his absence, that is, the following week, supposinc, 30s. was due to him for that week, he was only paid' 9s. This was a shame and a scandal, and the workmen ought to rise against it. (Applause.) The men engaged under one firm in Warrington were receiving periodical bonuses, but if a man happened to lose two hours before breakfast the sum of 10td. was stopped off him, though the men only received to Li is. a week. Was that fair? (A voice: "Yes," and loud laughter.) It was from these fines that the bonuses came, and therefore they were fictitious bonuses. Nonunion men in Warrington bad reported these grievances to the Union, and yet would take no adequate steps for their own protection. The speaker detailed how the Union in Bermondsey had com- pelled the removal by one firm of a sweating, bullying foreman,and forced another firm there to pay 20 per cent. advance on the wages paid prior to the formation of the Union, and prevented therA from succeeding in an at- tempt to discontinue the advance. He had heard of the boycotting that existed in Warrington as regarded the men in connection with the Union, and the system adopted to prevent a man bettering his position because his employer did not wish him to leave. Shame that the men of Warrington should allow this state of things to exist. (Applause.) From the year 1800 to 1848 dur- ing which period Trades Unions had sunk almost out of existence, wages had been low, but from the renewal of the unions in 1848 they had steadily risen. Professor GIFFEN, in his statistics on the condition of the working classes, said that by the year 1884 an advance of 30 per cent. had been gained in wages generally, and in many instances 50 per cent. In the leather trade they had advanced 35 per cent. In 1871 the last rise took place in at trade in Bermondsey. No such rise took place in ' Warrington,but in 1878 and in 1886 there were reductions of 10 per cent, each time. Why? Because the Warring- ' ton men were not organized. They attempted some little white back to get the tanneries closed at one o'clock on Saturdays, but were defeated through the masters taking advantage of their disorganised condition. The union in Bermondsey a short time back compelled a firm , there working till four on Saturday y to close at one, and if the men who refused to work after one had been dis- missed there was not a man who would have taken the place of one of them. Last week there was a firm in Bermondsey working 62 hours per week. (" That's nowt.") He understood in Warrington it was naught, but they thought the contrary in Bermondsey, and in- tended to alter it. They had reduced the hours of other firms to 56 a week, without any reduction of wages. The prices of labour in the trade in Warrington were very low at present. nd. per hide for fleshing was the price in Bermondsey; only one firm there paid less, and the Union intervied to make them pay the 21(1., and did not think that enough. But the Warrington men thought they would do very well if they could get _2d., indeed they were content with ltd. The yard- men in Warrington thought if they were getting £i per week they did well, but in Bermondsey yard-men got 235. a week and were not satisfied with that, and next week every employer would receive from him a circqlar demanding an..advance of 30 percent. for these men, and 6d. per hour overtime, the number of hours per week not to exceed 56. If Bermondsey could demand such terms why not Warrington? ,(" Just so.") Many of the men had been prevented from attending the meeting being held in Warrington by having to work till nine or ten at night, enough to crush the life out of a man. The masses were being reduced to nothing more than wealth- Providing machines. But men were not intended to be this; they were intended to have mental culture and recreation, not to be the slaves and drudges they were to-day, with but a bare pittance to live upon. The Speaker concluded by: strongly urging upon the tanners of the district to join the local branch of the Union. (Applause.) Mr. MALRIN proposed the following resolution : "That this meeting of tanners employed in Warrington and district, having heard the views of the Secretary of the Amalgamated Leather Trades Union, are of opinion that the only way to protect ourselves is by strengthen- ing our branch, and calling upon all workers in the trade ojoin at once ; and hereby pledge themselves to do all in their power to further the cause." The cause the pro- Poser remarked was he supposed, unionism; and he expatiated on the advancedt had made of late years, and the power it now exercised,; and urged his fellow-work- men to give in their adhesion to it. Mr. WARING seconded the resolution. He remarked that the tanners of Warrington were behind even those of Runcorn, ip point of wages. He thought the meetings had made a gt od impression, a great many men having decided to join the Union. Seine men thought that as soon as they joined it they should have a ten per cent. rise; and because this could not be, would not join. But they wouldcnot get to the top of the tree in a minute. The speaker strongly advocated co-peration with the

Mr. J. H. DABORN, of London, supported the resolu- tion. He observed that there was an idea in Warrington that the men there could do better by themselves than in combination, and contended that experience proved this to be a very great mistake. He defended the principle of trades unionism on scriptural grounds, the rebellion of the Israelites against Pharoah he said being nothing but the first strike—against having to make bricks with- out straw. The freedom of the labourer to-day he declared was nothing but the freedom to starve. He thought some of the Warrington tanners had not much of the spirit of Englishmen' if they allowed employers to Stop 235. out of 30s.—(loud applause)—and if a man were discharged for refusing to submit to it they ought to throw down their tools and refuse to wont till he was reinstated. As soon as the local employers realised that the men were in combination and in earnest, they Would learn a lesson ; and a dark blot would be removed from the trade of Warrington. (Applause.) . The motion was put and unanimously carried. Mr. PREECE moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman. tie assarted that the Sweating Commission had refused to accept the report of Lord Dunraven mainly because it ebutained a clause declaring that the condition of Workmen was better and their wages were higher where- ever trades unions existed. , Mr. Memix seconded, and the vote was carried by ac- clamation and responded to. ,As the result of the meetings in the district about 20 Vditional men had, up to Saturday night, joined the Ivarrington branch of the Union, which must now num- °er about 300.

THE W'ARRINGTO_V EXAMINER SAYS : "THE MARMALADE TRADE.—The severe" " weather we have recently experienced in" "this quarter has extended as tar south as' "Seville. It is in the neighbourhood of" "Seville, that the oranges best suited for" " marmalade making are grown. A recent" " frost (the like of which has not been ex-" " perienced for ten years), has played havoc" 'with the fruit, and, although though the" "full extent of the damage is not yet" " known, it is believed that fully one half" " the orange crop has been destroyed." "Luckily one shipment has been made to" " Liverpool before the disaster occurred, by" "SS " Zurburan," which has just arrived." "The Liverpool firm of W. H. Flett." "Limited, have been fArtunate enough to" "have a large consignment on Board this" "vessel, but they do not anticipate getting" "nearly sufficient to meet the demand for" "their well known marmalade, the sale of" "which is fast increasing."

QUESTIONS FOR "PLUTO."

Sir,—Your correspondent " Pluto " says that the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes "and that other genius of the same kidney, W. H. Stead, raised a moral smell around Par- nell" with the result that "Parnell is to-day the strongest man in the whole Irish Party." I ask your correspon- dent two questions-1. How can a " smell " (moral or otherwise) make a man strong (except in the sense of malodorous) ? 2. Whether the smell proceeded from Mr. Parnell or his accuser? I await your correspondent's reply with some curiosity.—Yours, &c.,

div.p: MASTER OF ARTS.
MINERS AND THE EIGHT HOURS MOVE- MENT.

Sir,—! have good reason to be satisfied with the com- ments and criticism upon my letters on the Eight Hours Movement, and none have been more fair and courteous than those which have appeared in your columns. Yielding to a widely expressed desire, I have collected and published my letters in pamphlet form, and that pamphlet will be sent to any applicant on payment of postage, one penny. My previous pamphlet on "Mine rents and mineral Royalties" has been and is being widely read and fairly considered ; I only ask similar consideration for my views on the Eight Hours Move- ment.—Yours, King-st., Wigan, 4th March, 1891.
C. M. PERCY
