" GAS " rEßsus COMMON-SENSE.

Sir,—The title of "Gas v. Common-sense" under -which " Pluto " writes in your last issue, is appropriate indeed; for a more perfect exhibition of the " Gas," and a more marked absence of the "Common-sense "- than distinguishes his letter would be hard to imagine. What truer thing could Rev. H. P. Hughes (whom '".Pluto "so viciously attacks) say, than "a Christian who voted for a brewer at an election was a Christian humbug ?"1 It must be admitted by all, that one of thu greatest barriers to the spread cf Christianity is that ex- cessive sale of" drink" by which the brewer prospers ; but theh2easures which are absolutely necessary in order to blot out the drink traffic (and thus save millions from its awful .curse) mean to the brewer financial ruin. Is he likely then in Parliament to further such measures? and if not, where's the Christian principle in one who votes for him?

But" Pluto "evidently regards is grossly inconsistent one who, while holding the opinion of Mr. Hughes as to the support of a brewer's political candidature, " is not above asking a brewer's help for a mission cause." The inconsistency I fail to see. Why should not the gains of the brewer, heaped up by the ruin of thousands, be used in raising again those fallen ones? By no means vote for a man whose best financial interests mean the ruin of happy homes, the blighting of highest hopes, and the loss of human souls ; but if from such a man's store, ill- gotten though it be, you can beg the means to reform one home, to fill one life with a new hope, or to save one soul, then for the sake of humanity, and for the sake of 'God, do it. The remainder of " Pluto's " letter is based on the assumptions (1) that Hr, Hughe's "words have done more mischief to any couse he advocates than aught else " (2) that "Parnell is to-day the strongest man in the whole Irish party." Whether such assumptions are well- founded I ask any man who reads, observes, and thinks, ta judge for himself.—l remain, yours &c, VERITAS, March 3rd, 1891.

div.head: COMMONSENSE V. "PLUTO."
div.p: COMMONSENSE V. "PLUTO."

Sir,—What on earth is the matter with my old friend? I fear his liver is out of sorts, or he would hever have written such an effusion as his last, of which lam cer- tain on calmer reflection, he must be utterly ashamed. Lel my friend give a single instance where the Rev. H. P. Hughes has solicited or obtained a subscription, how- ever small, from any brewer or publican, and then he may justly pour out upon him the full stream of his. wrath. But " Pluto "knows perfectly well that neither Mr. Hughes nor any other consistent man ever solicits aid for Christian work from so tainted a source, and Wes-

_ .-.leyan ministers of all men, insomuch as they are faithful , to the advice of the great founder cf their religious organ- isation will not forget in the centenary proceedings now pending, John Wesley's scathing denunciations of the ! " trade " and those who batten upon its ill-gotten gains. Y.: friend says further that the brewers are thankful •itil,t.-Mividenee has given them this "fulminating par.

son." Well ; we teetotallers are certainly grateful for I such a man, and I do not hesitate to say that given twenty sulh men, and we should have such a revulsion of feeling in regard to the drink traffic, created within the next few years as would certainly lead to the extinc- tion of at least half the licensed pest-houses which now exist. My friend must surely have drawn his inspiration from a very " mixed " source, or he would never have put Stead and Parnell, Booth and Hughes, all into the same epistle. I must beg to differ with him also in his opinion of Mr. Stead's action in regard to Parnell, and its results. Parnell, is to-day—spite of "Pluto's "assertion— of next to no account. True, he is making a gieat noise and attracting to himself all the worst element in Irish politics, but I venture to assert that Parnell dare not face an Irish audience in England, and like the Liberal Unionists, he knows perfectly well that the next General Election will give him his quietus. • "Pluto "talks about bigotry—did ever anyone write a more bigoted and intolemntletter than his last effusion? Nothing but crass ignorance and wilful blindness can account for such an exhibition of folly and bad temper. He says we don't want "self-constituted morality leaders." No sir, but we do want morality, and when " Pluto " has inown us how much the brewers and pub- licans have done for the moral and social improve- ment of the people of this country, then will be his time for criticising the actions of those whose only object is to lift up the people whose moral and physical degradation has been compassed by " Pluto's " clients. "The Trade" is damned and doomed, and all the raving and anathemas of all the " Plutos "will not save it.—Yours truly, FELIX. March 2nd, 1891.

div.head: ALLEGED POLLUTION OF KECKWICK BROOK.
div.p: ALLEGED POLLUTION OF KECKWICK BROOK.

Sir,—l notice in the report of the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, as published in your issue of the 14th ulto., that Messrs. Aaron and Whitlow have again been to the fore on the above-named subject. I often wonder why Mr. Earp does not reply to some of their charges, but I suppose he is like most other men who have to get their living by their brains,and has not the time to waste in refuting such clap-trap, or pro- bably he does not think it worth his while. However, when erroneous statements are made which are calculated to 'mislead the public, and cause them to form wrong . opinions, I think it is time some one spoke. _ _

Mr. Whitlow says he has had to change his mode of farming as his cattle would-not drink the water from this brook. Now, this is really very sad. I have known Mr. Whitlow ever since he came to live in the neighbourhood, and to my knowledge he has never had more than two cows, and these, I believe, have now been reduced to one cow and a calf; so the change Mr. Whitlow so much de- plores, has not been a very great one. Then again, Mr. Weir says his father and son have lost a number of cows in consequence of their having drunk the water from this brook. How does Mr. Whitlow re- concile this with his statement that his cattle would not drink the water? How he could get up and make such a statement as he did, and before a numberof gentlemen who were fully aware of all the circumstances, passes my understanding. I have not a report of the proceedings of the inquiry which was held sometime ago, but so far as I can re- member there were one or two facts brought out which, I think, go a long way towards explaining the silence of the Local Government Board (which I take to mean that the matter should be quietly shelved as there is no case against Messrs. Earp and Company). I. It was admitted' by one of the sitnesses (Mr. Weir) that the brook was as bad, if not worse, 25 years ago. 11. The Sanitary In- spector acknowledged that a quantity, of sewage was drained into Preston Brook, the water from which joins the water from Messrs. Earp's tannery and the two form the Keckwick Brook. 111. Mr. Earp conclusively, proved from the very analyis this wise authority pro- duced to strengthen their case, as they thought, that the water in Preston Brook was charged with matter detri- mental to health from 5 to 10 times as strong as the water that ran from the tannery. Now with these facts before the Local Government Board, what will be the result of the exuberant verbosity of Mr. Aaron and the bombastic attitude of Mr. Whitlow ? Why we shall have an elabo- rate sewage scheme which will involve the ratepayeks and property owners in a heavy expenditure; and all the outcome of the needless outcry of these two mal-contents. But no doubt the landlords and ratepayres in this town- ship will take due note of the action of their representa- tive on this Urban Sanitary Authority, and when .the time comes round, as it very soon will, for his re-election they will see that a fit and proper person is returned to look after the affairs and interests of this district.— Yours respectfully,
"RATEPAYER."
TIIE WARRINGTON MAGISTRATES AND THE
BIRCH ROD.

Sir,—There was reported in your paper a few weeks ago a case in which a man named Dunbobbin was charged with not sending his son regularly to school, and in which the magistrates, though imposing no penalty on the father, ordered the lad to be chastised with the birch rod.

Now, sir, considering that it was not the boy, but his parent who seas summoned before the Bench, this sen- tence on their part was an undue and unlawful exercise of authority-. There being no charge against that boy, no matter what the moral justice of the punishment might be, he was legally innocent, and that a severe physical castigation should be inflicted upon an un- charged, untried citizen, though a poor boy, whose in- dividual rights are as sacred as those of the wealthiest adult, seems to in,e a miscarriage of justice that ought not to pass uncommented upon. Even supposing the father had requested that the punishment should be in- flicted it would not be legal; and the practice on the part of magistrates of making themselves tile executants of the parents' will in this regpe-it is one, that on moral and social grounds, ought to be discouraged, as it would be open to grave abuses. I have looked carefully through the Education Act of 1870, and I defy anyone to find therein any authority whatever for the imposition, under any circumstances, of a penalty on a boy whose parent is charged with not sending him to school. Since the child is not charged in such cases any misconduct on his part, in the way of playing the truant, or otherwise, leading to his absence from school, is a private offence so far as the Bench are concerned; and the parent has no more right to bring him to a police court to be birched for that offence than he would have to bring him to be thug punished for swearing or telling a lie at home. We all know what an outcry was created by the recent discovery of the exis- tence in London of a private establishment to which parents were in the habit of sending unmanageable chit- dr,:n to be flogged. I say the unauthorised conversion of poh stations into flogging institutions for the con- y is an evil that ought magistrates, and school authorities ought no more to be tolerated in our midst than the vernence ence of such an anachronism as pri- vate whipping-house the class I have nr,n i t'oned. those individuals who are e.XI; siiion of such punishment g o: quite taemcobnyvi no convinced means tohneei m o. poe as birching is likely to be productlYe of good results. Public opinion has long since condemnz.'d as iniquitous the practice of such modes of disciplito in private schools; and certainly no one has dared to attempt the introduction of them into our Board schools. John Locke says—" Those children who have been chastised the most seldom make the best men," and Mr. Rogers, chaplain of the Pentonville prison, declares that "those juvenile criminals who have been whipped are those who most frequently return to prison." Certainly the birch- ing does not seem to have produced much impression upon the boy Dunbobbin. for since he suffered it his father has again been brought up and dealt with on oc- count of the youth's continued absences from school. But this is not to the point on which I am urging. I contend that the magistrates haveno right to impose the punishment of birching upon any boy whose parent may be summoned on account of his irregular attend- ance at school ; and the boy Dunbobbin would have a clear right of action for assault and illegal detention against those who birched him, and for the aiding and abetting of these offences against the magistrates who ordered'the punishment. I do not deny that the Bench— for unpaid justices are by no means impressive examples of legal erudition—probably, confusing moral with legal issues and what they could do in the case of convicted young thieves with what they could do in the case Pf a boy convicted of and charged with nothing, imagined that they were doing perfectly right in sentencing him as they did. I dare say they were convinced that it was more the fault of the boy than of the father that he did not attend school; and probably in any case the lad, morally speaking, only got substantial justice. But that Ignorance is no excuse for a breach of the law is a maxim often quoted by the magistrates, and therefore they must excuse me forgiving it an introversive applica- tion to themselves.

I have charitably allowed them above the alternative of ignorance as an excuse for their action. But there are certain other phases of the procedure of the War- rington magistrates as to which I shouldnot be inclined to make this concession. These I shall probably indicate in a future letter, and in easel do so I propose to deduce from the considerations in it, and my present letter, the moral that Warrington would be consulting its true interests by following the example of some adjacant towns, and having -a stipendiary magistrate.—Yours truly,
MANLIUS
THE AUTHORSHIP OF THE GOSPELS.

Sir,—Mr. Dignum characterises my last letter as an extraordinary effusion, and my argument re Professor Beet's statement as labyrinthine logic, and be says I am evidently -not acquainted with the best current literature on this subject. Well, I dare say my last letter would appear to be extraordinary to those NOV) had only read one side of this subject. What I said then I repeat now, that the Christian Fathers and early Christian literature can be made to prove anything.

First of all, though, let me go back to Professor Beet. Now, Mr. Dignum's manner of treating the Professor's statement is, i fear, much on a par with his manner of treating the other writers with whose works he professes to have such a profound acquaintance. Professor Beet makes a distinct and definite claim on behalf of the Epistles of St. Paul being the actual writings of the great apostle. He says they were accepted as genuine through- out the Roman Empire. But the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles, he admits, were anor4,mous, since the names attached to them do but embody a very ancient tradition. And yet in the face of this very clear statement—than which surely nothing can be clearer—my friend maintains that the Gospels were written by those whose names are attached to them; that, although anonymous, it was well known who wrote them. I could understand my friend better if he took up a position against the Professor. But no, he pretends to agree with him, and yet puts an inter- pretation upon his words absolutely opposed to that which they plainly and unmistakably convey. My friend makes a great parade of authorities.' Per- haps he will pardon my suggesting one or two additions to them :—Dr. Martineau, Dr. Abbott, and J. Estlin Car- penter. These are writers of the very highest position, and their writings are amongst the most recent of any on the authorship of the Gospels. In their works, Mr. Dignum will find statements very far removed from those of Drs. Westcott and Lightfoot. Dr. Abbott wrote the article on the Gospels in the "Encyclopedia Brit- annica." In t this article the authorship is all through treated as a tradition, and this article is my authority for the statement that the disciples, with the exception of Matthew,as pointed out by Mr. Dignum—were unable to write. Dr. Abbott repudiates the idea that God specially endowed them with ability to write. Dr. Martineau in his work just published,'" The Seat of Authority in Religion" also affirms the authorship of the Gospels to be a mere tradition, and says they are, "in spite of their traditional titles, practically anony- mous. They offer us no personal warrant for the accur- acy of their contents; and we are left to find out for ourselves the probable story of their origin, and the value of their materials. This in itself is surely a start- ling fact, utterly fatal to the claim of infallible authority constantly set up on behalf of Holy Writ. How is it possible to prove a divine right to be believed respecting a book that comes out of the dark, with no competent ' witness to vouch for it, and no self-confession of the hand that wrote it? On what ground can we attach a superhuman weight to the testimony of a masked and veiled witness, who does not even tell his name, or say how near he stands to the things which he relates? The evidence which he gives may have more or less of credibility, according to its degree of self-consistency, of verisimilitude, of apparent originality, and of agr9e- ment with parallel reports; but it can never acquire personal authority, or rise above the level of current tradition." J. Estlin Carpenter also expresses the opinion that the Gospels were nct written by those whose names are at- tached to them. He says that they were a tradition, and that the Disciples and Apostles were preachers, not writers. "Besides," he says, "it was the method of the times to pass on by memory the stores of accumulated learning ; and the Rabbis, who had piled up a mountain of oral law beside the Pentateuch, were in the highest degree averse to the idea of arranging it in literary form. Commit nothing to writing, was a well-known maxim of the schools." "The Christian tradition was no fixed

deposit, no rigid and unalterable form. It passed from mouth to mouth. Those who received and propagated it were gathered from the harbours,the market-place, the shop, and there was no guarantee that nothing should be added, changed, or dropped upon the way." My friend appears to attach great importance to the opinions of Ernest Renan, and it is quite touching to see the affection he lavishes on this "most cons ummate sceptic." Ernest Renan, the ablest of French sceptics,in his work "The Life of Jesus," admits the four Gospels to be "serious documents ".; and, as Renan " has spent al- most his life in the examination and sifting of ancient - documents," Mr. Dignum is accordingly properly grateful to him for this admission. Has it never struck my friend that it is, to say the least of it, a curious and significant circumstance that Renan should have "spent almost his life in the examination and sifting of ancient documents," that he should be an able and learned man in all matters pertaining to religious history and religious literature, and yet be "a most consummate sceptic " ? When writ- ing his " Life'of Jesus," he went to Palestine and visited ' all the scenes of interest connected with the life of Christ, and sought for documents, traditions, and everything else likely tc., cast any light on the subject of his boek,and yet he remained a "most consummate sceptic." Accor- ding to Mr.Dignum, he admits the Gospels to be "serious documents," and yet rejects everything of a miraculous nature in their contents! Perhaps Mr. Dignum will ex- plain. May I mention one more case in point? Professor Huxley has given years of consideration to these matters. Without a doubt he is an able and learned man. He commenced life as a believer, and now, when his head is white with the snows of age, but whilst his mental powers still retain all their pristine force and vigour, he is a sceptic, or, as he prefers to call Dimself, an AgniAtfic-. - Again, perhaps Mr. Dignum will explain. 'My friend gives a quotation from Mosheim—or what purports to be a quotation. If it is really a quota- tion, then his copy of Mosheim must differ somewhat from mine. The passage in my copy differs consider- ably from the one he gives. However, I will pass that by, and content myself with giving other quota- tions to prove inT statements. In vol. 1., page 84, Mosheinv tells us that in the first Century "Chris- tians adopted that absurd and corrupt custom amongst the Jews, of darkening the plain words of the Holy Scripture by insipid and forced allegories, and of draw- ing them violently from their proper and natural signifi- cation, in order to extort from them certain mysterious and hidden significations." Again, on page 87, he says, "The lives and manners of the Christians in this century [the first] are highly celebrated by most authors, and recommended to succeeding generations as unspotted models of piety and virtue. But many run into extremes upon this head, and estimating the lives and manners of all by illustrious examples of some eminent saints, or the , Sublime precepts and exhortations of certain, pious doc- tots, fondly imagine, that every appearance of vice and disorder was banished from the first Christian societies. The greatest part of those authors who have written concerning the innocence and sanctity of the primitive Christians, have fallen into this agreeable error. And a grcss error indeed it is, as the strongest testimonies too abundantly prove." In their controversies with Pagan and Jewish writers the Christian Fathers employed all the arts of sophistry and dissimulation to gain their points. Their object was victory not truth. Of this we have abundant prof in the writings of Moslieim, and the later authors whom I have mentioned. For a vivid picture of life amongst the earlier Christians let any one read the late Charles Kingsley's " Hypatia," not forgetting the preface. Mr. Dignum says that the story of the books jumping on the Communion table is an old wives' fable, and Mr. Jolley says it is as silly as it is untrue. I hope neither of these gentlemen snspect me of believing that thebooks did anything of the kind. And yet. is the story one whit more ridiculous than scores of others that are told in the Catholic Church, or in the Bible itself? Is it one whit more absurd than the story of Jonah and the • whale, or than many other stories equally incredible? I I have already exceeded the limits of space allowed by you, and so cannot in nay present letter deal with Irenreus, Papias, and the others whom Mr. Dignum mentions. With your permission, Mr. Editor. I will do so next week. In conclusion let me say that I think Mr.l Dignum will best consult his own dignity by refraining from the toneof self-conscious superiority assumed by him in his two last letters. I am not surprised when I meet with this in a really learned young man like Mr. A. J. Jolter ; but I certainly did not expect it from my friend Mr. Dignum whom I respect and admire very much,and for whom I entertain the kindest possible feelings. Let me assure him that I shall not require twelve months' close study to enable me to find him a few desperately hard nuts to crack touching the authorship of the Gos- pels. All knowledge on these subjects is not enshrined in the writings of Drs. Westcott and Lightfoot, nor is it even to be found in the person of Mr. Dignum. He need not for the present get hysterical about either the " im- pregnable rock "or the everlasting hills.—Yours truly, JOHN GANDY.

div.head: TILE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 7, 1891.
div.p: TILE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 7, 1891.
THE DUO D'ORLEANS.

Apart from his being the eldest son of the Comte de Paris, we only know of one thing which gives Louis Philipe Robert, Duc d'Orleans, any claim to distinction, and that is the gallant, or foolish— according to the view that is aken ot it—escapade of which le was the hero at the begin- ing of last year. In defiance

nibits the heads and the direct heirs of reigning Houses, from residing on French territory the Due went to Paris in the beginning of February last year, . and, going to a recruiting officer, stated who he was, and that, having just attained his majority, his name might be inscribed on the list of cons,3ripts, as he wished to serve his three years like an ordinary citizen. His presence being an offence, he was arrested on the 7th of February, ,taken to the Prefecture of Police, and afterwaris conveyed to the Conciergerie. He was brought to trial on the 12th of February, before thel Bth Chamber of Police Correctionelle, and sentenced to two years' imprisonment. On the 24th of the month he was removed from the Conciergerie in Paris to Clairvaux Prison, near Bar-sur-Aube. His imprisonment, however, did not last quite four months. A presidential decree of pardon arrived on the 3rd of June, and he was released from Clair- vaux, taken to the station to meet the evening train from Paris,and escorted to the Swiss frontier. From Bale he proceeded to Brussels, and thence to Eng- land, and thus harmlessly ended his little adven- ture.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse yesterday morning_ The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided. and there were also:present Messrs. W. Long, W. Houghton, Ifeaton, Swinton, Hnmphreys, Smitb,J. Houghton, Kilshall ;S. Sutton '(clerk) W. Owen (surveyor), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and Mr. F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector.) . A HEALTHY DISTRICT.—From the Medical Officer's re- port it appeared that during the past month there had been 36 births and 12 deaths. The death-rate was equal to 8-5 per 1,000, as against 10-2 during the last three months, and 34-8 in the corresponding month cif last year. The Chairman remarked upon thelow death-rate for the last month, which was, he said, about the same as that of Nantwich, which was being; quoted as having a particularly low death-rate.—Mr. J. C. SUTTON pointed out that in the county rates for 1889, the authority's returns stood third in the point of healthfulness.—Dr. SEPHTON said that they should also stand fairly well for ' Fast year. TfiE LIGHTING OF LATCHFORD.—Ther CLERK_ said, with regard to this subject, that he was riot yet in possession of the price which the Gas Committee of the Corporation would charge per lamp,but he had been told unofficially, that the charge would be £3 per lamp, which was 6s.per lamp more than was charged for the lamps in Liverpool- road.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON spoke in favour of again de- ferring the subject. The light nights were approaching, and no harm would be done byanother postponement.— Mr. J. C. SUTTON was also in favour of a postponement until the Gas Committee, which he had spoken to on the subject, hadcome to a decision.—The subject was accor- dingly postponed. NEW Housgs.—The Surveyor reported that plans had been submitted for two cottages, at Latchford, by Mr. John Hayes ; and two houses atPadgate, by Mr. Thomas Antrobus.—The report was confirmed.

The " Star " commenting on the return says : The worst monopolists live in the country districts, where in old times complacent Tory magistrates were only too ready to encourage Tory brewers, by multiply- in.. public-houses which could be used with telling effect ae'election times. In Lancashire and Cheshire, the great brewing firm of Greenall hold five hundred and thirty- eight full licenses. In the manufacturing town of St. Helens, where much beer is required to wash down the chemical fumes, Messrs. Greenall possess no fewer than one hundred and twenty-six licenses, most of which must have been granted by an admiring magistracy in recent years, inasmuch as St. Helens is a very new town. Warrington, close by, has sixty houses belong- ing to the same firm, and no wonder that it grate- fully returned its big brewer to Parliament, where- by he obtained a baronetcy, and built, we think, the usual church. Liverpool is a hard-drinking seaport, and there the firm of Peter Walker and Co. own one hundred .andlorty-three tied houses, the licenses of which, con- ferred in perpetuity as the Government proposed, would no doubt make a useful present. The big Liverpool brewer has diverged from the usual round of church building by building a picture gallery, and has earned a somewhat better right to his baronetcy than is usual with his class. Birmingham is too independent a town to be dominated by thepeople who make its drink ' • but the Holt Brewery Company possess one hundred and fifty-five tied houses, while no less than one hundred and fifty-nine are registered as the property of Sir Alfred Sherlock Gooch. Blackburn has one hundred and thirty- two tied houses belonging to Daniel Thwaites and Co. It is needless to say that Thwaites for Blackburn has been a great electioneering cry. Poor Thwaites, however, went out before the day of baronetcies arrived.

div.head: TWO HOUSES ON FIRE AT LATCHFORD,
div.p: TWO HOUSES ON FIRE AT LATCHFORD,

About half-past ten o'clock on Tuesday morning, the fire bell at Warrington rang Out its loud alarm, and the news soon circulated that the cause was the outbreak of a fire in Wash-lane, Latchford. On the fire brigade reaching the spot,, about eleven o'clock, two thatched cottages and a stable and coach house adjoining them were in flames, th 3 blaze, indeed, being so extensive that it was commonly remarked that there had seldom been a bigger one in Warrington. The property adjoins the burial ground of Christ Church, patt of the wall of that ground forming one of the walls of the coach- house, and belongs to Mrs. Broadbent,of the Mollies, Latchford. The cottages have been inhabited by Mr. Thomas Taylor, a carter, and Mrs. Bradshaw, a widow, who works as a charwoman. it has been supposed that the fire must have originated in the stable because a stove had been kept burning there, but this conclusion seems to have been premature. It appears that there was a horse in the stable at the time of the commencement of the fire, the ani- mal being kept there, under careful attention, be, cause it seemed likely to have an attack of pink It was necessary to keep the horse warm, and con- sequently a stove which stands in the stable had been kept burning. T. Jones, a young man who has had the horse under his care for Mr. Coxen, denies, however, emphatically that the fire broke out in the stable. He says Mrs. Bradshaw, who lived next door to the stable, has been in the habit of getting up early in the morning and lighting the fire for preparing her breakfast; before going out charring, and on Tuesday morninc, he was sitting reading in the stable, when he heard' the alarm of fire. He immediately led the horse out, and he saw flames coming from Mrs. Bradshaw's chimney and observed that she had a large fire-on in the kitchen. At that time there was no indication of fi're in the stable. He had let the stove fire out early in the morning. He states, however, it is only fair to say, that Mrs. Bradshaw denim that the tire originated in her house. The fire brigade under Superintendent Turner, was kept many playing on the burning building tillabout four o'clock, being placed at a disadvantage, as in conse- quence of the canal from which the supply of water was obtained being so distant, only one hosecould be brought into requisition. The property was reduced to ruins, onlv the walls being left standing,which will have to be pulled down, and new buildings will be put uryin their places. The amount of damage caused by theiz- destruction is estimated at £l5O, but is covered by insurance. The occupants of the cottages, managed, with the assistance of some neighbours to save most of their chattels, except their twabedsteads, a dress, and some articles of minor value. Mr. Conon had a quantity of hay—about £l2 worth—consumed ,besides some-harness and other things, his loss not being covered by insurance. A crowd collected to view the fire, ad considerable excitement prevailed. Had the wind been in a contrary quarter, a very extensive conflagration would in all probability have been the result.

By the capsizing of two vessels in the Tames RiveriVir- cinia. during a gale, twenty-three persons have been drowned. Work proceeded quietly at the Londen docks on Wed- necday, and negotiations are afoot for the settlement of the dispute at Cardiff. The Oxford and Cambridge (Rugby) football match which was played at West Kensington on Wednesday, ended in a draw of one goal each. Major James walker, chairman of the Midland Asso- ciation of Glassmakers, has been found dead in his tiarden from a gun shot wound in the head, but it is not known whether the'case is one of accident or suicide. At Durham Assizes, on Monday, the jury acquitted of. manslaughter a woman named Mary Quinn, who had found a neighbour named Mary Armstrong in her hus- band's eon-many, and next day assaulted her so severely that she died. A news agency states that two persons—a man and a woman—have been arrested at San Remo on the charge of murdering Dr. Lindemann, formerly of Manchester. The doctor's body was found in a ravine some months ago. It was at first thought that he had committed suicide, but the police, it is said, now believe they' have got another Eyraud ease. Police investigations resulted in the discovery of the fact that the doctor had been lured to the apartments of a female who had won his con- fidence, and there been robbed and murdered.
lIR. JUSTIN McCARTHY, M.P.

Mr. McCarthy, who is now the leader of the Irish Parliamentary party, was born at Cork in Novem- ber, 1830. Aftez receiving a liberal education there, he commenced his career as a journalist on a Liverpool paper in 1853. He entered the Reporters' Gallery of the House of Commons in 1860 for the "Morning Star," be- ame foreign editor .of that 'paper the following autumn

1864. In 1868 he severed his connection with the "Morning Star," and travelled through the United States for three years, visiting thirty-five of the thirty-seven states. On his return from America he joined the editorial staff of the "Daily News," from which he retired in 1886, but which he has since rejoined. He has also contri- buted to the "London Review," the "Fortnightly Review," the "Nineteenth Century," to several English magazines, and to many American periodi- cals. He is, it is needless to say, well-known as a Inovelist and historian, for, besides being the author of some pcpular works of imagination, such as "A Fair Saxon," "Dear Lady Disdain," " Linley Koch- ford," " Camiola," &c., he has written" A History of Our Own Times," "The Epoch of Reform," and "History of the Four Georges." In 1888, Mr. McCarthy brought out "The Right Honourable," and "The Ladies' Gallery," having written this latter work in conjunction with Mrs. Campbell Praed. He was first elected to Parliament. as a member for county Longford, Ireland, in 1879, and was re-elected when the dissolution took place in 1880, in both instances without a contest. At the general election, in 1885, he unsuccessfully contested Derry, but was again returned by a large majority for Longford. In 1886 he, for a second time, con- tested Derry, against Sir C. E. Lewis, who was returned by a majority of three. On petition, how- ever, Mr. McCarthy was declared to be the sitting member. After the recent rupture in the Irish party, ' Mr. McCarthy was elected by the majority of the Irish Parliamentary Party in opposition to Mr. ; Parnell.

div.head: SUPPOSED CASE OF SELF-DROWNING
div.p: SUPPOSED CASE OF SELF-DROWNING

Yesterday morning, about seven o'clock, Stephen Cork, labourer at the Ship Canal, who resides at 23, Ellesmere-st., Warrington, and James Harding, fireman on the Canal, who • lives at 20, Napier-st., were returning from their work, when on passing the three-corneied pit at Arpley, near the London and North-Western railway, they noticed the body of a man in the water which stands in the pit. They drew the body out of the water, which was about 2ft. deep, but found life extinct. JD the de- ceased's pockets were found a casual inmate ticket belonging to the Runcorn Workhouse with the name of Wm. Chard, upon it, issued on the 3rd inst. The deceased was seen by a boy named Richard Hol- croft, residing at Latchford, going to the iron bridge in the direction of the pit about half-past seven o'clock on Thursday evening. The body has been removed to the Higher Seven Stars Inn,pend- ing the inquest. It is supposed that the case is one of suicide.

div.p: MARKETS.

Cheese rules firm, with a fair consumptive demand; but Butter sells but slowly. Lard exhibits a firmer request at slightly enhanced rates. div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

THE CARDIFF DOCK STRIKE. The Cardiff Dock strike continues, and the Union men announce that they will fight it out. THE GREAT DROP IN PIG IRON. The withdrawal of the Pig Iron Regulation Bill has brought about a heavy fall in the Glasgow iron market. Yesterday morning Scotch dropped to 455. aid. ash, c Middlesbro' 40s. 9d., and hematite to 495. ed.

div.head: SUICIDE OF A LONDON BANKER
div.p: SUICIDE OF A LONDON BANKER

The" Globe" announces that Mr. Robert Lindsay Antrobus, son of Sir Edward Antrobus, and junior partner in the firm of Coutts and Co., bankers, was found dead in bed, yesterday morning, having evidently shot himself.

THE REMAINS FOUND IN THE REGENT'S CANAL. The inquest was held in London yesterday oq the por- tions of a woman's body found in the Regent's Canal, at Hackney. Medicsal evidence showed the remains had been crushed by barges and eaten by rats. A woman named Lloyd said she thought the remains were those of her sister, but was not certain. The jury returned a ver- dict of" Found drowned."

div.head: SIR CHARLES DILKE.
div.p: SIR CHARLES DILKE.

It is sugrested that Sir Charles Dilke will come forward as a candidate for the Forest of Dean Division, in succes- sion to Mr. Samuelson, the sitting Gladstonian member. There is reason, however, to believe that the Liberal leaders have intimated that they object to their late col- league re-entering public life, and, as Mr. Samuelson has no strong desire to give up the seat, it is probable that nothing more will be heard of Sir Charles Dilke's candi- dature.
CHARGE OF MURDER AT GREENOCK. A MAN'S NECK BROKEN. A young man called Joseph Robertson has been ar-

rested at oreenock on a charge of murder, and has been remitted to the Sheriff far trial. Early on Tuesday morning a ship carpenter named John Morrison was found lying dead at the bottom of the stairs of a house in Dalrymple-st., with his neck broken. It was then thought that he had fallen down stairs, but the police, after careful enquiries, came to the conclusion that he was pushed down, and they arrested Robertson.

div.head: DIED AT THE GAMING TABLE
div.p: DIED AT THE GAMING TABLE
NICE, FRIDA.Y.—Dr. Seegart, an English physician, while playing at Monte Carlo last night had an apopletic fit and fell dead on the gaming table.
GERMAN IRONCLADS. BERLIN. FRIDAY EVENING.—The Reichstag to-day voted the money for two new ironclads, and referred back to the Committee the remainder of the navy budget.
FIRE AT A HIGH SCHOOL. TWO _STUDENTS BURNED TO DEATH.

- - MUNROE, NORTH CAROLINA, FRIDAY.—The high school here caught fire and was burned down eialy yesterday morning. The girl students, who were on the ground floor, managed to escape unharmed, but two of the male students who were in the rooms ea the third floor were burned to death.

div.head: RESULT OF THE CANADIAN ELECTIONS.
div.p: RESULT OF THE CANADIAN ELECTIONS.

TORONTO, FRIDAY, 6 A.M.-.-.Of-ihe -2-175—;e-a-t;•In the Dominion House of Commons returns have been received of 211 elections, which show that, including those chosen by acclamation, the Ministcrialists have secured 118 seats and the Opposition 93. thus giving the Minis- terialists a majority of 25, including the Minister of Militia, who has been elected.
TORONTO, FRIDAY EVENING.—The" Empire," a govern- ment organ, estimates Sir John MacDonald's majority at 42. The opposition estimates range from 20 to 30.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat on" the w/oolsack a' a quarter past four.

THE ScurcH STRIKE—The Earl of WEBITSS called at- tention to thp strike of Railway servants in Scotland, and to the system of pieketini and the outrages by which it was accompanied. He asked whether Her Majerty's Government would take such measures as would in all future strikes insure due protection to unionists willing to work and to non-union workmen. Lord BRAMWELL said the law relating to intimidation should be rigorously enforced.—Lord LOTHIAN said the Government could not say what course in the future would be pursued uutil after the report of the Royal Commission had been received. The subject dropped, and the House adjourned at half-past six. FRIDAY.
HOUSE OF COMMONS

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. ROYALTIES FOR RAILWAYS.—The City and South Lon- don Railway Bill was read a second time.—Mr. T. H. BOLTON then moved that it be an instruction to the Committees upon the City of South London Railway Bill, the central London Railway Bill, and the South Kensing- ton and Paddington Subway Bill that, in order that the public should derive some advantage in return for the right to tunnel under the public roads, clauses should be inserted providing either for the payment of a royalty to the Local Authority or for specially reduced fares on the trains between hours most convenient for the working classes.—Mr. BARTLEY seconded, and Mr. ESSELAIONT opposed the instruction.— Mr. COURTNEY suggested that Mr. Bolton should wait until Committees had finished their labours, and call attention to the matter when the Bill came next before the House. The instruction was defeated by majority of forty. RAILWAY RATES AND C/lARGES.—On the motion for the second reading of the Provisional Order Bills confirm- ing the orders of the Board trade with respect to railway rates and charges, Mr. PHILIP STANHOPE moved that the House decline to proceed with the consideration of schemes based upon the recog- nition of legality of station terminal charges. Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH said he would never have ap- proached this matter had he thought at the outset that undertaking was one of such magnitude. The question had been dealt with in a very exhaustive way, and, al- though the principle of terminal changes was retained, it must be remembered that they were legal. Furthermore it was distinctly to the advantage of the traders to have these charges. if allowed, separated, from the ordinary rates. Ultimately, Mr. STANHOPE withdrew his amend- ment on the understanding that an opportunity should be given to discuss the composition of the committee to which the bill was to be referred.—The Bill was then read a second time.

THE CASE OF MRS. CATHCART.—The HOME SECRETARY, replying to a question, said Mrs. Cathcart was removed to a lunatic asylum under the order of a Commissioner of Lunacy made on the certificate of Drs. Bond and Savage. The inquiry the day following at the asylum wai by authority of the lady's husband. HOME RULE ALL ROUND.—On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Dr. CLARK called attention to the administration of and the mode of legislating for the domestic affairs of England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, and moved that in order to increase the efficiency of the Imperial Parliament to deal with Imperial affairs, and in order to give speedier and fuller effect to the special desires and wants of the respective nationalities constituting the United Kingdom, it was desirable to devolve upon the representatives of England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, respectively, the management and control of their domestic affairs. Mr. S. Evans, as a Welsh mem- ber, seconded the resolution, but the flouse'vras counted out, not forty members being present. The House adjourned at eight thirty-five.
The long-pending strike at Messrs. Lister and Co.'s silk mills, Bradford, underwent a further extension on Mon- day, the whole of the spinners and drawers turning out in sympathy with the weavers.

div.head: SHIP CANAL
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL

FATAL ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. Mr, J. E. Worsley, coroner, on Thursday afternoon, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court, on the body of William Ddvies, aged 39, a labourer on the Ship Canal, who lived at 4, Back King-st.—Emma Davies, the widow, said the deceased left home at half past eight on Monday night, in his usual health. Re was brought home injured abovt half-past ten. He said he had fallen into a dam and injured his spine and head. Dr. Mc- Dougall attended him until his death on Wednesday night.—Mr. G. Marshall (juror), asked if he was drunk. —Witness replied, no. certainly not. He was a great teetotaller.—Charles Inchcliffe, of 11, Waterloo-road, ganger, said on Monday night, at half-past ten, he was descending a ladder into a dam at No Man's Land. He told deceased to follow him. The deceased made a: stumble and fell to the bottom of the dam, a distance of about 24ft. The deceased had just got hold of the ladder when•he fell. The timber was very slippery at the tire owing to the tide having been recently over it, makrng it very wet.—A verdict of "Accidental Death" was re-, turned.

div.head: .LYMM.
div.p: .LYMM.

PRIMITIVE METRODIST BAND OF HOPE—A public meet- ing under the auspices of this Band of Hope society was held in the Institute on Tuesday evening. An interest- ing programme of songs, duets, part songs, dialogues, &c., was rendered by members and friends. Mr. Joseph Thorpe presided, and a collection wastaken in aid of the Band of Hope funds.

IMPROVE3IENT SoczETY.—The weekly meeting of the Baptist Mutual Improvement Society took place on Wednesday evening. Mr. Robinson occupied the chair. Various readings were given by members, followed by a paper, "Natural instinct," by Mr. W. Diamond. An interesting discussion followed on the debateable ground of where instinct stops and reason begins. THE PENNY CONCERTS.—.Q H Saturday evening, another enjoyable evening was spent at the Bridgewater Rooms. There was a crowded attendance, and the various per- formers were heartily applauded. The programme was entirely sustained by the members of the Oughtrington Church choir, who acquitted themselves admirably. Mr. 0. G. Smith, organist of Oughtrington Chercii, played the accompaniments in an accomplished man- ner.

WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.-1. successful public meet- ing and entertainment in Connection with the Wesleyan Band of Hope was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening. Mr. James Dodds was in the chair, and Mr. Luke Ellison, of Latchford, delivered a suitable address, and Mr. Thorpe also spoke. Mr. John Chorley gave a reading and Mr. Ellison a recitation. Several dialogues and recitations by the members completed the pro- gramme. THE WESLEY CENTENARY.—The scholars attending the Lymna Wesleyan Sunday School subscribed to the statue of John Wesley, which has been placed in the forecourt of Wesley's Chapel. in the City-road, London, and which was formally unveiled in the presence of a large assembly on Monday morning. The statue, the cost of which was. £7OO, is of bronze, and represents the great evangelist in his preaching robes. At the base is the inscription, "The world is my parish." The cost has been entirely defrayed by Wesleyan Sunday School children. INDUSTRIAL EXHIBITION. —An Industrial Exhibition, for which preparations have been going on all winter was. opened yesterday afternoon in the Lym m Congregational Schoolroom, by Mr. C. Lister, C.C. About 200 entries had been made in the various classes, some of them being of a highly interesting character. Considerable attrac- • tion was added to the event by a large number of "curios," in the form of African native carving, recent scientific instruments, microscopes, Ix. &c. Ballad ' concerts by the juveniles of the choir, and other enter- tainments, were provided. A good deal of interest is cen- tred in this first effort of the kind on the part of the Congregationalists, and as it has proved a success by the large number of entries, it is hoped to be made a perma- nent institution of the church.

div.head: LOCAL BOARD,
div.p: LOCAL BOARD,

The monthly meet-ink- of this- Board took place nn Thursday afternoon. Present :—Mr. El. Cam”ron (chair- man), Messrs. Dutton, Rogers, Brazendale, Gibbon, Swallow, Harrison, and Thkenason ; Mr. Ridgway (law clerk), Mr. W. Mullard (clerk), Mr. Mort (surveyor),and Mr. W. Severs (gas manager). NUMBERING THE STREETS.—The Surveyor reported that he had enquired as to the cost of name plates and the numbers for naming the streets and numbering the houses throughout the district, and he found the price of 36 plates to be about £7, and seven gross of iron num- bers about £2 95., making the sum of £9 9s. If paint- ings and fixing were included, about £l5. Other expenses would bring it to about £24. TIMBERING THE IRON BRIDGE.—Mr. Melt submitted .an estimate for covering the iron bridge with new planking two inches thick. Mr. Brazendale took objection t? tile thickness, to which the Surveyor replied that thicker timbar would be difficult to bend to tize—aurve,oi the roadway. Mr. Brazendale said three inches or four inches would bend just as easy as two inch, and he sug- gested that the matter stand over until next meeting, as timber could be got much cheaper than that quoted. The Chairman said there was timber and timber. Timber could be had at half the cost, no doubt. But it would be a serious matter if a horse were to get his foot through the timbered roadways. Mr. Brazendale: That is .all bosh—it is an absurdity. Mort says there is planking below.—lt was referred back. HEATLEY WATER SU PPLY . —The Surveyor was instructed to report on the water supply of He.atley to the next meeting. It was intimated that the Water Company bac, now completed the laying of the pipes in that neighbour- hood.

ROAD WIDENING.—The Chairman intimated that Mr. Dewhurst had instructed him to offer the piece of land at the old cottage (Johnnie Williamson's),in the Higher- lane, necessary for the widening of the highway (re- quired by the Board),on condition that the Board would put tin a fence along the boundary similar to that in the neighbourhood.—The offer was accepted with thanks. This was all the business.
The Cunard steamer Catalonia and the steamer Merchant Prince collided in the Mersey on Wednesday, the latter receiving such damage as will cause her to dock for repairs.

TO THE INHABITANTS OF RUNCORN.= COTTAGE HOSPITAL. In response tda numerously signed requisition asking me to convene a Town's Meeting for the purpose of considering the advisability of establishing a Cottage Hospital in Runcorn, I hereby give notice that a PUBLIC MEETING will be held In the BOARD Room, Tow x HALL, at 8 o'clock ON MONDAY BYENTNG NEXT, the 9th ixs.r., in respect of the above-named matter. SAMUEL TAYLOR. Chairman of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. Town Hall, Runcorn, 4th March, 1891.

RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. THE INFECTIOUS DISEASE (PREVENTION) ACT, 1890. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at a MEET- ING of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, duly convened and held at the Town Hall, Runcorn, on Thursday, the sth day of March, 1891, in pursuance of and In accordance with the provisions of "The Infectious Disease (Prevention) Act, 1890." It was resolved that the Runcorn Improvement Commis- sioners, being the Urban Sanitary Authority for the District of Runcorn, hereby adopt "The Infectious Disease (Preven- tion) Act, 1890. and declare that the provisions thereof shall be in force within the said Urban Sanitary District on and after the 13th day of April, 1891." Dated this sth day of March, 1891. E. MARSHALL, Secretary to the Authority.

DISTRICT OF WIDNES. PROPOSED INCORPORATION. IN-OTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the Honorable T. H. W. Pelham. Barrister-at-Law. the Commissioner appointed by the Lordsof Her Majesty's Privy Council,will be open an INQUIRY AT THE TOWN HALL, IN WIDNES, ON WEDNESDAY, THE 25TH DAY OF MARCH, 1891, at eleven o'clock in the forenoon and proceed,to take evidence in reference to the Petition that has been presented to Her Majesty in Coun- cil for the grant of a Charter of Incorporation to the District of Widnes according to the provisions of the Municipal Cor- porations Act, 1882, and further that all persons interested in the Insiniry. and who may wish to give evidence before the said Commissioner must then and there attend, and they will be heard. Dated this 2nd day of Mareh. 1891. This notice is published by direction of the said Commis- sioner by . JAS. T. ALLEN, Clerk to the Widnes Local Board.

Dutton; House Coal (Colliery to be named) ; Coke • Good Deal Coffins, specifying tize, and including plate with name, age, and date of death, to be delivered in the Union when and where required; Carting at per mile, and Funerals at per Funeral; also for the windingand care of the Clocks at the Workhouse, in Dutton, for twelve months. Parties Tender- ing for the supply of the above-mentioned Goods, will be required to deliver the same at the Workhouse, free of cost to the Guardians, how and when required. Tenders to be accompanied with samples, including Drapery Goods, as far as practicable. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any Tender. Persons desirous of Tender- ing must apply by letter, to my Office, in Frodsham, for a Printed Form of Tender, and none other can be entertained, where a schedule of the various articles required and further particulars can be obtained. Sealed Tender addressed to the Guardians, to be forwarded to the Clerk's Office, Frodsham, on or before Saturday the 21st day of March, 1891, endorsed "Tender for ." The Tenders will be opened and consi- dered at a Meeting of the Guardians to be held in the Board- -room, Dutton. on the 24th March 1891, at Two p.m. Parties whose Tenders are accepted must enter into a written contract, and be prepared to enter into a bond with two sureties, if required by the Guardians. By order of the Board. H. LINAKER, Clerk to the Guardians. Frodsharn, 2nd March, 1891.

"Dear Sir,—l am a poor hand at expressing my feelings on paper, but I should like to thank you, for your lozenges have done wonders tor me in relieving my terrible cough. Since I had the operation of ' Tracheotomy ' (the same as the late Emperor of Germany, and unlike him, thank God, I am still alive and getting on well) performed at St. Bartholomew's Hospital for abduct, or paralysis of the vocal chords, no one could possibly have had a more violent cough ; indeed, it was so bad at tim.es that it quite exhausted me. The mucus also. which was very copious and hard, has been softened, and I have been able to get rid of it without difficulty.—l am, sir, yours truly, " Mr. T. Keating." " J. HILL." MADICAL NOTE. FRODSHAM. __— PRIMITIVE METHODIST CITAPEL.—On Sunday evening. the service of song entitled, "Which was the Hero ?" was given in the above chapel to a large congregation. The musical portion of the service was fairly well done by the choir, assisted by a string band, in addition to the organ. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—A miscellaneous enter- tainment was given in the Trinity Schoolroom, Frodsham, last evening week, by the lady members of the class and several friends. The programme "consisted of a choice selection of solos, duets, trios (vocal and instrumental), choruses, and readings, and the performance throughout gave every satisfaction. CONCERT.—In aid of the Methodist Free Church organ fund, a concert was given in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Wednesday evening. A select party organised by Mr. John Holford, .G.T.S.C. of Runcorn, were assisted by Miss Olive Brock, of Nortiwich, who created a very. favourable impression. Mr. John Holland was, as usual, well received, and rendered his songs in good style, while Mr. R. Rogers fairly" brought down the house" by the rendering of his comic songs. Mr. Hibbert gave the pianoforte solo, "Bohemian Girl,"in a finished man- ner. Misses Heatherington and Culls and Messrs. Leathwood and Worrall were eminently successful in the songs set down to their names. Mastor and Miss Fother- gill gave a pianoforte duet in a very satisfactory man- ner. Miss Marlow. and Mr'. Holford sang the duet "To the Greenwood," and Mrs. Newall and Mr. Holford the duet" Love Divine " ; and the glee party gave a choice selection of part music. Mr. C. Le Couteur officiated as accompanist, and Mr. Holford as conductor. The hall was filled with a most appreciative audience, and the persistent demand for encores, whieh were the rule rather than the exception, showed that the efforts of their entertainers were highly appreciated.
